column2: Exploring Turn-taking Cues in Multi-party Human-robot Discussions about Objects
column3: The paper presents a multi-party card-sorting dialog system built on the Furhat robot head, which was exhibited in a museum and used by 373 interactions. Field data showed that gaze-away plus a filled pause, smile, or breath reduced users' likelihood of continuing to speak, and that Furhat's attention target strongly influenced which user responded.
column4: Technical system description combined with a field-trial analysis of 373 museum interactions, including systematic manipulation of the robot's turn-taking cues and attention.
column5: Field deployment in the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology over 9 days in November 2014, with visitors playing in groups of two.
column6: Data were recorded from 373 interactions with the system, averaging 4.5 minutes each; the total number of individual participants is not explicitly stated.
column7: Museum visitors of mixed ages: adults playing with adults (40%), children playing with adults (27%), and children playing with children (33%) of interactions.
column8: Two visitors and Furhat played a collaborative card-sorting game, discussing and sorting five cards by a criterion (e.g., invention order or running speed), with an average interaction length of 4.5 minutes.
column9: Three per session: two visitors plus one Furhat robot head.
column11: 2 visitors per session.
column12: Kinect-based tracking of users' head pose, speech recognition word and concept error rates on 9 transcribed and annotated dialogs, manual annotation of speech segments on a four-grade scale, and chi-square tests on user speech after turn-taking cues.
column13: Gazing away during a turn-taking cue significantly reduced the likelihood of user speech (main effect of gaze, p<0.001). Without cues, users continued speaking 33.8% of the time, versus 14.8% with the right combined cues. Furhat's attention target also strongly influenced which user responded (p<0.001).
column14: Robotic gaze-based attention
column15: The paper does not explicitly define robotic gaze or attention. It operationalises attention as Furhat's target (idle, item, user, or all), maintained by an Attention Flow that moves its gaze and neck.
column16: Gaze and attention serve turn-taking: the robot signals it is claiming the floor with gaze-away plus a cue (filled pause, breath, or smile), and gaze selects the next speaker (addressee selection). The robot also acts as a passive side participant through backchannels.
column17: Furhat's attention target strongly influenced which user responded after its questions (p<0.001). When the targeted user was looking back at Furhat, that user was more likely to take the turn (p<0.05).
column18: Built in IrisTK with two parallel controllers: a Dialog Flow for turn-taking and an Attention Flow that maps 3D target positions to neck and gaze movements. A Situation model fuses Kinect head tracking, close-talking microphones with two parallel cloud ASR recognizers, and touch-table events; a randomized belief model drives responses.
column19: Furhat robot head: an animated face back-projected on a translucent mask, with a mechanical neck.
column20: The paper argues that 2D animated agents suffer from the Mona Lisa effect because agent and user do not share physical space. Citing prior work, it states Furhat's back-projection on a 3D mask improves turn-yielding accuracy.

column2: Are you talking to me? Improving the Robustness of Dialogue Systems in a Multi Party HRI Scenario by Incorporating Gaze Direction and Lip Movement of Attendees
column3: The paper presents the humanoid robot Meka with an attention management system that prioritizes face, sound, and saliency cues so it can look at people, including those outside its view. In a multiparty study with 15 participants in 5 trials, mutual gaze at utterance end improved addressee recognition accuracy and precision, while lip movements alone performed poorly. Combining gaze OR lip movement gave the best accuracy and odds ratio.
column4: Experimental proof-of-concept user study with a humanoid robot in a multiparty interaction, in which addressee recognition approaches were evaluated against ground-truth annotation.
column5: Laboratory-style smart-home apartment (Cognitive Service Robotics Apartment, CSRA), with participants seated around a table, on a sofa, and in armchairs.
column6: 15 participants (2 female and 13 male) took part, across 5 trials totalling about 53 minutes of interaction.
column7: Participants were German native speakers; 2 were female and 13 male. No age or prior robot experience is reported.
column8: Participants picked a task slip from the table (e.g., turn lights on/off, ask the time, request information), told another participant to issue it to the robot, and that participant had to gain the robot's attention and repeat the request. A typical trial took about 10 minutes.
column9: One robot (Meka) with six people per session, as described for the experimental setup (three at the table, one on the sofa, two in armchairs).
column11: 6 participants per session, per the described setup (three at the table, one on the sofa, two in armchairs).
column12: Addressee recognition classifications were compared with a ground-truth annotation of each dialogue act, using a 2x2 confusion matrix to compute accuracy, recall, precision, and the diagnostic odds ratio (DOR). Recordings were annotated in ELAN.
column13: No statistical tests are reported. Mutual gaze kept recall at 93% and raised accuracy to 89%, against an 84% baseline, while lips-or-gaze reached 91% accuracy and the highest DOR (91.1 versus 5 for the baseline).
column14: Robotic gaze-based attention
column15: The authors do not give a general definition of gaze or attention. Operationally, mutual gaze is assumed when a person's gaze direction stays within a range of α around the robot's head, and the attention management system is based on hierarchical prioritization of multi-modal sensor input streams.
column16: Mutual gaze at the end of an utterance serves as a turn-yielding cue that helps the robot decide whether an utterance was addressed to it. Attention management lets the robot observe and turn toward persons outside its field of view.
column17: Effects were measured only on addressee recognition performance, not on the people themselves. Attention management was reported to facilitate addressee recognition when not all participants are visible, and lip-movement verification decreased false positive addressee recognitions.
column18: Autonomous system on the Meka robot: an attention manager arbitrates prioritized input streams (face detection, then sound source, then saliency) with override and gaze controllers over ROS/RSB. Addressee recognition uses a gaze detector with facial landmarks, classifying speaking from inner-lip distance variance and mutual gaze; speech recognition uses Sphinx and dialogue uses InproTK and Pamini.
column19: Meka, a humanoid M1 Mobile Manipulator with an omni-directional base, lift-controlled torso, two arms with four-fingered hands, and 37 motor-powered joints (including 2 in the head).
column20: Head movements of the robot caused motion blur, so gaze and lip features were sometimes not detected at the relevant moment. The attention system was designed to be exchangeable across platforms, such as NAO or iCub.

column2: Social Robot Haru Assisting Dynamic Group Discussion with Autonomous Eye Gaze Behavior
column3: The authors built a system for the social robot Haru to assist dynamic group discussion, combining LLM-based chat, a balancing and welcoming module, and an autonomous eye-gaze module learned by deep reinforcement learning in simulation and transferred to the physical robot. In a study with 50 participants in groups of three, adding balancing and welcoming improved satisfaction and perceived politeness over a chatbot-only Haru, and adding autonomous gaze further improved anthropomorphism, animacy, likability, perceived intelligence and satisfaction.
column4: Technical system development combined with an experimental user study comparing three conditions using physical Haru. The autonomous gaze policy was trained in a Gazebo simulation before being transferred to the robot.
column5: Simulated Gazebo environment for policy training, and a user study with physical Haru in which groups discussed a topic seated beside Haru on a table. The paper does not name a specific room or venue beyond recruiting from a university campus.
column6: 50 participants in total: 27 recruited for the user-perspective part (21 valid responses analysed) and 23 third-party evaluators.
column7: University campus participants. User-perspective group: aged 21-28 (mean 23.70, SD 1.438), 51.86% male, 40.74% female, 7.40% undisclosed. Third-party group: aged 20-27 (mean 23.41, SD 1.343), 60.87% male, 34.78% female, 4.35% undisclosed.
column8: Groups of three discussed a topic given by the instructor beside Haru, with one assumed extroverted, one introverted and one new user joining. Each group experienced three conditions: chatbot only, chatbot plus balancing and welcoming, and chatbot plus balancing, welcoming and autonomous gaze. Discussion duration is not stated.
column9: Three people plus one robot per session: two conversing users and one new comer joining, with Haru.
column11: Three human participants per session in the user study (two conversing users plus one new comer). In simulation, Haru randomly observed 2-4 users per training episode.
column12: Godspeed questionnaire for anthropomorphism, animacy, likability and perceived intelligence, plus satisfaction and eight custom conversation-experience items, all rated on 7-point Likert scales. Also two open-ended questions, Cronbach's alpha reliability checks, and ANOVA with Fisher LSD post-hoc tests.
column13: User ratings: Condition 3 scored significantly higher than Conditions 1 and 2 on all five measures (p<0.01), while Condition 2 beat Condition 1 only on satisfaction. Third-party ratings: Condition 3 beat both on all five measures, and Condition 2 beat Condition 1 on satisfaction, animacy and likability.
column14: Robotic gaze
column15: The paper gives no formal definition of gaze or attention. It describes Haru's gaze behaviours as designed to replicate human gaze movements, including vestibulo-ocular movement, during face-to-face interaction.
column16: Gaze is used to show politeness and to direct gaze to the current speaker, a less-engaged user (to encourage participation) or a new joiner. Haru shifts gaze between speakers via eyeball movement when they are close, and via body rotation otherwise.
column17: Compared with chatbot-only Haru, adding balancing and welcoming behaviour improved satisfaction and some perceptions, and adding autonomous gaze further improved anthropomorphism, animacy, likability, perceived intelligence and satisfaction in both user and third-party ratings.
column18: Gaze policy learned autonomously with soft actor-critic deep reinforcement learning in a Gazebo simulation, with a state of user positions, speaking indicators and motor angle, and actions of body rotation or eyeball movement, then transferred to physical Haru. Speech uses Google ASR, the Kimi LLM and TTS, and user positions and speaking are detected with Azure Kinect.
column19: Tabletop social robot Haru with five degrees of freedom: base rotation, neck tilt, eye movement, eye rotation and eye tilt. Each eye is a 3-inch TFT screen bordered by addressable LED strips, and an LED matrix simulates mouth movements.
column20: Eye-screen geometry limits the eye centre to a range to avoid an impolite whites-of-eyes look, and eye positions reset during body turns. Because Haru is fixed on a desktop, the state uses only the azimuth direction, and motor rotation is limited to a safe range.

column2: Social Robot Haru Imitating Human Gaze for Attention and Turn-Taking Coordination in Multi-party Conversation
column3: The paper presents the social robot Haru, which learns human-like gaze from real-world demonstrations using GAIL (trained in simulation and transferred to the robot) and uses ChatGPT for open-domain dialogue, so that gaze coordinates attention and turn-taking between two users. In a 22-participant study (11 pairs), adding the autonomous gaze module made Haru significantly better rated on social intelligence, satisfaction, and willingness to use than dialogue alone.
column4: Technical system description combined with an experimental within-subjects user study in which all 22 participants experienced both conditions (dialogue only vs. dialogue plus autonomous gaze).
column5: Real-world user study with participant pairs recruited from a university campus; gaze policy was trained beforehand in a Gazebo simulation.
column6: 22 participants (11 groups of 2).
column7: Aged 22 to 27 years, 15 males and 7 females, university campus recruits; 59.1% had experience in social robotics and 40.9% had no relevant experience.
column8: Pairs of participants talked on a topic assigned by an instructor while interacting with Haru; each group experienced both the dialogue-only condition and the dialogue plus autonomous gaze condition in randomized order, with a short break between them.
column9: 2 humans plus 1 robot (Haru) per session.
column11: 2 per session.
column12: Godspeed questionnaire (anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence, perceived safety), selected PSI items, four custom satisfaction questions and two custom willingness-to-use questions, all on 5-point Likert scales, analysed with Cronbach's alpha and paired t-tests.
column13: Haru was rated significantly better in Condition 2 than Condition 1 on all GODSPEED and PSI dimensions (paired t-tests, p<0.01; e.g., anthropomorphism t = -8.737). Participants also reported significantly higher enjoyment, perceived attentive listening, overall satisfaction, willingness to re-engage, and willingness to use and recommend Haru in Condition 2 (p<0.01).
column14: Robotic gaze-based attention
column16: Haru's gaze is used to follow the current speaker and to orient toward the middle between users when both are talking or silent, coordinating attention and turn-taking in the group conversation.
column17: Participants rated Haru more favourably with gaze behaviour: they preferred it when it maintained mutual gaze, and were more inclined to use it in daily life and to recommend it to others in Condition 2 (p<0.01).
column18: Gaze policy learned with GAIL from human expert demonstrations, using relative azimuth angles and speaking status as state and head-rotation change as action; trained in a Gazebo simulation for 1500 episodes and transferred to the real robot. Users were tracked with an Azure Kinect for skeleton and sound localization, and dialogue used ASR, ChatGPT and TTS.
column19: Haru, a desktop social robot placed on a tabletop; its gaze direction is produced by rotation restricted to a predefined range of [−90°, 90°].
column20: Hardware constraints restricted Haru's rotational movement to [−90°, 90°], which defined the range of its gaze actions in the study.

column2: The Power of a Glance: Evaluating Embodiment and Turn-Tracking Strategies of an Active Robotic Overhearer
column3: The authors equipped a NAO robot with moving-pupil eyes and tested, through a video-rating study with 29 participants, how an active overhearer of recorded dyadic conversations should time gaze and head turns. Moving eyes were rated significantly higher than fixed eyes, and oracle-timed models beat random turning, while reactive and predictive timing did not differ significantly.
column4: Experimental video-rating study in which participants judged videos of a NAO robot overhearing recorded conversations under six behaviour models.
column5: Participants watched the robot videos one at a time on a computer screen with headphones, using a GUI with a single play button; the paper does not name a lab or field setting.
column6: 29 participants.
column7: Students or otherwise affiliated with Bielefeld University, all native German speakers; mostly female (six male), aged 17-55 (mean 24, median 23). Two had prior HRI study experience and three had other robot experience.
column8: Participants watched 18 videos (six per audio part) of a NAO robot acting as an active overhearer of recorded dyadic conversations, then rated how well it followed the discussion and how close its behaviour was to a human's. Each video covers an interaction part of about 60-65 seconds.
column9: Two humans in the recorded conversation plus one NAO robot as overhearer; the robot is not a live participant and the raters are not part of the interaction.
column10: One NAO robot per session, taking the role of an active overhearer.
column11: Two humans per interaction (a dyadic conversation); the stimuli were drawn from three dyadic interactions.
column12: Two custom questions rated on unbounded scales (how well the robot followed the discussion; how close its behaviour was to a human's), analysed with ranking and z-scores, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests; a post-experiment questionnaire included a 0-5 task difficulty rating.
column13: Moving-eye models were rated significantly higher than their fixed-eye counterparts for all pairs (Friedman χ2=75.88, p<0.001; Wilcoxon post-hoc, Bonferroni-adjusted α=0.0033). Oracle models (PRD, RCT) clearly outperformed the random baseline (RND), most strongly with moving eyes, while PRD and RCT did not differ significantly.
column14: Robotic gaze
column15: The paper gives no formal definition of gaze or attention; it describes gaze as the eyes rotating so the pupil turns toward a target, which is distinct from head turning.
column16: As an active overhearer, the robot turns its head and eyes toward the currently active speaker, following the turn-taking structure so that it signals to other observers that it is attentive and engaged.
column17: Moving eyes considerably increased ratings of the robot's attentiveness, ability to follow the discussion, and naturalness. The randomly timed model with moving eyes was rated higher than the fixed-eye reactive and predictive models, though these differences were not statistically significant.
column18: Eyes are two Arduino-driven TFT screens showing pupils; pupil displacement is computed from a linear regression fitted to eye-tracker data, with separate head and eye controllers. Overhearer models (RND, RCT, PRD) use turn timing from transcripts, so they are oracle models rather than autonomous.
column19: Aldebaran NAO humanoid robot with a pair of small displays (1.77 inch) as eyes behind a paper mask with a 3D nose. The NAO head has only yaw and pitch degrees of freedom and cannot tilt.
column20: The physical 3D mask and eyes placed in physical space let the robot avoid the Mona Lisa effect, and the NAO head's lack of tilt meant the pupil model ignored tilted head posture.

column2: Skantze et al. - 2015 - A Collaborative Human-Robot Game as a Test-bed for Modelling Multi-party, Situated Interaction
column3: The paper presents a collaborative card-sorting game in which two visitors and the Furhat robot head jointly discuss cards on a touch table, with Furhat's gaze directed to maintain joint attention. The system was exhibited for nine days in a museum, yielding 373 recorded interactions. It is proposed as a test-bed for collecting data and building data-driven models of gaze and turn-taking, but no gaze effects were measured.
column4: Technical/system description: a demonstration paper presenting a test-bed for collecting data and testing models of multi-party situated human-robot interaction. The system was deployed in a museum and data was logged.
column5: Field deployment in a public museum: the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology, where the system was exhibited for nine days in November 2014.
column6: The paper reports 373 recorded interactions with the system, averaging 4.5 minutes each. The total number of participants is not explicitly stated.
column7: Museum visitors of mixed ages, including both children and adults. No further demographic details are reported.
column8: Two visitors at a time play a collaborative card sorting game with Furhat, sorting cards (e.g., inventions by year or animals by speed) on a touch table while discussing the solution together. After completing one game, players could choose to continue; 58 of the pairs who completed the first game chose to do so.
column9: Each interaction session includes two human visitors and one robot (Furhat), i.e., three participants in total.
column10: One robot (the Furhat robot head) per interaction session.
column11: Two humans (visitors) per interaction session.
column12: The paper does not describe questionnaires or outcome instruments. Data was recorded from the interactions, and users' attentional behaviour is approximated by head pose.
column13: No statistical results are reported. Qualitative claims include that the system proved fairly robust against speech recognition errors, that children and adults enjoyed the game, and that 58 pairs chose to continue playing.
column14: The paper uses the concepts of visual focus of attention (VFOA) and joint attention, with Furhat's attention directed to targets such as users or cards. It does not use the term robotic gaze-based attention explicitly.
column16: Furhat's gaze is used to maintain joint attention on the cards and exclusive mutual gaze with users. Users' head pose determines whether they are addressing Furhat or each other, which decides whether Furhat contributes or only gives backchannels.
column17: No effects of Furhat's gaze were measured in this paper. The authors state, citing prior work, that shared visual focus of attention has a clear effect on turn-taking behaviour.
column18: Autonomous system built in the IrisTK framework. column2: The furhat back-projected humanoid head–lip reading, gaze and multi-party interaction
column3: The paper presents Furhat, a back-projected humanoid head, and three experiments on lip reading, gaze perception and multi-party turn-taking, plus a museum deployment. It found that a 3D head avoids the Mona Lisa effect, giving much better turn-taking accuracy (84% vs 53%) and shorter response times than a flat-screen agent in a five-person setting.
column4: Experimental: three lab-based experiments (lip reading perception, gaze perception, and multi-party turn-taking), plus a technical description of the Furhat back-projected head and an uncontrolled public museum deployment.
column5: Controlled lab environments for the three experiments, and a public museum setting (London Science Museum Robotville exhibition) for the field observation.
column6: Study I used 10 normal hearing subjects, Study II used 18 subjects, and Study III used two sets of five subjects (ten subjects in total). The museum exhibition involved thousands of visitors.
column7: Study I subjects were normal hearing with normal or corrected to normal vision; Study II subjects had normal or corrected to normal vision. Museum visitors included many children. The paper does not report further demographic details.
column8: In the lab, participants identified acoustically degraded Swedish sentences with a lip-synced head, placed a tagging object on the grid square they believed Furhat was gazing at, and answered route questions from an agent in a multi-party dialog. In the museum, visitors answered Furhat's survey questions about the future of robots over four days.
column9: Study III: five human subjects plus one animated agent per session. Public exhibition: Furhat interacted with two users at a time, with two podiums and microphones.
column10: One robot head (Furhat) or one animated agent per interaction session.
column11: Study III: five subjects per session. Public exhibition: two users present at a time in the two-user condition.
column12: Sentence intelligibility accuracy (words correctly identified) in Study I; perceived gaze location on a grid, with angles and distances computed from a geometric model in Study II; manually annotated video turn-taking data, confusion matrix and response times in Study III.
column13: Study III: turn-taking accuracy targeting the intended subject was 53% in the 2D condition and 84% in the 3D condition. Response time was significantly shorter in 3D (1.38 s) than in 2D (1.85 s), F(1)=15.821, p<0.001. Study I found Furhat significantly more intelligible than the flat screen.
column14: The paper does not give a formal definition of robotic gaze-based attention. It frames the topic as robotic gaze and its perception, with Furhat directing its attention using eye gaze and head pose and the Mona Lisa effect as the central concept.
column15: No explicit definition is given. The paper describes the Mona Lisa effect: because a 2D agent is not spatially co-present, either all observers perceive it as looking at them or none do.
column16: Gaze serves turn-taking control, addressee selection and deictic reference. Gaze is used to address a particular person and to regulate multiparty dialogue turn-taking.
column17: On 2D displays, the Mona Lisa effect limits gaze-based turn-taking. A 3D back-projected head improved turn-taking accuracy and reduced response time. In the museum, open questions were answered by the addressee in 92.2% of cases, and Furhat's lip-synced face was more intelligible than a flat screen.
column18: In Study III gaze shifts were controlled by a Wizard-of-Oz setup. In the museum, Furhat's behavior was autonomous, using handheld microphones, ultrasound proximity sensors and audio-level comparison to choose the addressee, with the IrisTK toolkit.
column19: Furhat is a back-projected, human-like robot head: a micro projector projects an animated face onto a 3D-printed mask, mounted on a pan-tilt-roll neck. The animated eyes have separately controllable pupils, irises and eyelids.
column20: The physical 3D mask, compared with a flat screen, eliminated the Mona Lisa effect and made gaze exclusive to one person. The static mask also enlarged the perceived lips, which may explain the higher intelligibility. Calibration of gaze may need to differ by robot design.

column2: On the Benefit of Independent Control of Head and Eye Movements of a Social Robot for Multiparty Human-Robot Interaction
column3: The authors analysed a three-party teleoperated conversation and found that the pilot's head contribution to gaze was weaker when addressing both players than when addressing one. An online evaluation with 50 participants on a Furhat robot showed that a policy replaying the human's decoupled head and eye movements was rated most natural.
column4: The study combines an analysis of human pilot gaze and head behaviour in a recorded three-party conversation with an online crowdsourced subjective evaluation of four head-eye coordination policies on a Furhat robot.
column5: The evaluation was conducted online as a third-party video rating study. The interaction data come from the RoboTrio corpus of a collaborative word game recorded with an iCub robot.
column6: 50 participants' submissions were analysed in the online evaluation, after 51 people completed it and one submission was rejected.
column7: Online evaluation participants were French speakers aged 18 to 60 residing in France, Belgium or Switzerland, with a balanced number of females and males. The recorded human players in the corpus were pairs of men.
column8: Players played a collaborative word game (Unanimo) with a robot animator in the recorded corpus. In the evaluation, subjects rated 15 short clips (about 10.5 seconds on average) selected from five annotated sequences.
column9: Each interaction session involved two human players and one robot teleoperated by a human animator. The evaluation clips show only the virtual robot with the participants' soundtracks in stereo.
column10: One robot per interaction session. In the corpus this was an iCub teleoperated by a pilot, and in the evaluation clips a virtual Furhat robot.
column11: Two human players per interaction session, plus the human animator who teleoperates the robot.
column12: Participants rated the perceived naturalness of each clip on a 0 to 100 slider scale in the HEMVIP interface and then completed a general questionnaire about their familiarity with robots. Gaze and head focal points were also annotated from the corpus using GMM classification and OpenFace.
column13: Policy significantly affected naturalness ratings (chisq(3)=744.53, p<0.0001). The EyesHead policy was rated significantly higher than the others, while Furhat and EyesOnly did not differ from each other but were rated significantly lower than HeadOnly and EyesHead.
column14: The authors frame robotic gaze as a combination of head and eye movements, where the robot's gaze generation involves identifying where to focus attention and a control policy that directs attention through body segments, with the head treated as an attention vector.
column15: The authors state that gaze is essentially a combination of eye and head movements with their own kinematics, and that gaze is the addition of head and eye movements whose kinematics differ.
column16: Gaze and head orientation regulate multiparty conversation, contributing to addressee identification and next speaker identification, and the head orientation helps communicate to whom the robot is addressing.
column17: Driving only the eyes or only the head was rated less natural than replaying the original human behaviour with both channels. The Default Furhat policy, which aligns eyes and head at the end of the movement, obtained low scores compared with the other policies.
column18: Gaze targets and head movements were taken from a teleoperated iCub recording and replayed on a Furhat robot under four head-eye policies. The Furhat controller computes eye trajectories toward targets, and clips were rendered with the Furhat simulator and presented via HEMVIP.

column3: The authors implemented an autonomous gaze algorithm on the EveR-4 android that gives each detected face an importance value based on its distance and how long it has been tracked, then gazes at the highest-importance person. column4: Technical system description: the authors implemented an autonomous gaze algorithm on an android robot and informally observed people's reactions to it at an exhibition.

column16: Gaze divides attention among everyone present to acknowledge them and set up a platform for inviting conversation. It also helps ensure smooth transitions as people enter and leave the conversation.

column2: Identifying the Focus of Attention in Human-Robot Conversational Groups
column3: The paper proposes a hidden Markov model that estimates a group's focus of attention from participants' head positions and orientations, so a robot can direct its gaze to the group's focal point, including objects and people outside the group. It reached 81.6% accuracy on the Babble dataset versus a 53.8% baseline, and 94% accuracy in a live Fetch robot experiment with groups of 3 to 7 including the robot.
column4: Technical system description with evaluation: an HMM-based focus-of-attention method tested on the public Babble dataset and in a live laboratory experiment with a Fetch robot.

column8: In the live experiment, the robot acted as an active listener within an F-formation while participants held informal conversation about topics such as favorite movies and restaurants. A researcher moderator randomly selected a participant to leave the group every 4-5 minutes, and a poster was later brought near the group to test focus shifts to outside objects.
column9: Live sessions were reported with group sizes ranging from 3 to 7 including the robot. F-formations of size 2 were excluded from testing.

column13: On the Babble dataset the HMM achieved 81.6% accuracy versus 53.8% for the naive voting baseline. In the live experiment the system reached 94.00% accuracy, and all errors were false negatives.
column14: The paper frames the concept as the group's focus of attention: the visual point at which a majority of participants direct their gaze in a conversation, which the robot detects. It does not use the term robotic gaze-based attention.
column15: The group's focus of attention is defined as the person or object that receives the majority of the attention within or outside the conversational group. It can be a person inside the group, an object inside the group, a person outside the group, or an object outside the group.
column16: Knowing the group's focus of attention lets the robot adjust its gaze to the conversational dynamics and behave more naturally. It also gives context that can reduce ambiguity in conversations, such as when two people share a name.
column17: The authors state that the algorithm enabled the robot to exhibit more natural gaze behavior in realistic group interactions. The paper reports no measured effects on human participants or interaction outcomes.
column18: Autonomous pipeline: Vicon motion capture tracks head position and orientation, REFORM detects F-formations, and an HMM with forward-algorithm updates infers the focus of attention among candidate targets using normally distributed head-orientation likelihoods. column2: Implementing a gaze control system on a social robot in multi-person interactions
column3: The authors implemented a gaze control system on the RASA humanoid robot that chooses which person to look at in multi-person interactions, using social cues and proximity and orientation weights calibrated from human gaze data. In an 80-second real-life scenario the robot's gaze matched participants' average gaze pattern 76.9% of the time, and most participants felt the robot sometimes really looked at them.
column4: A technical system description of a gaze control system on the RASA robot, supported by experiments: two calibration experiments with volunteers watching animations and an evaluation with a new group of volunteers comparing robot gaze with participant gaze plus a questionnaire.

column10: One robot: the RASA humanoid robot.

column14: The paper frames robotic attention as a gaze control system that directs the robot's attention to the most appropriate target in multi-party interactions by selecting an attention target and adjusting the head and eyes.

column16: The gaze behaviour selects which person the robot looks at in a multi-person scene, based on social cues and proximity and orientation. It also serves as a deliberate redirection away from the audience and rotates attention so the robot does not fixate on one person.
column17: In the evaluation, the robot's gaze matched participants' average gaze pattern on 10 of 13 attention shifts (76.9%). Also, 86% of the 21 participants gave a positive score that the robot sometimes really looked at them, with a mean of 4.33 out of 5.
column18: The gaze control system runs as a ROS package within a cognitive architecture. Kinect sensor inputs feed a Perception Unit for social cues, a rule-based Logic Unit selects the target using an elicited attention score, and an Action Unit moves the head and eyes. The gaze shifts are controlled autonomously, with a PID controller for the neck.
column19: RASA is a humanoid robot designed for teaching Persian Sign Language. It has 32 degrees of freedom, including 3 neck DOF, and a face projected on an 8-inch screen with adjustable eyes, plus a Kinect sensor in its chest.

column2: Embodied Mediation in Group Ideation – A Gestural Robot Can Facilitate Consensus-Building
column3: The authors studied groups of three planning a five-day vacation with a small, non-humanoid whiteboard-mounted robot that used gestures including following speakers with gaze. Participants often described the gaze as supportive, and groups with the robot spent more time consensus-building than groups without it; some participants also felt monitored or judged.

column2: Assisting Group Discussions Using Desktop Robot Haru
column3: The authors built a desktop robot system that combines autonomous gaze, dialogue assistance, and verbal prompts to balance participation in two-person discussions. In the study, the combined gaze and dialogue-balancing condition received higher ratings for Haru’s effectiveness and discussion quality, though the study does not isolate gaze’s contribution from the verbal prompts.
column4: Experimental user study and technical/system description.
column5: University campus recruitment; in-person group discussions at a table with Haru positioned between participants; the gaze policy was trained in Gazebo simulation and evaluated on the physical robot.
column6: 40 participants total: 24 in the group-discussion study and 16 teacher-role video evaluators.
column7: The discussion participants were 20–25 years old (mean 23.3, SD 1.127); 54.17% male, 33.33% female, and 12.5% undisclosed. They were paired as a “talkative” and a “shy” student. The video evaluators were 21–25 years old (mean 23.5, SD 1.212); 68.75% male, 25% female, and 6.25% undisclosed.
column8: Two participants discussed a topic supplied by a staff member acting as a teacher, with Haru assisting. Each group completed three conditions: chatting only; chatting plus dialogue balancing; and chatting, dialogue balancing, and autonomous gaze. Participants familiarized with one another for five minutes beforehand; no discussion duration is specified.
column9: Three per interaction session: two human participants and one Haru robot.
column11: 2 discussion participants per group; the paper considers two users conversing with Haru.
column12: Godspeed-derived ratings of anthropomorphism, animacy, likability, and perceived intelligence; a custom four-question, 7-point Likert scale; teacher evaluations of discussion videos using the questionnaires; and recorded video. The paper reports no gaze-tracking or behavioral coding instrument.
column13: Student ratings showed significant condition differences across all assessed perspectives (p < 0.01); Condition 3 outperformed Conditions 2 and 1 on Haru’s effectiveness and discussion quality, and Condition 2 outperformed Condition 1 (p < 0.01). Teacher ratings showed the same pattern, except Condition 2 versus 1 differences in animacy and perceived intelligence were near significance (p = 0.03 and p = 0.02).
column14: The authors frame the behavior as “autonomous gazing behavior” and non-verbal gazing behavior, which they associate with politeness and assistance in group discussion. They do not explicitly define “robotic gaze,” “robotic attention,” or “robotic gaze-based attention.”
column16: The gaze behavior directs Haru toward the current speaker, toward the middle when both participants are silent or speak simultaneously, and toward the least-spoken participant when Haru encourages her. The authors present this as politeness and as part of assisting group discussion.
column17: With dialogue balancing and autonomous gaze together, participants rated Haru’s effectiveness and discussion quality higher than in the other conditions. The paper attributes increased perceived politeness and discussion quality to the system, but does not isolate gaze’s effect from dialogue balancing in Condition 3.
column18: The gaze policy used soft actor-critic deep reinforcement learning, trained in Gazebo simulation and transferred to physical Haru. It used user positions and engagement state to select a motor movement angle; Azure Kinect supplied user skeletons and sound locations in the study. The paper describes the behavior as autonomous.
column19: Haru is an experimental multimodal desktop robot with five degrees of freedom: base rotation, neck tilt, eye movement, eye rotation, and eye tilt. Its body has addressable LEDs for mouth movements; its eyes contain a 3-inch TFT display bordered by LED strips.
column21: The authors built a desktop robot system that combines autonomous gaze, dialogue assistance, and verbal prompts to balance participation in two-person discussions. column2: Towards Robot Autonomy in Group Conversations: Understanding the Effects of Body Orientation and Gaze
column3: The authors tested middle versus attentive body orientation and random versus attentive eye gaze with Chester, a mobile robot interacting with groups of three or four people during laboratory brainstorming. Attentive gaze made the robot’s motion seem more natural and led participants to stand closer, while attentive orientation made participants feel that the robot looked at them more; orientation did not significantly alter feelings of group inclusion.
column4: A 2×2 between-subjects experiment, with automated orientation and gaze behaviors and wizard-managed speech and study sequencing.
column5: Laboratory room set up for group brainstorming, with 4.4 × 4.4 meters of free space.
column6: 69 participants in 20 groups (5 groups per condition).
column7: Adults (18 or older), fluent in English, raised in the U.S.; mostly university students. Mean age 24.8 years (SE 1.0); most used computers daily and reported limited robot familiarity. Seven sessions included participants who knew one another.
column8: Participants joined a robot-led brainstorming session about useful tasks the robot could perform in the lab. The robot introduced itself, facilitated six minutes of brainstorming, and closed the session; participants wrote ideas on slips and deposited them in color-coded boxes, which prompted natural departures and re-entries. Four conditions crossed middle or attentive orientation with random or attentive gaze.
column9: Each session involved one robot and three or four human participants (four or five group members total).
column11: 3 or 4 participants per session.
column12: Post-test survey, including the Inclusion of Other in Self (IOS) scale and Williams et al. survey on belongingness and ostracism; Likert ratings of robot impressions. Objective measures included participant–robot distance, group membership, and idea-slip counts. Researchers also used coder annotations of group membership, speaker/addressee transcription, robot eye-fixation inspection, system logs, and teleoperation records.
column13: Attentive gaze (AG) made the robot’s motion seem more natural than random gaze (RG) (M=4.71 vs. 4.00; p<.05). Attentive orientation (AO) increased ratings that the robot looked at participants compared with middle orientation (MO) (M=4.72 vs. 4.11; p<.01). Participants stood farther away with RG than AG during the final brainstorming minute (2.29 m vs. 2.09 m; p=.02); the MO+RG group was farther from the robot than MO+AG (2.40 m vs. 2.03 m; interaction p=.04).
column14: The paper frames gaze as a way for the robot’s eyes to communicate mental states and attention, and examines gaze and body orientation as coupled behaviors in group conversations.
column16: Attentive gaze attempts to establish mutual gaze with the person who is the robot’s addressee or current speaker, or with a moving group member when the group is silent. The authors present gaze as communicating attention and contributing to perceived naturalness of robot motion.
column17: Attentive gaze improved perceived naturalness of robot motion and was associated with participants standing closer to the robot than under random gaze. Attentive orientation increased the perception that the robot looked at participants. Gaze and body motion influenced perceptions of one another. The orientation behaviors did not significantly change feelings of inclusion or belonging; the authors report similar feelings for MO and AO.
column18: The study used an integrated multimodal perception system to track people and the robot, detect conversational groups and the current speaker, and control orientation and gaze. Participants wore baseball caps with UWB beacons; a Kinect contributed skeleton and audio data. The behavior conditions ran autonomously for most of the interaction, while a hidden wizard managed speech and event sequencing and occasionally repositioned or corrected the robot. MO oriented toward the mean direction of group members; AO biased orientation toward the addressee or speaker. AG directed pupils toward the focus of attention, while RG used random small pupil shifts when no scripted eye animation was scheduled.
column19: Chester, a mobile furniture platform with a differential-drive base, fixed face, and back-projected eyes.
column20: The fixed head meant gaze was manipulated through eye direction, while the robot’s design constrained the behaviors studied. column2: Regulating Turn-Taking in Multi-child Spoken Interaction
column3: The study tested gaze cues during trivia games with pairs of children and a human or robot moderator. Robot head-eye cues supported directed turn-taking as well as the human moderator, while eye movement alone led to more errors; head-eye cues also produced the most balanced participation on open questions.
column4: Experimental study comparing programmed robot gaze cues with a human moderator.
column5: Laboratory setting.
column6: 44 children (22 pairs recruited); 19 pairs were included in analysis.
column7: Children aged five to nine; 20 female among 44 participants. Children in each pair were familiar siblings or friends and generally similar in age.
column8: Pairs played a Disney trivia quiz with directed and open questions, first with a human moderator and then with the robot. Robot questions used either eyes-only or coordinated head-eye cues.
column9: Three participants per session: two children and one moderator, human or robot.
column11: Two children per session; the moderator was either human or robot. Robot sessions also involved a human wizard/experimenter.
column12: Behavioral video/audio coding by two study-blind annotators; turn-taking, response type, and moderator interruption measures; interface event logs and recordings.
column13: For directed questions, correct turn-taking was 70.0% with robot head-eye cues versus 51.4% with eyes-only; eyes-only produced significantly more errors than head-eyes (χ²=9.272, p=.002) and human natural movement (χ²=8.73, p=.003). In open questions, head-eyes produced the most even participation distribution; the paper does not report a significance test for that comparison.
column14: Gaze is framed as the combination of eye and head movement and as a nonvocal cue for regulating turn-taking and identifying addressees.
column15: The paper explicitly defines gaze as the combination of eye and head movement; it does not give a separate definition of robotic attention.
column16: Gaze cues regulate turn-taking and signal the intended addressee or inclusion of both children.
column17: Coordinated head-eye movement improved children’s directed turn-taking accuracy over eyes-only cues, reaching performance comparable to the human moderator. In open questions, head-eyes yielded the most balanced participation; eye-only cues were associated with more imbalance and fewer ties.
column18: A dialog system used a Kinect person-tracking module to locate the two players and direct robot gaze. A human wizard supplied high-level input; programmed cues were eyes-only or coordinated eye and head movement.
column19: Sammy, an anthropomorphic robot head with an adult-like form, rear-projected facial animation on a 3D-printed mask, and a two-degree-of-freedom neck.
column20: The authors report that eye movement alone on this anthropomorphic head did not reliably signal addressee to young children, while prominent head rotation in coordinated gaze supported turn regulation. They compare this with adult studies using the same robot head.

column2: When a Robot Is Your Teammate
column3: This paper presents cohesion as a framework for designing, developing, and evaluating robotic teammates and reviews four prior use cases. In its multiparty gaze study, autonomous responsive and attentive gaze improved perceived teamwork, with attentive gaze rated as more fluent than responsive gaze.
column4: Conceptual framework paper presenting four use cases from previous work, including experimental user studies and a technical system description.
column5: The paper describes multiple settings: an online video-rating study and game-based human–robot interaction studies; the setting for all studies is not specified.
column8: Tasks included playing a four-player trick-taking card game in two human–robot teams, a collective-risk musical-band game, and watching scripted videos of a silent coordination task to rate teamwork. Durations are not stated.
column9: Groups varied by use case: four members (two humans and two robots) or three members (one human and two robots). The gaze study used a triadic team of one robot and two humans.

column13: In the gaze study, both responsive and attentive gaze improved perceived teammate perception and team fluency versus baseline; attentive gaze was rated more fluent than responsive gaze. Teams where both humans displayed gaze were rated more coordinated, fluent, and united than teams where only one human did so. Statistical values are not provided.
column14: Robotic teammate gaze behavior is framed as a nonverbal behavior supporting task cohesion through joint attention and structural cohesion through signaling roles and communication structures.
column15: The paper does not give a standalone definition of robotic gaze or robotic gaze-based attention; it describes responsive and attentive gaze strategies by what gaze targets they detect and how the robot responds.
column16: Gaze supports mutual gaze and joint attention, conveys communication structure and roles, and is examined as a means to affect team coordination and fluency.
column17: Responsive and attentive gaze positively affected perceived teammate quality and team fluency; attentive gaze yielded higher perceived fluency than responsive gaze. More human teammates displaying gaze was associated with higher perceived coordination, fluency, and unity.
column18: An autonomous gaze system detects human teammates’ gaze. In the responding-gaze condition, the robot detects gaze toward itself and looks back at that person. In the attentive-gaze condition, it also detects gaze between human teammates and looks at the same person they are looking at. The baseline only blinks.
column20: The paper states that gaze response depends on the communication structure the robot perceives, and more generally that embodiment affords different ways of expressing emotion. It does not describe a specific robot platform or explain how the gaze-study robot’s body affected the study or results.
column21: This paper presents cohesion as a framework for designing, developing, and evaluating robotic teammates and reviews four prior use cases. In its multiparty gaze study, autonomous responsive and attentive gaze improved perceived teamwork, with attentive gaze rated as more fluent than responsive gaze.

column2: Meet me where i'm gazing: how shared attention gaze affects human-robot handover timing
column3: The authors tested three PR2 gaze conditions during one-to-one bottle handovers: no gaze, gaze toward the handover location, and gaze that then shifted to the participant’s face. Participants reached significantly earlier with shared-attention gaze than with no gaze; turn-taking gaze showed some nonsignificant favorable trends in subjective ratings.
column4: Human-human observational handover study followed by a controlled human-robot paired-comparison experiment.
column5: Controlled room during a university orientation event.
column6: The human-robot experiment recruited 102 volunteers; data from 96 participants were analyzed. The human-human study included 12 volunteers.
column7: The human-robot experiment analyzed 96 participants (63 male, 33 female; mean age 23, SD 5.59); participants were recruited as naïve volunteers. The human-human study had 12 volunteers (10 male, 2 female).
column8: Participants received a water bottle handed over by the PR2 under two gaze conditions per participant, then placed the bottle in a box and returned for a second handover. The experiment compared no gaze, shared-attention gaze toward the handover location, and turn-taking gaze that shifted from the handover location to the participant’s face.
column9: Two per human-robot interaction: one robot and one participant.
column11: 1 participant per human-robot handover interaction.
column12: Measures included video-based frame-by-frame coding of human-human giver gaze; infrared motion sensors for participant reach time; robot event timestamps; and a custom post-handover questionnaire comparing preference, naturalness, and perceived timing communication.
column13: Participants reached for the object earlier with shared-attention gaze than with no gaze (M=1.91 vs. 2.54 seconds; p<.005). No significant reach-time differences were found between shared-attention and turn-taking gaze or between turn-taking and no gaze. Subjective comparisons showed trends favoring turn-taking gaze, but no significant overall differences.
column14: The paper frames its behavior as robot gaze during handovers, including shared-attention gaze at the projected handover location and turn-taking gaze that adds a look toward the receiver’s face.
column15: The paper defines deictic gaze or shared visual attention as one person following another’s direction of attention to look at a fixed point in space.
column16: Shared-attention gaze is intended to direct the human’s attention to the projected handover location and convey where the handover will take place. The added look to the receiver’s face was tested as a timing cue and as a way to improve subjective experience.
column17: Shared-attention gaze led participants to reach for the offered object significantly earlier than no gaze, with mean reach occurring before the robot finished moving. Turn-taking gaze showed trends toward better preference, naturalness, and timing judgments in some comparisons.
column18: The PR2 expressed gaze through head orientation. The robot tracked its end-effector while acquiring the bottle, then changed gaze during the transition from ready position to handover location; software modules controlled the arm and head, and a sensor array detected participant reach.
column19: The study used a PR2 humanoid mobile robotic platform with a pan-tilt head and two 7-DOF arms, each with a two-fingered, 1-DOF gripper.

column2: Deliberate delays during robot-to-human handovers improve compliance with gaze communication
column3: In a one-person block-sorting task with HERB, the robot suggested a box by looking toward it during an object handover. Delaying release increased participants’ attention to HERB’s head, recognition of the gaze suggestions, and compliance; the joint-attention versus mirrored-gaze manipulation had no significant effect.
column4: Experimental study
column5: In-person human–robot interaction experiment in Pittsburgh; the paper does not explicitly label the setting as a laboratory.
column6: 32 participants
column7: 18 female participants; mean age 34; recruited from the Pittsburgh area through Carnegie Mellon University's online participant pool.
column8: Participants took part in a block-sorting handover task. HERB handed them five colored blocks; participants sorted each into a yellow or blue box according to their preference. For ambiguous and semi-ambiguous blocks, HERB suggested a box by looking toward it. The interaction lasted about 2 minutes 20 seconds.
column9: One robot and one participant per interaction session.
column11: 1 participant per interaction session
column12: Task performance (whether participants followed HERB’s suggestions); custom written post-task questionnaires, including free-response and Likert-scale items; semi-structured interviews; and video recordings coded for looking at HERB’s face/head and noticing suggestions. No named standardized questionnaire or eye tracker is reported.
column13: Handover delay increased compliance with HERB’s semi-ambiguous-block suggestion (19% without delay versus 63% with delay; χ²(1, N=32)=6.77, p=0.0092), increased head-looking time (24.7 versus 50.6 seconds; F(1,31)=12.9828, p=0.0012), and increased self-reported recognition of suggestions (75% versus 38%; p=0.0302). Gaze type did not significantly affect compliance.
column14: The paper frames robotic eye gaze as a non-verbal communication channel that can provide information and influence human motor behavior. Its focal use is a gaze cue that suggests where a handed-over object should be sorted.
column15: The authors do not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or robotic attention. They describe gaze communication as non-verbal communication and operationalize the cue as the robot orienting its head toward a box.
column16: The robot’s gaze communicates a sorting suggestion about where to put the object after the handover. A deliberate release delay is used to redirect human attention toward the robot’s head so people notice the gaze cue.
column17: The delay increased attention to HERB’s head, recognition of gaze suggestions, and compliance with counterintuitive suggestions. The social-gaze manipulation (joint attention versus mirrored gaze) did not significantly affect attention or compliance.
column18: HERB used pre-scripted trajectories and a force/torque sensor to detect when the participant grasped the block. On each trial it turned its head toward a box; in the delay condition it released only after completing the head turn, while in the no-delay condition release and head turn began simultaneously. The experiment ran autonomously with real-time force feedback; no real-time vision was used.
column19: HERB (Home Exploring Robot Butler) is a bimanual assistive robot with two 7-DOF WAM arms, each with a 4-DOF three-finger Barrett hand. It has a pan-tilt head with a Microsoft Kinect and camera; the visible round cameras on the Kinect front serve as its eyes. Only the right arm was used.
column20: The authors suggest that HERB’s relatively abstract, non-anthropomorphic head may have affected how well participants perceived joint attention; they propose that a robot with more defined eyes might yield different results. The paper reports no significant effect of gaze type in this study.
column21: In a one-person block-sorting task with HERB, the robot suggested a box by looking toward it during an object handover. column2: Multi-party Interaction with a Robot Receptionist
column3: The paper compares four video-based robot receptionist policies for coordinating turn-taking with two users, varying eye gaze, head pose, and speech. The combined gaze, head pose, and speech policy was rated more favorably on several social and cognitive traits, while using head pose alone without speech was rated least polite.
column4: Within-subjects video-based experiment comparing four robot engagement policies, followed by an online questionnaire.
column5: Online questionnaire study using video demonstrations; the interaction depicted is a robot receptionist scenario.
column6: 110 submissions were considered in the analysis, from 120 recruited participants.

column2: Model for controlling a target human's attention in multi-party settings
column3: The paper proposes and tests a five-phase, non-verbal model for directing one person’s attention in a multiparty interaction. Experiments with paired participants and robot heads indicate that head motion effectiveness depends on viewing position, while blinking, gaze avoidance, and gaze back can help the robot engage a target, shift their attention, and signal disinterest in non-targets.
column4: Experimental study with two experiments and a technical system description.
column5: University experimental setting; the paper describes participant pairs seated and interacting with robot heads in an arranged room setup. It does not explicitly label the setting as a laboratory.
column6: Experiment 1: 20 participants in 10 pairs. Experiment 2: 36 graduate students.
column7: Experiment 1 participants were 15 males and 5 females, average age 27.92 years, recruited from Saitama University. Experiment 2 participants were graduate students, mean age 26.5 years (SD 3.4).
column8: Experiment 1: pairs played a card game while perceiving a robot head’s turning or shaking motions. Experiment 2: pairs looked around at paintings while the robot attempted to attract a selected target’s attention and direct it toward a left or right table object; there were two trials per pair.
column9: Each interaction session involved two humans and two robot heads: one moving or attention-control robot and one stationary robot.
column11: 2 participants per session.
column12: Custom 1–7 rating questionnaires; paired t-tests for the first experiment; video observation for time to attention shift and success ratio; ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey tests for experiment 2 questionnaire and timing results.
column13: In experiment 1, head shaking attracted more attention than head turning in the far peripheral field of view (FPFOV; p < .0001 for both participants); head turning was sufficient in the near peripheral field of view, and neither motion attracted attention out of view. In experiment 2, the proposed method had shorter time to attention shift (1.72 s) and higher success ratio (58.3%) than methods 2 (2.71 s; 25%) and 3 (1.80 s; 33%); timing differences were significant between methods 1 and 2 (p = .0076) and methods 2 and 3 (p < .05), but not methods 1 and 3. Proposed method ratings supported eye contact, intended attention direction, and conveying non-communicative intention to non-targets.
column14: The paper frames its approach as a five-phase attention control process for directing a particular human’s attention among multiple people, using non-verbal robot behaviors.
column15: The authors define attention control as gaze (head) control that shifts someone’s gaze from one direction to another intended by the initiator.
column16: The process selects and engages a target person, establishes eye contact, signals non-communicative intent to non-targets, and directs the target’s attention to a referential object.
column17: Robot head motions attracted attention depending on the target’s viewing position: turning worked in near peripheral view, shaking was needed in far peripheral view, and non-verbal motions could not attract someone out of view. In the second experiment, eye blinking and gaze back were associated with faster, more successful attention shifts and stronger perceived eye contact; looking away helped non-targets perceive less communicative intent.
column18: The system uses a finite-state-machine model, head and body tracking, situation and face detection, eye blinking, and pan-tilt control. It turns toward the target, shakes its head if needed, waits about four seconds for a response, blinks after face detection, avoids a non-target by turning away, returns its gaze if the target responds, and shifts gaze/head toward the object.
column19: A custom robot head with spherical 3D mask, projected CG eyes, laser range sensor, three USB cameras, and pan-tilt unit.
column20: The authors state that the robot heads’ human-face-like appearance could itself attract participants, even without robot actions; the study used a static robot as a comparison for this reason.

column2: Entrainment Effect Caused by Joint Attention of Two Robots
column3: The study tested joint attention in interactions between two Robovie-R robots and one person. Gaze toward the person was associated with greater gaze following and immersion in robot communication, while synchronous robot gaze helped participants identify the shared target more accurately.
column4: Experimental study with two experiments.
column5: In-person laboratory-style experiment; the paper describes a controlled setup but does not explicitly name the setting.
column6: 20 participants.
column7: 17 male and 3 female participants; no age or prior robot experience is stated.
column8: Experiment 1: participants watched two robots converse and then jointly gaze at an object, then guessed the object's color and conversation content. Experiment 2: participants watched synchronous or asynchronous joint gaze and identified the target object's color over 13 trials. Duration is not stated.
column9: Three individuals per interaction: two robots and one human participant.
column12: SMI eye-tracking glasses; custom questionnaires; participant responses identifying target colors and conversation content; target identification accuracy and distance from the correct object.
column13: Participants in Condition 1-A (robots gazed at the participant before shifting to an object) followed the robots' gaze more than in Condition 1-B (p .05) and tended to be more immersed in communication. In Experiment 2, synchronous gaze yielded more correct target guesses than asynchronous gaze (p .01); guessed-object distance also differed (p .01). Participants reported Condition 2-B was easier to understand (p .05).
column14: Joint attention, considered through two effects: sharing recognition and building relationships via communication entrainment.
column15: Sharing recognition means people share individuals' focus on an object; building relationships concerns communication entrainment, including drawing a person into a group through joint gaze.
column16: Joint gaze is framed as supporting shared recognition of a target and entraining or immersing a person in group communication.
column17: When both robots gazed at a person before gazing at an object, participants followed their gaze more and tended to be more immersed in communication. Synchronous robot gaze improved target identification compared with asynchronous gaze, although participants said asynchronous gaze was easier to understand.

column2: Cooperative gazing behaviors in human multi-robot interaction
column3: The authors tested two Nao robots interacting with one human who taught them object names, while the robots used different gaze strategies triggered by the human’s attention. Participants responded to those strategies: the active robot received more face looks, and active-following sessions produced more speech utterances and fewer attention shifts between objects around naming events.
column4: Experimental behavioral study with a real-time gaze-contingent platform; includes a technical system description.
column5: University laboratory setting; participants interacted with robots at a table. The paper does not explicitly label the study as a laboratory study.
column6: 21 participants included in the two conditions: 10 in the active-following condition and 11 in the passive-following condition. Five additional participants were excluded due to technical issues.
column7: Undergraduate students at Indiana University; age and gender are not reported in the provided paper text.
column8: Participants taught two robots the names of four novel, single-colored objects per trial, using artificial two-syllable names. They completed three trials of about three minutes each. The active-following condition paired a stereotype robot with an active robot; the passive-following condition paired a stereotype robot with a passive robot.
column9: Three agents per session: one human participant and two robots.
column11: 1 human participant per session; the paper describes each participant interacting with the two robots.
column12: Head-mounted Eye-Trac 6000 eye tracker and real-time gaze/ROI tracking; recorded first-person videos, robot head movements and gaze directions, and participant speech. Utterances were segmented by a speech-silence endpoint detection algorithm and transcribed by three human coders. Robot gaze behavior and successful gaze-following rates were also evaluated. Post-experiment interviews are mentioned, with no instrument specified.
column13: Participants looked more frequently at the active robot than at the passive robot (p = 0.03); they produced more spoken utterances in the active-following condition (26.45 vs. 20.71; p = 0.03). Around naming events, participants in the passive-following condition made more shifts between different objects than those in the active-following condition (before: F(1,59) = 127.69, p < 0.0001; after: F(1,59) = 350.52, p < 0.0001).
column14: The authors frame the topic as cooperative gazing behavior in human multi-robot interaction, including robot gaze behaviors contingent on the human’s attention. They identify following the user’s gaze, actively directing the user’s gaze, and encouraging attention toward other robots as possible cooperative behaviors.
column15: Cooperative behavior is defined as an action performed by robots that are not capturing the user’s direct attention. The paper does not provide a distinct formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or robotic gaze-based attention.
column16: Robot gaze behaviors can elicit or redirect the user’s attention, coordinate attention between the human and robots, and shape group communication and teaching behaviors. The active robot’s face looks were intended to attract the teacher’s attention when the teacher looked at its peer.
column17: Participants were sensitive to distinct robot cooperative gaze behaviors: active gaze elicited more frequent face looks and more speech utterances, while passive gaze did not direct more attention to its robot peer and was associated with less attention to the passive robot. Active-following participants also showed fewer object-to-object attention shifts around naming events, which the authors characterize as better teaching signals. No significant difference was found in object-look duration or naming-event counts between conditions.
column18: A gaze-contingent system used a head-mounted eye tracker and first-person video to detect the participant’s gaze target among four objects and two robots. A robot control unit received the target ROI; each robot’s control was independent. Robots followed gaze after a buffer of 30 gaze data points, requiring more than 50% to indicate the same ROI. Reported mean response time was 657 ms. Robot behaviors were programmed as stereotype, active, or passive strategies; no Wizard-of-Oz control is described.

column2: Are you looking at me? Perception of robot attention is mediated by gaze type and group size
column3: The authors built programmable MyKeepon robots and tested whether people could identify which robot was looking toward them in groups of four, six, or eight. Participants identified attention more accurately when fixations were short and frequent, and accuracy declined as robot group size increased.
column4: Experimental mixed between- and within-subjects study, with a technical platform description.
column5: Laboratory experiment.
column6: 53 participants took part; 51 were analyzed after two were excluded.
column7: 20 male and 33 female participants; age, population, and prior robot experience are not stated.
column8: Participants watched groups of robots perform random movements and occasional gaze fixations, then identified which robot appeared to be paying attention to them and rated their confidence. They completed 30 trials, each lasting 30 seconds, across fixation durations of 0, 1, 3, or 6 seconds.
column9: Each session included one participant and either 4, 6, or 8 robots.
column11: One participant per session.
column12: Custom trial-level robot-choice responses and a 0–100 confidence rating; accuracy of identifying the target robot was analyzed.
column13: Identification accuracy was significantly higher for 1- and 3-second fixations than for 0- or 6-second fixations. Accuracy differed by group size; the four-robot group outperformed the eight-robot group, with four versus six robots marginal. Overall accuracy across fixation durations was 37%, 28%, and 26% for groups of four, six, and eight robots, respectively.
column14: The authors frame the study as perception and detection of robot visual attention, operationalized through robot gaze fixations directed at the participant. They call their approach a “sociophysical level of analysis.”
column15: The paper operationalizes an attention fixation as a gaze fixation directed at the user; it does not provide a broader formal definition of robotic gaze or attention.
column16: Robot gaze fixations are used to convey or indicate that the robot is attending to the participant; the experiment tests whether participants can detect that attention among distractor robots.
column17: Multiple short fixations were more accurately recognized as attention than fewer, longer fixations. Increasing the number of distractor robots reduced accuracy.
column18: The researchers modified MyKeepon toys for computer control using Arduino Uno boards and motor shields. Robot motions were pre-scripted and sent over USB/serial; motor commands were cached on the boards and played sequentially. Target robots were hand-calibrated to orient toward participants.
column19: Programmable MyKeepon toys: small, yellow, snowman-like robots with two eyes and a nose and four degrees of freedom, controlled by three DC motors.
column20: The robots’ imprecise motors made perfectly direct gaze difficult, so target gaze was oriented toward or near participants; the authors note that gaze offset may have contributed to generally low accuracy. The body moves as a whole to orient gaze.

column2: A considerate care robot able to serve in multi-party settings
column3: The authors developed a mobile care robot that acknowledges a second person’s request by turning its gaze toward them while it is serving someone else. In a two-person snack-delivery experiment, gaze acknowledgment improved perceived recognition and ease of calling, while satisfaction ratings did not differ significantly.
column4: Technical/system description with a controlled comparative experiment and ethnographic observations.
column5: An experimental room with participants seated in chairs; the robot’s mobility was also tested moving around tables and obstacles. The paper additionally reports observations at a Japanese elderly day-care center.
column6: 40 participants.
column7: Undergraduate students in the university’s Faculty of Liberal Arts; the paper does not state their age, gender, or prior robot experience.
column8: Participants played person B, called the robot by raising a hand after it began moving to person A, and experienced either gaze acknowledgment or no gaze acknowledgment. The robot delivered snacks to two people, serving A before B.
column9: Two humans and one robot per experimental interaction.
column12: Four custom 1–7 response questions; a 28-pair Semantic Differential impression evaluation on seven-degree scales; video analysis/counting of hand raises and observed calling behaviors; statistical comparison of question scores. WoZ was used to avoid request recognition errors.
column13: Gaze acknowledgment produced higher average scores on all four questions, with significant differences for perceived recognition (Q2) and ease of calling (Q3), p<0.05; Q4 satisfaction did not differ significantly. Participants without gaze acknowledgment raised their hands more than once, while the participant shown after gaze acknowledgment put her hand down.
column14: The paper frames gaze as a nonverbal acknowledgment that projects the order of service provision and signals which requester will be served next.
column16: Gaze acknowledges a subsequent request, projects the service order, and communicates to the waiting person that they will be served next, allowing the robot to continue serving the first person while the second waits.
column17: Gaze acknowledgment improved perceived robot recognition and ease of calling; participants gave higher scores across all four questions, though satisfaction did not differ significantly. Without acknowledgment, participants repeated hand raises and some used emphatic waving or said “excuse me.” Impression ratings also suggested more positive evaluation with the nonverbal gesture.
column18: CCR autonomously circulates while looking around, detects hand-raising requests using a body-mounted laser range finder and human-shape tracking, and, when a second request is detected en route to the first person, momentarily stops and turns its gaze toward the second person before continuing. The comparative experiment used WoZ to avoid request-recognition errors.
