column2: Multi-person human-robot interaction system for android robot
column3: The paper presents an Actroid-SIT system for multiparty interaction that plans interruptible, parameterized gestures and gaze toward talkers or objects. In a field experiment, the interruptible and parametric condition had a 62% induction rate and the longest mean conversation residence time (52.5 seconds); the authors linked the induction result to the robot’s idling motion and longer interaction to interruptibility.
column4: Technical system description and field experiment.
column5: Field study at the Heijo palace site during the 1300th Anniversary of Nara Heijo-kyo Capital, Japan.
column6: 570 subjects across three conditions (226 + 165 + 179).
column7: Visitors of various age groups; age, sex, and character were discussed as sources of variation. The paper does not state further participant demographics.
column8: Visitors could approach and speak with Actroid-SIT using a microphone. The study compared three conditions: non-interruptible/non-parametric, interruptible/non-parametric, and interruptible/parametric interaction. Residence time ran from when a subject started speaking until returning the microphone to its stand; consecutive speakers without a break counted as one duration.
column9: One robot interacted with visitors; the number of humans in each interaction group/session is not stated.
column12: The study counted visitors and subjects to calculate induction rate, and measured residence time using the microphone return as the endpoint. It reports comparisons and t-tests for residence time.
column13: Induction rate was highest in the interruptible, parametric condition (62%, versus 48% and 38%); residence time was longest in that condition (52.5 s versus 33.3 s and 48.6 s). Residence-time differences between conditions 1 and 2, and 1 and 3, were significant at the 1% level; the authors attribute improved induction to the home-position idling motion and longer communication to interruptibility.
column14: The paper describes gaze motion planning alongside gesture adjustment for multiparty communication. It presents gaze as coordinated head and eye direction and as a way to look toward talkers or object locations.
column16: Gaze motion is used to look toward talkers and object points, including an idling motion that tracks a talker’s direction. The system also rapidly switches attention between people to support multiparty communication.
column17: The authors report that the home-position idling motion was associated with a higher induction rate, with the parametric and interruptible condition reaching over 60%. They report longer residence time with interruptible interaction and significant differences between the non-interruptible condition and both interruptible conditions.
column18: The system uses a camera and microphone-color markers to detect talker location and count nearby people, speech recognition and keyphrase extraction, and an episode-rule selector. RMDB generates parameterized, interruptible body gestures; gaze direction is computed from head and eye angles with a sharing-rate model and convergence for object points. Components communicate through a Key-Value Store. The paper does not state that interaction was Wizard-of-Oz controlled.
column19: Actroid-SIT, an android robot with a human-like figure and 42 degrees of freedom: 29 for body gesture and 13 for facial expression.
column20: The authors state that robot appearance and body gesture affect human impression, and that the android's human-like appearance is expected to help present multimodal information. They do not isolate or measure an embodiment effect in the experiment.

column2: Neural network based reinforcement learning for audio-visual gaze control in human-robot interaction
column3: The paper develops an autonomous deep reinforcement learning system that controls a Nao robot’s head to find people, keep multiple people in view, and favor speakers using audio and visual sensing. Offline, simulated, and live experiments show that audio-visual fusion works best overall, with late fusion slightly better on the recorded dataset; the paper does not report participant outcome measures.
column4: Technical/system description with offline dataset evaluation, simulation, and live robot experiments.

column8: The system learns to orient a robot head to find people, maximize the number of people in its camera field of view, and favor people who speak. Evaluation includes simulated moving/talking people, recorded group footage, and live two-person and other unspecified participant scenarios.

column11: Not specified for live sessions; the paper gives a two-person live example, and the simulated environment uses one or two people.
column12: System/technical performance measures: reward (face and speaker reward), computed from visible faces and speech source presence; comparisons of architecture and parameter settings. No human outcome instruments are reported.
column13: Key technical result: audio-visual fusion produced the best overall performance; on the simulated environment early and late fusion were indistinguishable as best, while late fusion was slightly better on AVDIAR. No inferential statistical tests are reported.
column14: The paper frames robotic gaze as gaze control: orienting a robot head to find people, maximize visible people, and favor speakers; it also describes gaze as directing attention toward groups.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or attention beyond describing gaze control as head orientation toward people, maximizing visible people and preferring speakers.
column16: Gaze control is used to gather useful information about people in group interaction: find and track people, maximize the number visible, and favor speakers.
column17: The paper reports system behavior and gaze-control performance, not measured effects on participants or interaction outcomes. The authors state that gaze and verbal behavior can affect turn-taking in general, but do not test that effect here.
column18: Autonomous deep reinforcement learning: an LSTM recurrent neural network estimates Q-values; audio and visual streams are fused early or late, with audio-only and vision-only variants also evaluated. column19: Nao humanoid robot with a rotating head, two rotational degrees of freedom, a head-mounted camera, and four microphones.
column20: The head-mounted camera and two-axis head constrain the visual field of view and available actions; the planar microphone array provides only horizontal sound localization. Full-body pose detection helps the robot orient from visible limbs toward a person's face.

column2: Robot Gaze Behavior and Proxemics to Coordinate Conversational Roles in Group Interactions
column3: The authors built an autonomous system for Pepper that uses participants’ distance and orientation to estimate conversational roles and adapt the robot’s gaze. In a pilot trivia study with pairs, role-coordinated gaze was associated with closer participant positions and higher ratings of adaptability, sociability, social presence, and feeling attended to.

column6: 16 participants, recruited in 8 pairs.
column7: Participants’ average age was 27; gender, population, and prior robot experience are not stated.

column12: Human–robot distance and orientation angle (α) were extracted every six seconds. Subjective outcomes were measured with the ALMERE questionnaire and additional questions about feeling attended to; analyses included factorial ANOVA with Tukey HSD and one-way ANOVA.
column13: Participants in the conversational-role-coordinator condition stood closer overall than in basic awareness (mean 1.31 m vs. 1.637 m; F(1, 44)=7.635, p=0.01); bystander participants also stood closer (1.68 m vs. 2.03 m). Orientation-angle differences were not significant.

column2: What happens when a robot favors someone? How a tour guide robot uses gaze behavior to address multiple persons while storytelling about art

column2: Using Random Forests for the Estimation of Multiple Users’ Visual Focus of Attention from Head Pose
column3: The paper evaluated a Kinect-based system that estimates one or two people's visual focus of attention from head pose while they looked at images on a screen. Precision fell from 0.82 with one user to 0.62 when tracking two users, and to 0.39 when both users had to be correct simultaneously; the study did not test a robot's gaze behavior.
column4: Technical system evaluation with single-user and two-user experiments.
column5: Controlled indoor setup in front of a television with a Kinect camera.
column6: 18 participants; arranged into 14 two-person couples for multi-user tests.
column7: 18 participants: 14 males and 4 females. Age and prior robot experience are not stated.
column8: Participants followed images appearing for four seconds in randomly selected regions of a six-quadrant television screen; they were asked to look at each image. In two-person sessions, both participants did this task simultaneously after sequential calibration.
column9: One human in single-user sessions; two humans in multi-user sessions. No robot was present in the interaction group.
column11: One or two per session.
column12: Kinect RGB-D sensor with OpenNI skeleton tracking and DRRF head-pose/VFOA estimation; screen-region hit and miss counts over each four-second image display, summarized as precision (also sensitivity in this setup).
column13: Mean precision was 0.82 for single users, 0.62 for individual users tracked in two-person sessions, and 0.39 when both users had to be correctly recognized at the same time. Single-versus-multiple-user precision differed significantly (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.0157); simultaneous joint attention recognition was described as unattainable in this setup.
column14: The paper frames the topic as estimation of multiple users’ visual focus of attention (VFOA) from head pose, or head gaze, in multiparty interaction.
column15: The paper treats VFOA as a person's focus of attention estimated from head pose; it does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or robotic gaze-based attention.
column16: The paper describes head gaze/VFOA as a social cue that can signal attention to a person or object, regulate turn-taking, inform whether to initiate interaction, and help estimate user engagement. These roles are discussed as motivation rather than tested with a robot.
column17: The system's VFOA estimation performance declined when tracking two users compared with one; jointly recognizing both users' attention to a screen region was poor. The study did not measure effects of a robot's gaze behavior on people.
column18: Autonomous estimation combines Kinect RGB-D depth images with OpenNI skeleton tracking and a Discriminative Random Regression Forest (DRRF) to identify heads and estimate nose position and Euler head-rotation angles. The estimated head pose is mapped to tracked users and projected onto a vertical plane to calculate VFOA.
column21: The paper evaluated a Kinect-based system that estimates one or two people's visual focus of attention from head pose while they looked at images on a screen. column2: TOP-JAM: A bio-inspired topology-based model of joint attention for human-robot interaction
column3: The paper presents TOP-JAM, a neural-network model for representing and tracking joint attention in interactions involving multiple humans and robots. In a lab experiment with two people and Pepper, it tracked pairwise attention states with stable estimates; the paper also reports simulation computation times.
column4: Technical/system description with computational simulation and a real-robot triad experiment.

column12: Behavioral observations were captured using a Qualisys motion-capture system with markers on participants and robot. The main technical outcome was TOP-JAM's estimated joint-attention state over time; the paper also reports computation time in simulation.
column13: TOP-JAM tracked joint-attention states for each actor pair with stable estimates; computation times in simulation were 38.48 ms (SD 2.77) for 144-unit CANNs and 94.64 ms (SD 2.05) for 576-unit CANNs. No statistical significance tests are reported.
column14: The paper frames its focus as joint attention in HRI and proposes TOP-JAM to represent and track joint-attention states from behavioral data. It describes social attention as a continuum of individual attention and four states with increasing jointness: monitoring, common, mutual, and shared.
column15: Joint attention is characterized through typologies of social attention and corresponding levels of common knowledge; the paper's scale ranges from individual attention through monitoring, common, and mutual to shared attention.
column16: The paper presents joint attention as supporting coordination, sharing, understanding, cooperation, shared goals, and rapport. TOP-JAM is intended to provide JA-state estimates that can support robot interaction skills such as initiating, responding to, or ensuring joint attention.
column17: The study reports that TOP-JAM tracked joint-attention states in the triad, with stable estimates for actor pairs and activations coherent with the proposed attention typologies. It does not report measured effects on participants or interaction outcomes.
column18: TOP-JAM estimates pairwise attention states from behavioral inputs including head position and direction, torso position and yaw, hand position, object position and properties, and speaking probability. It uses continuous attractor neural networks and logical feature operations; experimental behavior was controlled in closed loop, and observations were captured with motion tracking. Speech recognition was simulated because it was not operational during the experiment.

column2: The vernissage corpus: A conversational Human-Robot-Interaction dataset
column3: The paper presents a multimodal dataset of 13 sessions in which a humanoid NAO robot guides and quizzes two people, with robot gaze and nodding controlled by a Wizard-of-Oz. It provides gaze-related annotations and sensor data for studying visual focus of attention and addressee estimation, but does not report measured effects of robot gaze on people.

column2: Synchrony as a tool to establish focus of attention for autonomous robots
column3: The paper presents a Nao robot that uses optical flow and synchrony to select a moving interaction partner and direct its focus of attention toward that agent. In tests with a human and a one-degree-of-freedom automaton, the robot synchronized with the agent whose movement frequency was close to its learned frequency, and its attention direction followed that agent.
column4: Experimental technical/system description.
column5: Laboratory setup.
column8: The system was tested in rhythmic movement interaction: the robot synchronized its arm movement with a human or one-degree-of-freedom automaton, selected a partner among multiple moving agents, and oriented its focus of attention toward synchronized motion. Conditions included agents moving at similar or different frequencies and changing location.
column9: The described tests included the robot with one human, one automaton, or both a human and an automaton; in the two-agent condition, the interaction group comprised one robot, one human, and one automaton.

column13: The system synchronized with the agent moving at a frequency close to Nao’s learned frequency, as indicated by rising PLV; the focus-of-attention direction followed that synchronized agent and shifted when the synchronized partner changed. No statistical significance tests are reported.
column14: The paper frames focus of attention as a synchrony-based mechanism for selecting an interaction partner and locating the synchronized region of motion; it presents immediate synchronous imitation as a communication tool.
column15: The authors describe focus of attention as locating the synchronized region of movement, using prediction of synchrony to attract robot attention.
column16: Attention behavior helps the robot select an interaction partner from multiple agents and direct its attention toward that agent’s synchronized movement.
column17: The robot’s focus shifted toward whichever agent synchronized with it, and followed that agent as it changed location. The paper reports system behavior, not measured effects on human participants.
column18: An autonomous neural network architecture uses camera-derived optical flow and an oscillator model. column2: Social balancing effect of eye contact
column3: In a simulated job interview with one participant, a confederate, and a humanlike android, the researchers varied whether the confederate made eye contact with the android. Participants in the eye-contact condition reported a more positive impression of the android, supporting the authors’ proposed social balancing effect in triadic interaction.
column4: Experimental study.
column5: A controlled experimental room configured to simulate a job interview.
column6: 30 participants.
column7: Japanese adults; mean age 21.2 years (SD 2.01); 15 participants per condition, with eight men and seven women in each condition.
column8: Participants acted as job interviewers, asking eight prepared questions of a confederate interviewee and rating each answer from 5 to 7. In condition 1 the interviewee made eye contact with both participant and android; in condition 2 the interviewee looked away from the android at the corresponding times. No duration is stated.
column9: Three agents per session: one participant, one confederate, and one android.
column11: 2 humans per session: a participant and a confederate.
column12: A custom post-interaction questionnaire measured impressions and perceived relationships, including eye contact. Recorded video was observed and coded for gaze duration and counts, eye-contact duration and counts, and synchronized nods; inter-rater reliability was assessed with Cohen’s kappa.
column13: Participants who perceived eye contact between the interviewee and android reported a more positive impression of the android than those in the no-eye-contact condition (questionnaire item a, p < .01). They also rated the interviewee as having a more positive impression of the android (item c, p < .01). Participant gaze and synchronized behavior toward the android did not differ significantly between conditions.
column14: The authors frame eye contact as synchronized nonverbal behavior and study its “social balancing effect” in triadic interaction, using Heider’s balance theory.
column15: The paper describes social balancing effect as social relationships being attracted to a balanced state because of synchronized behavior between two agents. Eye contact is treated as a representative synchronized nonverbal behavior.
column16: Observed eye contact between the other two agents served as a cue for the participant to perceive their relationship and influenced the participant’s social cognition toward the android in the triadic interaction.
column17: Observing eye contact between the confederate and android was associated with a more positive impression of the android. The paper reports no significant condition differences in the participant’s gaze at or eye contact with the android, or in synchronized nodding with it.
column18: The android’s actions were prepared in advance and triggered by a remote operator (Wizard of Oz). The confederate’s gaze was trained and varied by condition; in condition 1 they made eye contact with the android, and in condition 2 the confederate looked toward the opposite side.
column19: Repliee Q2, a humanlike android resembling a Japanese woman, with movements driven by pneumatic actuators.
column20: The authors state that the humanlike android appearance was part of the setup’s rationale for presenting it as a human-modeled recording device. They do not report a comparison testing how embodiment influenced the results.
column21: In a simulated job interview with one participant, a confederate, and a humanlike android, the researchers varied whether the confederate made eye contact with the android. Participants in the eye-contact condition reported a more positive impression of the android, supporting the authors’ proposed social balancing effect in triadic interaction.
column22: RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5. column2: RoboTrio2: Annotated Interactions of a Teleoperated Robot and Human Dyads for Data-Driven Behavioral Models
column3: The paper presents RoboTrio2, a multimodal corpus of 23 cooperative game interactions between a teleoperated modified iCub robot and pairs of human players. It describes how gaze was recorded and categorized, and reports that the robot/pilot looked between players and game information while players often looked at the robot, which the authors interpret as inclusion in the conversation.
column4: Technical/system description of a multimodal corpus, with descriptive behavioral statistics and initial analysis.
column5: In-person interactions in a controlled setup: two humans sat before a robot, while its pilot operated it remotely from another room.
column6: 23 human dyads (46 human players) and one pilot; the same pilot operated the robot for all interactions.
column7: Human players participated in pairs; the paper describes the pairs as either male or female. The robot was teleoperated by the same human pilot throughout. No participant ages or prior robot experience are stated.
column8: Two human players cooperatively played a word-association game. For each of nine themes, they supplied five answers; the robot acted as game animator and referee, guiding the players and taking part in conversation.
column9: Three in the interaction: two human players and one robot. The human pilot remotely controlled the robot.
column11: 2 players per interaction, plus one remote human pilot controlling the robot.
column12: Multimodal audio/video and motion-capture recordings; pilot eye/head tracking; robot eye cameras and microphones; fixed HD cameras and headset microphones for players; OpenFace for players’ head, eye, and facial-action measurements; ELAN annotations; GMM-classified gaze targets. No questionnaires are reported.
column13: Descriptive gaze findings: the pilot looked at both players equally overall, looked more at the tablet while speaking, and often looked at a speaking player while listening. Players looked at the robot frequently. Statistical significance tests are not reported.
column14: Gaze is presented as an important non-verbal cue in human–robot conversations and as part of natural, ecological interaction behavior. The paper does not give a formal definition of robotic gaze, attention, or gaze-based attention.
column16: Gaze helps the robot address and monitor one or both players, support conversational regulation, and retrieve game information from the tablet. The paper discusses gaze behavior in relation to speaker/listener roles and multiparty footing.
column17: Players looked at the robot frequently, which the authors interpret as indicating that they included it in the conversation. The paper reports descriptive observations, not a controlled test of gaze effects.
column18: The robot was controlled in real time by an immersive remote human pilot using a VR headset and eye tracking; the pilot’s gaze and head movements were mapped to the robot’s eyes and neck. Pilot gaze targets were classified after saccade detection using GMM; user gaze was similarly classified from OpenFace head and eye positions. The paper notes prior use of the corpus to train a robot gaze-control model.
column19: A modified iCub humanoid robot with an articulated mouth, mobile eyes with embedded VGA cameras and three degrees of freedom including vergence, a three-degree-of-freedom neck, and microphones in human-shaped ears.
column20: The authors state that the embodied robot’s sensors and actuators shaped the collected signals and that immersive teleoperation produced fluid interactions adapted to the robot’s capabilities. They also frame the corpus as allowing study of changed expectations and behavior around robotic bodies, without reporting a specific measured embodiment effect.

column2: Robotic Gaze Responsiveness in Multiparty Teamwork
column3: The study implemented two autonomous gaze-response strategies for an EMYS robot head and evaluated them through online ratings of silent videos showing a two-human, one-robot coordination task. Both strategies improved perceived fluency, work alliance, and robot teammate traits versus no response; only attentive gaze significantly improved coordination, and shorter response delays increased ratings across all measured dimensions.

column6: 300 recruited; 244 included in the statistical analysis after exclusions.
column7: Participants stated they were fluent in English; ages 22–66 (M = 26.3, SD = 10.0); 43% female, 56% male, 1% preferred not to answer. Two human actors performed the scripts and were volunteers.
column8: Participants watched five randomly selected short, silent video scenes from a coordination task inspired by The Mind, in which two humans and one robot coordinate card-play actions using non-verbal cues. Robot gaze condition varied by responsiveness strategy and response delay; a no-response control was included. Survey completion averaged around 8.5 minutes.
column9: Three teammates per interaction: two humans and one robot.
column11: 2 humans per interaction.
column12: Video-based third-person ratings using items from Hoffman’s subjective human–robot fluency metric (fluency, teammate traits, work alliance), plus three coordination items based on questions for singing ensembles. Attention checks and manipulation-check items were also used. Statistical comparisons used non-parametric tests.
column13: Both attentive gaze (AG) and responding gaze (RG) improved perceived fluency, work alliance, and positive teammate traits versus control. AG improved perceived coordination versus control; RG did not significantly do so. Shorter reaction delay improved all four assessed teamwork dimensions. No significant interaction between gaze strategy and delay was found.
column14: Robotic gaze responsiveness: the robot perceives teammates’ gaze and produces a corresponding gaze reaction. The paper studies two heuristics, Attentive Gaze and Responding Gaze.
column15: Gaze responsiveness is defined as perceiving others’ gaze behaviours and the robot’s corresponding gaze reaction or response.
column16: The authors frame gaze as a monitoring and communication mechanism that can support intention prediction, information sharing, joint attention, common ground, synchrony, and implicit coordination in collaborative multiparty work.
column17: In third-person video ratings, responsive gaze was associated with better perceived teamwork: AG and RG improved fluency, work alliance, and teammate traits over control; AG also improved coordination. Shorter robot response delays increased ratings across all dimensions. The study measured perceptions, not objective team performance.
column18: Autonomous robot perception and response. Human gaze behaviours were detected using OpenFace Head Pose Live at 25 fps; gaze targets were classified by comparing head pose and gaze direction with a prior calibration. Robot gaze targets were predefined static angles; modules ran on Thalamus, with animation and behavior planning from SERA. AG responded to gazes toward any target, while RG responded only when a teammate looked at the robot.
column19: EMYS robotic head, an autonomous robotic teammate. The setup included cameras for sensing each human teammate and tablets for human input and a shared screen.

column2: Picking favorites: The influence of robot eye-gaze on interactions with multiple users
column3: The study tested a Magabot guide telling three-person groups about two artworks, varying whether it gazed only at participants or also at the artwork and whether it favored one person. Artwork-directed gaze drew attention toward the robot instead of reliably creating shared attention to the artwork, while favored participants perceived more attention from the robot and tended to like it more.
column4: Experimental study; 2 × 2 mixed factorial design.
column5: University of Twente laboratory arranged as a museum-like exhibition, with two artwork posters.
column6: 57 participants.
column7: University students and staff; mean age 25.6 years (SD 7.585); 41 male and 16 female; 78.9% studied or worked in IT; 91.2% reported little or no robot experience; 56.1% had prior knowledge of one or both artworks.
column8: Participants in groups of three listened to the robot tell stories about two artworks, with gaze varied by condition; sessions lasted approximately 30 minutes.
column9: Four per session: one robot and three human participants.
column11: 3 participants per interaction group.
column12: Questionnaire using Source Credibility, Godspeed, and Social Presence subscales; video annotation of attention direction and compliance; participant positioning/proximity; knowledge questions about story and artworks.
column13: Object-oriented gaze drew participants’ attention toward the robot rather than the artwork at explicit and implicit compliance moments (F[1,35] = 25.395, p = 0.000; F[1,35] = 21.902, p = 0.000). Favored participants reported more attention received from and given to the robot (F[1,53] = 91.740, p = 0.000), and greater perceived presence/awareness (F[1,53] = 37.786, p = 0.000). At explicit compliance moments, participants looked more at the artwork in the person-oriented than object-oriented condition (F[1,35] = 5.218, p = 0.029).
column14: Robot gaze is framed as a non-verbal cue for indicating or engaging in shared attention toward an object, directing visitors’ attention, and distributing attention among group members.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or robotic attention; it describes the gaze conditions operationally.
column16: Gaze is used to direct visitors toward artworks and establish shared attention, while gaze toward people distributes the robot’s attention among group members and can signal favoritism.
column17: Object-oriented gaze attracted attention to the robot but failed to produce shared attention toward the artwork; favored participants perceived more attention and awareness from the robot and tended to like it more. The object-oriented condition also yielded a more human-like perception and closer participant proximity at the halfway point; recall did not differ by gaze condition.
column18: The robot’s gaze was controlled remotely by an experimenter in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. It turned its front and moved its displayed eyes toward participants or artworks; gaze durations and favoring schedule are described.
column19: Magabot robot with a table structure and basic custom shell without anthropomorphic features; laptop on top displayed anthropomorphic eyes.
column20: The paper suggests robot movement may have distracted participants and drawn their attention to the robot rather than the artwork; it does not attribute this effect specifically to the robot’s body design.

column2: Optimization of a Robotics Gaze Control System
column3: The paper optimizes stimulus weights for a competitive gaze-control network and evaluates it with a robotic head in multiparty interactions. The network produced smooth attention shifts and matched the teacher-annotated focus choice in 99.03% of test cases; the paper does not report a separate measure of how the robot’s embodiment affected outcomes.

column14: The paper frames gaze control as selecting whom to attend to in a multiparty conversation, using a competitive network to determine a focus of attention and transition between participants.
column15: The paper describes gaze control as determining a stable focus of attention from different stimuli, and specifically treats deciding who to pay attention to in a multiparty conversation as a central problem. It does not give a formal definition of “robotic gaze” or “robotic attention.”

column2: Optimal robot selection by gaze direction in multi-human multi-robot interaction
column3: The paper presents an autonomous vision system in which three people select among three mobile robots by looking at them. column2: MGpi: A Computational Model of Multiagent Group Perception and Interaction
column3: The paper presents MGPI, a neural model that learns to weight nearby agents’ gaze, position, and conversational cues to predict social actions and identify groups. Tests use simulated multigroup conversations and human group-layout datasets; there are no robot embodiments or participant studies reported.
column4: Technical/system description with simulation-based experiments and real-data group-identification evaluation.
column5: Simulated multiagent social-party/group-conversation scenarios, with evaluation on real-world datasets of people’s positions, gaze directions, and group assignments.
column8: The technical system models agents’ conversational actions in static and dynamically changing multigroup conversations, then uses learned social attention to identify conversational groups. Interaction episodes were simulated for 600 steps; real-data group identification was evaluated on initial layouts from three datasets.
column9: Layouts contained 6–12 people organized into several groups. The evaluated human-robot group size is not stated.
column12: Technical measures: mean average precision and cross-entropy loss for action prediction; precision, recall, and F1 score under the |G| criterion for group detection. No human-participant instruments are reported.
column13: MGPI outperformed the action-prediction baselines in static and dynamic scenarios on mean average precision and test loss. For group detection, the KPM gate achieved the highest overall mean precision (0.74 static, 0.75 dynamic) and F1 (0.73 in both); reported overall recall was 0.72 in both.
column14: Social attention / social signal gating: selective weighting of nearby agents’ non-verbal and conversational signals, learned as part of a computational model of multiagent group perception and interaction.
column15: Social signal gating is defined as attending to people in one’s conversational group while suppressing verbal and non-verbal information from nearby groups. The KPM gate weights each neighboring agent’s influence using relative position and orientation.
column16: It filters and weights neighbors’ social cues to select influential agents, supports conversational action selection, and provides an implicit basis for identifying group membership.
column17: No effects of robot gaze or attention on human participants were measured. In the model, higher attention weights indicate greater neighbor influence on the agent’s next conversational action; learned gating also enabled group identification.
column18: MGPI is an autonomous, end-to-end trainable deep neural network learned by imitation (behavior cloning) from simulated demonstrations. It encodes histories of relative gaze direction, relative position, neighbors’ conversational actions, and the agent’s own actions with GRUs; a two-layer MLP KPM gate weights each neighbor before pooling, and an interaction policy predicts the next action.
column21: The paper presents MGPI, a neural model that learns to weight nearby agents’ gaze, position, and conversational cues to predict social actions and identify groups. column2: Maintaining awareness of the focus of attention of a conversation: A robot-centric reinforcement learning approach
column3: The paper evaluates reinforcement-learning methods in simulated conversations where one robot tracks the active speaker by turning toward them. Model-based methods, especially TEXPLORE, generally performed best, and the learned policies generalized to groups with different numbers of people; no real participants were studied.
column4: Technical study evaluating reinforcement-learning agents in simulation.

column8: A simulated multiparty conversation in which the robot learns to orient toward the active human speaker. Simulations generally ran for 18,000 steps (one hour); generalization runs lasted 3,000 steps (10 minutes).
column9: Usually five interactants total: one robot and four people. Generalization was tested with two, three, five, or six people interacting with the robot.
column11: Usually four people; generalization tested with 2, 3, 5, and 6 people.
column12: Simulation-derived technical metrics: reward, proportion of steps receiving a positive bonus, failures to orient within 10 degrees, and angular offset from the speaker.
column13: The model-based agents performed best at orienting toward speakers; TEXPLORE achieved the highest cumulative reward. Increased look-at noise reduced performance. Pretrained agents outperformed agents learning from scratch in conversations with different group sizes.
column14: The paper frames the behaviour as conveying attentiveness to, and maintaining awareness of, the conversation's focus of attention by turning toward the speaker.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or attention; it operationalizes attention as turning the robot toward the active speaker.
column16: The robot's orientation signals attentiveness to the current speaker and maintains its awareness of the conversation's focus. Body orientation can also induce spatial reconfigurations that redirect conversational focus.
column17: The paper measures the robot's simulated orientation performance, not effects on human participants. It reports that more noisy human head orientation reduced the agents' performance.
column18: The robot uses a front-mounted camera to detect people and their head/body orientations, plus a microphone array to estimate speaker direction. column2: Learning Gaze Behaviors for Balancing Participation in Group Human-Robot Interactions
column3: The paper learned autonomous robot gaze policies from prior group game interactions using imitation learning and batch reinforcement learning, then compared them with heuristic gaze behaviors in a user study. The RL policy increased participant turn-taking relative to one heuristic, and the IL policy increased active participation relative to another; neither improved participation balance, and perceived robot attributes did not differ by condition.
column4: Between-subject experimental user study comparing learned gaze policies with heuristic policies, alongside offline policy evaluation.
column5: University campus and surrounding areas for recruitment; interactions took place in a conference room.
column6: 50 newly recruited participants; analyses also included participants from the prior study, yielding 102 valid participants (51 dyads).
column7: Participants were 18–67 years old; 27 identified as female, 22 as male, and 1 preferred not to say. Thirty-two had never interacted with a robot before, and 8 reported interacting with robots regularly. Dyads paired a native Swedish speaker with a Swedish language learner.
column8: Dyads played the With Other Words language game with the robot for 15–20 minutes. Participants described words using hints, and the robot guessed the words; gaze policy conditions were IL, RL, and prior heuristic conditions GA and SL.
column9: Three participants per interaction session: two human participants and one robot.
column12: Behavioral measures included active participation from voice activity detection using individual close-talk microphones, turn-taking frequency from speaker changes lasting over a one-second backchannel threshold, and speech-time participation unevenness. Questionnaires assessed demographics, Big Five extroversion and agreeableness, willingness to communicate, Swedish proficiency, RoSAS warmth and discomfort, and custom ratings of intimidation, being ignored, and staring.
column13: Condition significantly affected participation unevenness, turn-taking frequency, and active participation. Unevenness differed between GA and SL (SL lower); RL participants took more turns than GA; IL participants were more actively participatory than SL. No condition effect was found on robot perception measures.
column14: The paper frames the work as learning robot gaze behaviors to balance human participation in group HRI, with gaze treated as a nonverbal behavior and policy action.
column15: The paper operationalizes participation unevenness as the summed absolute difference between each participant’s share of total human speech and the mean share. It does not provide a general definition of robotic gaze or attention.
column16: Gaze is used to shape and balance participation, including by directing attention between the speaker and listener, and the RL formulation aims to subtly incentivize conversational floor switches and turn-taking.
column17: The learned policies did not compromise interaction quality. RL increased participants’ turns relative to GA, while IL increased active participation relative to SL. Learned policies did not improve participation balance over prior work; robot perception ratings did not differ by condition.
column18: The robot operated autonomously. Gaze policies were learned offline from data in 26 prior groups using behavioral cloning (decision tree, SGD, or KNN) and batch reinforcement learning with Double Deep Q-learning and a turn-based reward. State features were collected at 2 Hz; actions were gaze at speaker, gaze at listener, gaze aversion, or do nothing.

column2: Investigation of the Impression of Storytelling with Robots to Multiple Children
column3: The paper tested storytelling with two children using either one reader robot or a reader and listener robot, with gaze directed among the children, display, listener, and environment. Children enjoyed storytelling in both conditions, with no significant condition differences in parental ratings; the study did not isolate gaze's effects.
column4: Within-participant experiment examining one-robot and two-robot storytelling conditions, alongside a system description.

column6: 16 children and 16 parents (15 mothers and 1 father).
column7: Children aged 4–5 years (mean age 4.69, SD 0.46), participating in pairs of friends; their parents participated as observers/questionnaire respondents (15 mothers and 1 father). The paper's extracted text obscures the child and girl/boy counts.
column8: Children listened to interactive storytelling from one or two robots using picture books, with opportunities to talk and ask questions. Each child pair completed two sessions in different robot-number conditions; average robot reading times were 5.5 minutes for the Olfers book and 3.5 minutes for the Rivas book.
column9: Each interaction session involved two children and either one or two robots.
column10: One or two robots per session: one reader robot, or a reader robot plus a listener robot.

column12: Custom parent questionnaire using 1–7 ratings of perceived child concentration and enjoyment, kindergarten use, and increased storytelling opportunities; direct post-experiment questions to children about enjoyment; observations of child behavior. column13: No significant differences were found between one- and two-robot conditions for parental ratings of child concentration (t(15)=.144, p=.887, r=.019) or enjoyment (t(15)=.397, p=.697, r=.043). All children said they enjoyed the storytelling. The paper also reports no significant condition differences for parents’ kindergarten-use and increased-opportunity ratings.
column14: The paper frames gaze as an autonomously controlled robot behavior used to support natural storytelling in a multiparty setting; it does not explicitly define robotic gaze, attention, or gaze-based attention.
column16: The reader robot's gaze behavior allocates attention among the display, children, listener robot, and environment as part of storytelling; the paper does not explicitly state that gaze serves turn-taking or addressee selection.
column17: Children's gaze shifted with storytelling timing: they generally looked at the reader robot when it began speaking and then at the display. Children sometimes approached or pointed at story content; with two children, they sometimes talked together during the story. The study does not isolate gaze as the cause of these observed effects.
column18: A gaze model selects targets and changes gaze every three seconds. It uses sentence timing and specified target ratios; a Kinect V2 provides children's head positions. column3: The paper presents an autonomous robot system that estimates people’s engagement from multimodal behaviours and uses a fuzzy model to choose a person to attend to in multiparty interaction. column2: Integrating vision and speech for conversations with multiple persons
column3: The authors describe an autonomous humanoid robot system that uses vision and speech-related sensing to maintain beliefs about multiple people and direct its gaze. In laboratory demonstrations with two people, it made short eye contact with a secondary person and shifted attention when that person became more important; human outcomes were not measured.

column2: Human-Oriented Interaction With an Anthropomorphic Robot
column3: This paper presents BARTHOC, an anthropomorphic robot with autonomous gaze-direction classification, speaker localization, and memory-based tracking for attention to multiple people. In tests, it usually responded to the intended addressee and rarely disturbed people talking to one another; the paper also reports better ratings for emotional mimicry than neutral responses.

column13: Key technical results: voice recognition/validation was immediate in 70% of 20 trials and rose to 90% when a second call was allowed; correct addressee response was 85% of 20 trials; gaze classification disturbed human-human conversation in 1 of 18 trials; mimicry ratings were significantly better than neutral confirmation (t(26)=1.8, p=0.05, one-tailed, as printed).

column17: The system enabled addressee-directed response and usually avoided disturbing human-human conversations; gaze classification caused one disturbance in 18 trials. The authors report that emotion mimicry was rated significantly better than neutral confirmation and increased acceptance by 50%.
column18: Autonomous real-time perception and attention: two eye cameras detect faces and classify horizontal face/gaze direction in 20° steps; two microphones and SPLOC estimate one or more sound-source directions. Face detections validate sound sources; memory-based tracking preserves trusted, stationary people temporarily outside view. The system combines reactive tracking and deliberative dialog through a three-layer hybrid architecture and XML-based module communication.
column19: BARTHOC is an anthropomorphic humanoid torso robot, about adult-sized from the waist up, with a movable head, facial-expression actuators, two eye cameras, arms, and five-finger hands; two shoulder-mounted microphones support speech and speaker-direction detection.

column2: How Can Robot's Gaze Ratio and Body Direction Show an Awareness of Priority to the People With Whom it is Interacting?
column3: The authors tested a humanoid robot’s gaze ratios and body direction while it gave smartphone information to pairs assigned VIP and follower roles. Biased gaze toward the VIP was rated more positively than balanced gaze, with preferred ratios depending on body direction: 80:20 or 90:10 when the body stayed front-facing, and 100:0 for some outcomes when it turned toward the VIP.
column4: Exploratory mixed factorial experiment testing gaze ratio and body direction in a social robot’s interaction with two people.
column5: In-person experimental setting; the paper does not explicitly label it as a laboratory study.
column6: 20 participants
column7: Adults; 20 participants, ten female and ten male, average age 30.25. Participants were assigned VIP or follower roles, and did not know one another beforehand.
column8: In 12 sessions, pairs listened to a two-minute robot explanation about a smartphone. Six contents were assigned randomly; participants were assigned VIP or follower roles, with six gaze ratios and two body-direction conditions.
column9: Three per interaction session: one robot and two human participants.
column12: Custom post-session questionnaires measured intention to use, politeness, understandability, and total impression on 1–7 scales. The paper reports no behavioral coding, interviews, or eye tracking as outcome measures.
column13: Biased gaze ratios were generally rated more positively than the 50:50 gaze, non-priority-oriented baseline. For intention to use, 80:20, 90:10, and 100:0 with non-priority-oriented body direction, and 100:0 with priority-oriented direction, were higher than baseline. For politeness and total impression, 70:30, 80:20, and 90:10 with non-priority-oriented direction were higher. For understandability, all priority-oriented ratios and non-priority-oriented 70:30, 80:20, 90:10, and 100:0 were higher. Reported significant interactions and main effect: intention-to-use gaze ratio × body direction, F(5,90)=2.561, p=.033, partial η²=.125; politeness interaction, F(1,18)=3.797, p=.004, partial η²=.174; understandability gaze-ratio main effect, F(1,18)=12.483, p=.001, partial η²=.410, and interaction, F(1,18)=4.749, p=.001, partial η²=.209; total-impression interaction, F(1,18)=2.615, p=.030, partial η²=.137.
column14: The paper frames gaze ratio and body direction as social gaze behaviors that can signal awareness of differences in authority or priority among people in multiparty interaction.
column16: Gaze ratio and body direction convey awareness of people’s differing authority or priority during information provision; gaze is directed toward the VIP more often, while body direction may turn toward the VIP or remain front-facing.
column17: Biased gaze ratios and body direction affected perceived impressions. In non-priority-oriented direction, 80:20 or 90:10 was more positively evaluated across all measurements; in priority-oriented direction, 100:0 was positively perceived in some measurements, and all ratios improved understandability compared with baseline. The role factor showed no significant differences.
column18: An autonomous gaze controller used Kinect V2 head-position estimates to track people; roles and positions were manually entered. The controller selected gaze targets among the two addressees and the environment, changed targets every three seconds, and varied gaze ratios and body direction by condition.
column19: Sota, a 28 cm tall desktop-sized interactive humanoid with eight degrees of freedom, humanlike physical expressions, voice synthesis, and a blinking mouth LED.
column20: The authors state that using only Sota limits generalizability across robot appearances. They discuss how available movement modalities affect design implications: robots able to turn face and body can use either body-direction condition; face-only robots use non-priority-oriented direction, while body-only robots use priority-oriented direction. These embodiment comparisons are recommendations, not tested effects in this experiment.

column2: Gaze Behavioral Adaptation Towards Group Members for Providing Effective Recommendations
column3: The authors tested three ways for a NAO robot to distribute gaze while recommending movies to groups of three people, targeting the member who rated a movie lowest with longer or more frequent gaze. Group acceptance was highest with more frequent gaze toward that member, while participants did not significantly distinguish the gaze behaviors in perceived naturalness or persuasiveness and tended to prefer standard gaze.
column4: Between-subjects experimental study (as stated in the abstract); the Methods section describes a within-subjects, repeated-measures experiment.
column5: Movie recommendation study with groups seated around a robot at a table; the paper does not explicitly label the setting as a laboratory or field study.
column6: 30 participants in 10 groups.
column7: Italian high-school or master students; 25 male and 5 female; average age stated as “20 6”; all had moderate familiarity with robotics applications.
column8: Each group received three movie recommendations, presented using three gaze behaviors. Participants rated movies, gave individual and consensus group accept/reject responses, completed a short satisfaction questionnaire after each condition, and stated a preferred interaction mode.
column9: 4 people per interaction group: one robot and three humans.
column12: Custom questionnaire (including familiarity, personal and group acceptance, persuasiveness, naturalness, and preference items); acceptance/reject responses; statistical analyses of acceptance and questionnaire responses. No named validated scale or video/eye-tracking measure is stated.
column13: Personal acceptance was strongly associated with group acceptance (F(1, 90)=53.083, p<0.001; ρ=0.613, p<0.001). In a two-way ANOVA, gaze behavior and personal acceptance had significant main effects on group acceptance, but their interaction was not significant. Acceptance rates were 52% for standard gaze, 67% for longer gaze toward the lowest-rated member, and 75% for more frequent gaze toward that member. Gaze behavior did not significantly correlate with reported persuasiveness or perceived naturalness; plot length had a weak positive correlation with perceived naturalness (ρ=0.2, p=0.05).
column14: The paper frames gaze as a non-verbal social cue that can convey attention and influence group decision-making and acceptance during recommendations. It examines gaze frequency, fixation duration, and head-turn allocation toward group members.
column16: The gaze behavior is used to direct and distribute the robot’s attention among group members during a recommendation, especially by giving more or more frequent gaze to the member who rated the recommended movie lowest. The authors aim to elicit that member’s attention and influence group decision-making and acceptance.
column17: Gaze behavior produced different group acceptance rates when considered with personal acceptance; frequent gaze toward the lowest-rated member yielded the highest observed rate. Participants did not report significant differences in perceived naturalness or persuasiveness and preferred standard gaze overall.
column18: Three heuristic gaze models vary the robot’s head turns and gaze duration: standard gaze allocates equal gaze time to all members; longer gaze assigns a 7-second fixation to the lowest-rated member and 3 seconds to others; frequent gaze inserts a second non-adjacent section for that member, doubling their gaze time and head turns. A face-tracking module tracks participants’ positions and movements; head orientation provides gaze because the robot cannot move its eyes.
column19: Softbank NAO T14 humanoid robot with a torso, 14 degrees of freedom (two for the head and 12 for the arms), no eye movement, and LEDs positioned in its eyes to reproduce blinking.
column20: The robot’s lack of eye movement meant gaze was implemented through head orientation; the paper states that head orientation is fundamental for recognizing gaze in multiparty human-robot settings. No further effect of embodiment on study outcomes is reported.

column2: Facilitation of telepresence robot turn-takings by gesture exaggeration
column3: The paper presents a telepresence robot that detects a remote participant’s attention directions, nods, and back-channels and exaggerates them as robot motions to help the participant become an addressee and take turns in multiparty teleconferences. Preliminary tests evaluated cue-recognition modules, but the effect on multiparty interaction was left for future work.

column2: Eye contact as a key component in human robot interaction
column3: The paper describes a museum robot that selects a face from people in front of it, tracks that face with stereo cameras on a movable head, and uses the behaviour to support directing speech to a person. In small demonstrations, tracking kept the cameras focused while subjects remained in view, and subjects often perceived the robot as looking at them; the evidence is technical and informal.
column4: Technical/system description with demonstrations and performance tests of a robotic face detection and tracking system.
column5: A planned public museum exhibit at Questacon in Canberra, Australia; the reported tracking tests used subjects in front of the robot. The paper does not explicitly state whether testing took place in the museum or a laboratory.
column7: Participants are described only as test subjects; no demographic characteristics or prior robot experience are reported.
column8: Technical tests evaluated selecting and tracking a face as subjects moved in view of the robot, including a two-subject tracking test. column9: Tests included one subject and two subjects in the scene; the robot platform was one Questacon Robot.
column11: The reported tests included one-subject and two-subject scenes; total participant count is not stated.
column12: System/technical metrics: time to transition from face detection to tracking, tracking duration, and error between required camera position and camera image centre. The authors also report informal feedback from test subjects.
column13: The key technical result was that the system maintained camera focus on subjects while they remained in view, including in the two-subject test. Test subjects said the robot seemed to look at the selected person and described tracking as natural, though one called it “freaky.” No statistical significance tests are reported.
column14: Eye contact as a communication prompt and a means for the robot to direct speech to a particular human in a group; implemented through active-head face tracking.
column15: The authors characterize eye contact as a key communication prompt that indicates who conversation is directed at. They do not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or attention.
column16: The behaviour selects and follows a face in a group so the robot can direct verbal output to that person; the active head's movement is also intended to signal that the robot is focusing on the selected user.
column17: The authors report that subjects believed the robot was looking at the selected person and considered tracking natural; one subject called it “freaky.” They state that the combination of eye contact and verbal interaction drew people into an interactive experience, but provide no controlled comparison or statistical results.
column18: A stereo camera pair on a motorized active head detects faces with Viola–Jones and correlates detections across cameras. CAMSHIFT tracks the selected face using a hue histogram; the head moves to minimize the offset between the face centre and camera image centre. Periodic restricted-area face redetection handles cases where a subject turns away. The paper describes an autonomous system.
column19: The Questacon Robot has a stereo vision head mounted on a CEDAR Head mechanism with independently panning cameras, tilt control, and a motorized shaft simulating a human neck. The robot also has microphones and other sensors.

column2: Estimating human interest and attention via gaze analysis
column3: The study analyzed gaze from groups of three to five people watching a stationary Nao give three building tours in different styles. Participants looked toward locations indicated by the robot, and physical gestures drew more gaze than verbal references; group-level gaze timing and duration were associated with reported engagement.
column4: Experimental, within-participant study analyzing hand-coded video and survey data.
column5: In-person study in the Gates Building at Carnegie Mellon University, with presentations at three indoor locations.
column6: 34 participants in nine tour groups; the coded subset included 13 participants.

column8: Participants attended three Nao robot tour-guide presentations about features of the building, each at a different location and in a different presentation style. Presentations lasted about three minutes in the analyzed videos; participants completed surveys after each presentation.

column12: Hand-coded participant head pose from Kinect RGB video; labels for robot topics, gaze, and deictic gestures; post-presentation surveys with two custom 7-point engagement/entertainment ratings; contingency analyses, t-tests, and ANOVA.
column13: Robot topic was associated with audience gaze: 91% of upward gaze occurred during ceiling-feature discussion and 99.2% of leftward gaze during window-feature discussion. Deictic gestures elicited more looks toward indicated locations than verbal topic alone (57% vs. 38% upward; 50% vs. 31% toward the window). At group level, first-look timing and time spent looking predicted engagement significantly (p=.0085 and p=.0014).
column14: The paper frames joint attention as coordination between the robot’s indication of surrounding features and its human audience, and treats audience gaze responses as cues to interest, attention, and engagement.
column15: A deictic gesture is defined as an indicatory gesture such as pointing, arm position, body orientation, or an indicatory nod. In this study, deictic gestures specifically refer to large arm gestures referencing a physical location.
column16: Robot gaze and gestures coordinate information by directing listeners toward indicated objects or locations; the study examines group attention and whether audience gaze can indicate engagement.
column17: Physical deictic gestures directed audience gaze toward indicated locations more than verbal references alone. Gaze timing and duration showed group-level associations with self-reported engagement; the authors describe some individual-level gaze-feature trends as weak.
column18: A stationary Nao used scripted verbal presentations with head and limb deictic gestures. column2: Effects of Observing Eye Contact between a Robot and Another Person
column3: The authors ran two controlled job-interview experiments with two people and a human-like android, varying whether a confederate appeared to make eye contact with the robot. In both experiments, observers who saw the eye contact rated the android more positively; the study used Wizard-of-Oz robot control and did not find differences in subjects’ own gaze behavior toward the android.
column4: Experimental study with two experiments.
column5: Controlled laboratory setting.
column6: 60 participants total: 30 in each experiment; each experiment initially assigned 15 participants to each of two conditions.
column7: Japanese adults, mean age 21.2 years (SD 2.0 in Experiment 1; SD 2.01 in Experiment 2); each experiment included 16 men and 14 women. Participants were recruited through a temporary employment agency. No prior robot experience is stated.
column8: A simulated job interview: the subject acted as interviewer and asked eight prepared questions, listening to and scoring the confederate’s answers; the android was presented as an Intelligent Android recorder and acted as sub-listener. The confederate either established eye contact with the android while answering or looked away at the same times. The interaction duration is not stated.
column9: Three agents per session: two humans and one android.
column11: 2 humans per session: a subject and a confederate.
column12: Custom post-interaction questionnaire measuring impressions of the android, the confederate, and their perceived relationship, plus perceived eye contact; video observation/coding measured looking time, subject-android eye-contact duration and frequency, and synchronized nods. Inter-rater reliability was assessed with Cohen’s kappa.
column13: In both experiments, subjects who observed confederate-android eye contact reported a more positive impression of the android than those who did not (Experiment 1: mean 5.50 vs. 4.14, p < .01; Experiment 2: mean 5.27 vs. 4.43, p < .05). The perceived relationship between confederate and android was also more positive in the eye-contact conditions. No significant condition differences were found in subject gaze or synchronized behavior toward the android.
column14: The paper frames the behavior as observing eye contact between a robot and another person, a form of non-verbal interaction that may influence an observer’s impression of the robot in triadic interaction.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or robotic gaze-based attention. It describes eye contact as synchronized non-verbal behavior.
column16: The robot’s gaze toward the current speaker, combined with a confederate’s gaze toward the robot, creates observable apparent eye contact. The authors study whether witnessing this non-verbal interaction affects an observer’s impression of the robot and its potential mediation role.
column17: Observing eye contact between the confederate and android was associated with more positive impressions of the android in both experiments, regardless of whether subjects were directed to feel positively or negatively toward the confederate. The authors suggest it may also raise perceived mediation ability, while noting an alternative interpretation; evidence for Heider’s balance theory was only partial overall.
column18: Wizard-of-Oz control: an operator monitored the interaction remotely and triggered the android’s predesigned actions. The operator triggered greeting nods and gaze toward the current speaker; the confederate was trained to look at the android in one condition or away from it in the other.
column19: Repliee Q2, a human-like android resembling an actual Japanese woman, with duplicated facial details and pneumatic actuators to reduce motor noise.
column20: The authors selected a human-like android because they expected its appearance to make it easier for subjects to recognize when it established eye contact with the confederate. column2: Designing robot eyes for gaze communication
column3: The paper presents projected robot eyes with stereo cameras and tests how eye shape, iris size, and gaze movement affect gaze reading and perceived friendliness. Round eyes with a large iris performed best, and dynamic gaze had smaller average reading errors than static gaze; the experiments involved individual participants rather than multiparty interaction.
column4: Technical/system description with experiments evaluating gaze readability and friendliness of robot-eye designs.
column5: Online survey for the friendliness comparison and a face-to-face experimental setup for gaze reading; the paper does not explicitly name a lab or field setting.
column6: 105 participants in the friendliness study; 36 participants in the gaze-reading study. The sample size for the later projected-eyes versus mechanical-eyes comparison is not stated.
column7: The friendliness study participants were Japanese university students. Other participant characteristics are not stated.
column8: Participants compared pairs of robot-eye images for friendliness. In a separate task, they identified which marker the robot appeared to look at across static and dynamic gaze conditions. Each gaze-reading participant saw five target markers with three iris sizes, 15 judgments total; gaze displays lasted five seconds with five-second intervals. A later comparison asked participants to rate projected versus mechanical eyes on questions about looking and expressiveness.
column12: Thurstone paired-comparison scaling (case III) for perceived friendliness; marker identification and average gaze-reading error for gaze accuracy; 1–7 ratings comparing projected and mechanical eyes.
column13: The round outline with a large iris was reported as most suitable for gaze reading and friendliness. Dynamic gaze had lower average reading errors than static gaze; motion did not erase the pattern associated with eye shape. No inferential significance statistics are reported.
column14: The authors frame robot gaze as nonverbal gaze communication: robot eyes should both see and show gaze, enabling gaze reading, eye contact, and joint attention. The paper does not frame or define multiparty robotic attention.
column15: The paper gives no formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or gaze-based attention. It describes gaze communication as showing gaze so that users can read it, including to establish eye contact and joint attention.
column16: Gaze is presented as a nonverbal communication channel that can establish eye contact and joint attention; the introduction also cites its role in turn-taking. Multiparty interaction is not studied.
column17: Eye shape and iris size affected gaze-reading accuracy and perceived friendliness: round eyes with a large iris performed best. Moving gaze improved average reading errors relative to static gaze. In the later comparison, projected eyes were preferred on looking-at-something and expressiveness ratings.
column18: Computer-generated eyes were rear-projected onto hemisphere screens by laser projectors. Two cameras and stereo triangulation estimated a target's 3D position; coordinate correspondences enabled the eyes to be rotated independently toward it. The paper describes a system implementation, not a Wizard-of-Oz setup.
column19: A custom robot head used a removable mask, projected eyes on hemispherical screens, mirrors, laser projectors, and cameras. The system was also embedded in a Robovie-R ver.3 robot.
column20: The projected eye system allowed changes in eye appearance, accurate gaze representation, and smooth, speedy movement; the authors report that projected eyes appeared more lively than the original mechanical eyes. No multiparty embodiment effects were studied.

column2: Designing LED Lights for Communicating Gaze with Appearance-Constrained Robots
column3: The paper explored LED parameters for simulating gaze on a Roomba and evaluated the resulting left-to-right scanning signal in online video surveys. Participants understood the robot’s intent more readily when objects were shown as a reference, while the lights rarely led them to describe the robot as eye-like or gaze-like.
column4: Pilot study with a design session and an online survey evaluation.
column5: Design session with a physical robot; evaluation via online survey using a Japanese crowdsourcing platform and demo videos.
column6: 126 participants total: 6 designers and 120 online survey participants.
column7: Six designers, one female; 120 online survey participants recruited in Japan. Other characteristics are not stated.
column8: Designers explored LED gaze parameter combinations and commented on their designs. Survey participants watched one of two videos of the robot scanning; one showed the robot alone and the other showed three objects in front of it, then answered two open-ended questions.
column9: Not specified for a live interaction session; videos showed one robot, with either zero or three objects. Human-robot group size is not reported.
column10: One robot in each demo video.
column12: Custom open-ended questionnaire; participants’ written descriptions were analyzed. No named scale, behavioral coding scheme, or eye-tracking device was used in this study; eye tracking is proposed for future work.
column13: No statistical significance tests or statistics are reported. The central reported outcome was that participants found the intent hard to understand when the robot appeared alone and easy to understand when objects were shown; descriptions in the object condition often interpreted the lights as scanning the objects.
column14: Gaze is framed as a communication cue that provides information and regulates interaction; light-based gaze signals are explored as a way for functional robots to communicate intent.
column16: The paper presents gaze as communicating a robot’s intent and directing people’s attention; this study examines whether light expressions can be recognized as gaze, particularly when objects provide a reference.
column17: With objects present, participants more readily understood the robot’s intent and often attributed agency by describing it as observing or choosing among objects. When the robot appeared alone, participants commonly interpreted its behavior as cleaning, searching for garbage, charging, or waiting for commands. Almost none explicitly described the lights as eye-like or gaze-like.
column18: A NeoPixel LED strip was controlled by an Arduino Uno R3. The light-based gaze was configured with a bright green pupil and dim gray sclera; the selected example used 2 pupil pixels, 3 sclera pixels, and 4 pixels between the eyes. The robot scanned left to right in two cycles in the demo videos.
column19: An iRobot Create 2 (Roomba) with a one-meter, 60-pixel NeoPixel LED strip installed on it.
column20: The authors expected the Roomba’s mechanical embodiment and the LED strip’s neutral shape to make the robot seem hardly anthropomorphic, potentially making the light expressions difficult to interpret as gaze. column2: Designing an artificial attention system for social robots
column3: The paper presents an artificial-attention architecture and evaluates parts of it through simulation and a one-human, one-robot object interaction scenario. The system showed strong engagement and acknowledgement results but struggled to shift gaze toward the human's focus of attention; no effects on people or multiparty interaction were tested.
column4: Technical system description with simulation and experimental validation of perception and action modules.
column5: Controlled experimental setup: a robot with an active head faces a table of objects; interlocutors interact with it at 1 to 4 metres. The setting is not otherwise identified as a particular venue.
column8: Technical scenario: test free-view attention and a sequence in which the robot detects an interlocutor, responds to an object shown by the human, uses the object's colour as a bias, and searches for a similar object. In reciprocal HRI trials, interlocutors picked up a red, yellow, or blue object; no other scripting or spatial or temporal instructions were given.
column9: One robot and one human interlocutor are described in the tested interaction scenario.
column11: 1 interlocutor per described interaction; total participant count is unstated.
column12: Visual assessment of whether expected fixation behaviours occurred in the correct order; recorded individual interactions were classified according to reactions. System performance metrics included module frame rates and percentages for expected behaviour, mirroring, and completed joint-attention tasks.
column13: Key technical results: robot behaviour met expected engagement, visual-search, and acknowledgement criteria at 76.44%, 52.72%, and 69.30% overall, respectively; object fixation was 35.66%. In simulation, mirroring response was 67%, completed joint-attention tasks were 78.40%, and 47.21% of IJA events were initiated by the robot. No statistical significance tests are reported.
column14: Artificial attention / attentional system; the paper frames attention as a multisensory process and builds social reciprocity and awareness into its design. It does not use the specific term “robotic gaze-based attention.”
column15: Attention is defined as allocation of perceptual resources to analyse part of the surrounding world at the expense of other parts.
column16: The proposed system uses attention to support reciprocal social interaction, including joint attention, gaze following, engagement, visual search, and acknowledgement. The paper describes this role as a framework aim and tests system behaviour; it does not establish effects on multiparty interaction.
column17: The system showed coherent behaviour in tests, with high rates for engagement, visual search, and acknowledgement, but low success shifting gaze to the interlocutor's focus of attention, attributed mainly to missing gaze inference and gist modulation. Effects on human participants or multiparty interaction were not evaluated.
column18: ROS-based artificial-attention architecture with perception, top-down control, action, and behavioural-reorienting modules. It segments sensory input into proto-objects, combines feature contrasts into a saliency map modulated by an attentional set, stores attended objects and spatial saliency in working memory, and selects gaze shifts (saccades or smooth pursuit). The simulated top-down controller uses a probabilistic joint-attention state machine and an attention schema; the implemented reorienting module currently responds to auditory signals. Gaze inference was still missing from the complete implementation.
column19: A robot with an active head is shown in the experimental setup; a detailed specification of the robot head and its sensors is referenced elsewhere, not provided here.

column2: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Audio-Visual Gaze Control
column3: This paper presents an autonomous deep reinforcement learning system that controls a Nao robot’s audio-visual gaze in group scenarios, aiming to keep people visible and favor speakers. In dataset, simulation, and live robot evaluations, audio-visual fusion performed well, and the learned policy outperformed handcrafted strategies under equal movement limits.
