column8: The system learned to orient a robot head toward a group of people to maximize visible people and favor speaking people. Evaluation included AVDIAR recordings, simulated people who moved and spoke, and a live two-person Nao scenario.
column9: The paper reports a live example with two people and describes evaluations with groups of people, but does not specify a total group size per session.
column10: One robot per described interaction; the live platform was Nao.
column11: Not specified as a fixed number per session. A live example includes two people.
column12: Technical performance measures: reward based on visible faces and whether a speech source is in the camera field of view; comparisons report reward scores.
column13: The paper reports technical rewards rather than statistical significance tests. Audio-visual fusion performed best overall, and the learned LFNet outperformed handcrafted policies under equal head-motion speeds; on Nao, the authors report successful transfer of exploration and tracking abilities.
column14: Audio-visual gaze control: combining controlled robot motion with acoustic and visual observations to direct the robot head toward groups of people.
column15: The authors describe gaze control as selecting head motions using audio-visual observations to direct the robot toward people; the stated objective is to maximize visible people and possibly favor those engaged in speech.
column16: Gaze control maintains people in the robot’s visual and acoustic fields of view so it can receive instructions and favor speaking participants; it supports group awareness and information gathering.
column17: The system’s reported effects are on technical performance: audio-visual fusion and reinforcement learning improved gaze-control rewards relative to unimodal or handcrafted approaches. No measured effects on participants are reported.
column18: Autonomous deep Q-learning with an LSTM-based Q-function; inputs are motor positions, visual landmark grids and audio speech-source grids. Actions rotate the head left, right, up, down, or stay still. Training used simulation and the learned model was transferred to Nao.
column19: A Nao companion robot with a camera and two microphones mounted on a head with pan and tilt; the live robot has four microphones and a 640×480 camera.
column20: The robot’s head and acoustic properties shaped sensing and action: two rotational degrees of freedom defined pan/tilt control, while speech-source elevation was difficult to estimate, so the audio grid used only yaw information. The paper does not report embodiment effects on human responses.

column3: The authors trained cascaded LSTM models to predict a robot animator’s gaze targets and head movements in a three-party word game. Online raters found the predicted gaze control viable, while context-aware head movement generation was not rated significantly differently from a heuristic control.
column4: Technical/system description and evaluation: the authors developed data-driven gaze and head-movement models, evaluated their performance, and ran an online perception study.
column5: Online perception study of video clips; the underlying interactions were three-party collaborative-game sessions collected using immersive teleoperation.
column6: 30 raters in the online perception study; the training and evaluation corpus comprised 11 recorded game sequences.
column7: The online raters were native French speakers, with equal representation of men and women. The corpus used different pairs of human players and the same robot pilot; their demographics are not stated.
column8: Two human players collaborated in a word-scoring game while a robot animator reported themes, invited proposed words, and reported scores. Online raters judged short clips of robot behavior and gaze for relevance to context.
column9: Three-party interaction: one robot and two human players.
column11: 2 players per interaction; the robot was controlled by a human pilot.
column12: Objective technical measures: gaze-target classification accuracy/F1 and head-angle MSE, using nine-fold cross-validation. Subjective outcome: HEMVIP video ratings from 0 to 100; ratings were analyzed with beta regression and pairwise comparisons. A closing survey about robot familiarity and general feeling was also collected.
column13: The gaze-target model achieved average accuracy of 52.9 ± 1.4%; the head-angle model's average MSE was 7.93 ± 0.51. Control type significantly affected video ratings (χ²(3)=16.511, p=0.0008), with Shifted Ground Truth differing significantly from each other control. LSTM and heuristic controls did not differ significantly, nor did Simulated Ground Truth from those two controls.
column14: The paper frames its subject as robotic gaze control and attention control in multiparty HRI, including prediction of gaze targets and generation of head movements.
column16: The paper describes gaze as a social cue that regulates conversation, including turn-taking and identifying the next speaker or current addressee. The proposed model predicts where the robot should direct attention based on interaction context and communication intent.
column17: In the online ratings, the proposed LSTM gaze control was rated as appropriate as the original behavior, but it showed no significant advantage over the heuristic control for context-aware head movement generation. The authors report no significant differences between Simulated Ground Truth and the LSTM or heuristic controls.
column18: Two cascaded LSTM models predict gaze target and head angles from multimodal inputs about robot-pilot activity and the two users; the head model also receives pilot-gaze features. Pilot gaze was classified from recorded movements, verbal features were manually annotated, and user gaze features automatically annotated. The training data came from an iCub teleoperated by a human pilot; evaluation clips were rendered on a virtual Furhat. Four control conditions were compared.
column19: The interaction corpus was collected with an iCub humanoid robot whose head and eyes were controlled via immersive teleoperation; all head and eye movements, including vergence, were reproduced in real time with 3+3 degrees of freedom. Perception clips used a virtual Furhat robot.
column20: The authors note that the physical robot was not used for the perception evaluation; future work proposes testing with raters facing the physical robot to examine engagement. column2: Coordinating turn-taking and talking in multi-party conversations by controlling robot's eye-gaze
column3: The authors tested a small humanoid robot as a silent side-participant in a three-person, nonverbal balance game. The robot’s gaze affected who took the next turn and, in a second experiment, how closely the next challenger’s points matched the previous challenger’s; the authors conclude that gaze can help coordinate turns and talking.
column4: Experimental study with two within-subjects experiments.
column5: Laboratory setting at Shizuoka University; participants played around a table in a controlled experimental environment.
column6: 45 participants total: 24 in Experiment 1 and 21 in Experiment 2.
column7: Japanese informatics students at Shizuoka University; Experiment 1 had 20 males and 4 females; Experiment 2 had 21 males. Ages and prior robot experience are not stated.
column8: Participants played a nonverbal cooperative balance game, taking turns pulling sticks and selecting the next challenger. Experiment 1 involved four games of 24 trials; Experiment 2 involved two games.
column9: 4 per interaction session: 3 humans and 1 robot.
column12: Mouse clicks to identify challengers and measure time between turns; Kinect sensors to measure face direction; game points and challenger transitions to assess behavior. No named questionnaire or interview is reported.
column13: The gaze condition during turn-taking significantly affected the ratio of participants becoming the challenger (F(3, 69)=14.59, p<.01); the Challenge gaze factor was marginal (F(3, 69)=2.64, p<.10), and their interaction was significant (F(9, 207)=3.25, p<.01). In Experiment 2, turn-taking gaze condition significantly affected point differences (F(3, 69)=14.59, p<.01); FROM differences were smaller than TO and NONE, and EC smaller than NONE (p<.05).
column14: The paper frames robot eye-gaze as a way for a side-participant robot to coordinate turn-taking and talking in multiparty conversation. It also describes gaze as conveying attention and willingness to talk.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or robotic attention; it describes gaze as a cue that can convey attention, intention, and willingness to talk.
column16: The side-participant robot’s gaze can encourage participants to take the next turn, influence who becomes the next speaker, prompt other participants to gaze at the selected participant, and adjust the context of talking.
column17: Robot gaze changed the ratio of participants becoming challenger and was reported to smooth turn-taking. In Experiment 2, gaze during turn-taking affected the point difference between successive challengers; participants gazed at by the robot could plan to get points close to the previous challenger's score.
column18: The robot randomly turned its face toward one participant during the Challenge and Turn-taking phases. Whether it turned its face changed between the first and latter halves of each game; participant face direction was measured with Kinect sensors. No autonomous inference model or Wizard-of-Oz procedure is described.
column19: Robovie-mR2, described as a small humanoid robot.

column2: Contingency scaffolds language learning
column3: The study compared an iCub robot that responded contingently to a tutor’s gaze and looming actions with a non-contingent feedback condition while tutors taught it words for cube markers. The contingent condition elicited more language production and learning words, with a non-significant statistical trend in change in learned-word percentage; the study was dyadic rather than multiparty.
column4: Longitudinal comparative study of contingent versus non-contingent robot feedback strategies.

column7: Naive users; all fluent English speakers. Mean age was 24.6 in the tutoring spotter condition and 28.9 in the non-tutoring spotter condition. Tutoring spotter: 2 female, 7 male; non-tutoring spotter: 1 female, 8 male.
column8: Participants explained the colors and shapes on three different-sized cubes to the iCub robot in three sessions, each lasting 2 minutes in total, with at least one day between sessions. The robot gave no verbal feedback in session one and verbal feedback in sessions two and three. Participants wore a headset; their utterances were transcribed between sessions.

column13: The learned-word percentage change from session one to session two showed a non-significant trend favoring contingent feedback: tutoring spotter 6.3 (SD 7.7, SE 2.4) versus non-tutoring spotter 0.26 (SD 9.8, SE 3.11), Mann–Whitney Z = -1.739, p = .082. The authors report more learning words overall and more total language production in the tutoring spotter condition; SUS results were not significantly different.
column14: The paper frames its subject as contingent robot behavior involving responsive eye gaze and looming/pointing feedback to support tutoring and language learning. It does not explicitly frame or define “robotic gaze-based attention” as a standalone concept.
column15: Contingency is described mainly as a temporal pattern in which one event occurs in response to a previous event; the paper also describes spatial and intensity contingency. No explicit definition of robotic gaze-based attention is given.
column16: Responsive gaze and pointing/looming feedback are presented as contingent feedback intended to support tutoring, signal participation, and help elicit scaffolding language from a human tutor. The study involves dyads, not multiparty interaction.
column17: The contingent tutoring-spotter condition was associated with more learning words overall and more tutor language production; learned-word percentage change showed a non-significant trend favoring that condition (p = .082). Participants in that condition also used “we” more frequently. These are dyadic interaction findings, not multiparty effects.
column18: The tutoring spotter detects three gaze classes—gaze at robot, away, or at an object—and the robot responds by matching gaze or following the tutor’s gaze. Language feedback uses the same learning system in both conditions; verbal feedback begins in session two.

column2: Attention Mechanisms for Social Engagements of Robots with Multiple People
column3: The paper presents a mobile robot system that combines face, sound, and speech inputs into decaying attention signals to manage engagement with multiple people. In its demonstration, the robot ignored a second person's greeting while engaged with the first, then tried to engage the second person after the first interaction waned.

column2: A robotic framework for shifting the target human's attention in multi-party setting
column3: The authors built and evaluated a robot head that selectively captured one person’s attention from a pair of people, established eye contact, and directed that person toward an object. In a controlled study, blinking during eye contact and turning both eyes and head toward the object improved success, response time, and participant ratings compared with two alternative methods.
column4: Experimental study validating a robotic framework, with a technical system description.

column8: Pairs watched paintings while the robot selected one participant as its target and attempted to capture their attention, make eye contact, then shift their attention to one of two objects on the table. Each pair completed three sessions, each corresponding to a viewing direction and lasting approximately 120 seconds.
column9: Three agents per session: one robot and two humans.
column10: 1 moving robot per interaction session; a second static robot was also present in the experiment.
column11: 2 humans per interaction session: a target and a non-target participant.

column13: The proposed method (eye blinking during eye contact and combined eye-and-head turns for shifting) had a higher mean success ratio (0.94) than methods 1 (0.60) and 2 (0.74), with significant condition differences reported (F(2,58)=4.7, p=0.001, η²=0.10). It also required less time (1.72 seconds versus 3.01 and 2.55), with significant condition differences (F(2,18)=45.07, p=0.01, η²=0.79). Questionnaire ratings for shifting-attention impression and communicative intention also significantly favored method 3.
column14: The authors frame the work as robot-initiated shifting of a target human’s attention selectively from multiple humans, in three phases: capturing attention, making eye contact, and shifting attention.
column15: Attention shift is defined as reorienting or reallocating attention to a target because it is the object of another person’s attention.
column16: The robot selectively captures a target human’s attention, establishes eye contact, and redirects that person’s attention to an intended object; the design aims to avoid interrupting non-target people.
column17: The proposed gaze-awareness and combined eye-and-head shifting method produced higher attention-shift success, shorter response time, and higher participant impressions of shifting attention and communicative intention than the two alternatives.
column18: The system tracks human head direction and body position, classifies the target’s viewing situation, and uses situation-dependent attention-capturing actions. It detects a frontal face to identify response, blinks to signal gaze awareness, then turns eyes and head toward the target object; attempts are checked for success with a two-second response window. The implementation uses a finite-state machine and sensor-processing modules.

column2: A Collaborative Human-Robot Game as a Test-bed for Modelling Multi-party, Situated Interaction
column3: The paper presents a public museum test-bed where two visitors collaboratively sort cards with the Furhat robot head. Furhat uses head pose and eye gaze to direct attention to people or cards and support mutual gaze and joint attention; the paper reports no formal evaluation of gaze effects.
column4: Technical/system description and demonstration of a test-bed for multiparty situated human–robot interaction.
column5: Public exhibition at the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology, over nine days.
column6: 373 interactions were recorded; the number of individual participants is not stated.
column7: Visitors of mixed ages, including adults and children. The paper does not report participant gender or prior robot experience.
column8: Two visitors and Furhat collaboratively sorted cards on a touch table according to a criterion, such as inventions by year or animals by running speed. Interactions averaged 4.5 minutes; after one game, players could choose to continue.
column9: Three per interaction: two human visitors and one robot head.
column12: The paper describes a multimodal recorded dataset from 373 interactions, including sensor inputs such as user head pose and card movement. It does not report questionnaires, interviews, or formal outcome measures.
column13: The paper reports no statistical significance tests or quantitative performance results. It states that visitors enjoyed the game and that some returned to play more.
column14: The paper frames visual focus of attention as something that interlocutors share between one another and objects under discussion; Furhat signals its attention with head pose and eye gaze.

column2: Robot Gaze Can Mediate Participation Imbalance in Groups with Different Skill Levels
column3: Pairs of a native Swedish speaker and a language learner played a word guessing game with a Furhat robot whose gaze adapted to speaking participation. Adaptive gaze led to more balanced speech participation, while overall speech amount and social presence measures did not significantly change.
column4: Between-subjects experimental study.
column5: Laboratory study conducted in a meeting room.
column6: 72 participants recruited in 36 pairs; 54 participants in 27 groups were included in the analysis.
column7: Participants were aged 18–67; 35 identified as female, 36 as male, and one did not say. Each pair included one native Swedish speaker and one Swedish language learner. Most participants were unfamiliar with each other; 39 had never interacted with a robot before and 19 reported interacting with robots regularly.
column8: Pairs played a Swedish-language word-description and guessing game with the robot as guesser. Participants collaboratively described target words, without saying the target word, and the robot attempted to guess. They played easy, medium, and hard levels; interaction lasted 15–20 minutes.
column9: Three participants per interaction: two humans and one robot.
column11: 2 human participants per interaction.
column12: Voice activity detection (VAD) duration measured active participation; turn counts and unevenness of speech participation were calculated from speech time. Questionnaires measured personality (Big Five Inventory dimensions of extroversion and agreeableness), familiarity, Swedish proficiency (CEFR levels), social presence (Networked Minds co-presence and attentional allocation scales), and willingness to communicate (Ryan questionnaire).
column13: Unevenness of participation was significantly lower (more balanced) in the adaptive gaze condition than in control, F(1, 72) = 5.717, p = 0.019. Extroversion and participant language proficiency were significantly related to active speech amount; learner proficiency was significantly related to group turn count. Robot condition did not significantly affect active participation; the condition effect on turn count showed a trend (p = 0.065).
column14: The paper frames robotic gaze as an adaptive, non-verbal behavior that can influence group dynamics and balance participation by shifting attention between participants based on speaking activity.
column16: The adaptive gaze behavior aims to encourage the less active participant and balance participation. The robot attends equally while the dominant participant speaks; when the non-dominant participant speaks or there is silence, gaze is distributed based on relative speech amounts.
column17: Adaptive gaze produced significantly more balanced speech participation than control, but did not significantly affect overall active participation. Turn-taking showed a trend toward increasing in the experimental condition. The gaze manipulation did not significantly change co-presence, attentional engagement, or willingness to communicate.
column18: An autonomous algorithm used each participant’s accumulated speech time to calculate a relative speech ratio and adapt gaze target, gaze duration, and head pose. column2: Human Communicative Responses to Different Modes of Gaze Management by the Robot
column3: In a table-based storytelling experiment, one participant at a time told stories to two F-2 robots that either returned the participant’s gaze or looked away. Participants who noticed the gaze difference tended to prefer the responsive robot, and some showed more iconic gestures with it and frustration or attention-directing behaviors with the gaze-avoiding robot.
column4: Experimental study of human communicative responses to two robot gaze behaviors.
column5: The study took place in an experimental interaction setting at a table, with participants and two robots.
column6: 46 participants.
column7: Mean age 27 years; 33 females. The paper identifies a core group of 15 participants who noticed the difference between robot behaviors and had higher Understanding of Emotions of Others scores.
column8: Participants told six stories to two robots using picture cards from Herluf Bidstrup, arranged in random order. Each robot reacted to the participant's gaze in a different way.
column9: Three people/robots per interaction: one participant and two robots.
column11: 1 participant interacted with the two robots at a time.
column12: The study used the EmIn Emotional Intelligence Test, a post-experiment questionnaire, a computer-vision component that identified face orientation as a proxy for gaze, and observation/analysis of participant behavior and gestures.
column13: Participants with higher Understanding of Emotions of Others scores were better at recognizing the difference between robot gaze patterns (p 0.05, Mann-Whitney U-test). Those who recognized the difference more often preferred the responsive-gaze robot (p 0.01, Spearman correlation).
column14: The paper frames gaze as both an attention behavior and an expressive communicative signal. It studies robot gaze management as responsive versus aversive gaze, and discusses joint attention as shared attention between communication partners.
column15: The paper describes gaze as an expressive means for indicating an object's attentional status, directing another participant's gaze to support joint attention, and expressing positive or negative evaluation. It describes joint attention as shared attention between two communication participants.
column16: Robot gaze served as a communicative response to the participant's gaze and provided or withheld attention feedback. Participants sometimes followed the robot's presumed attention or attempted to gain its attention through joint attention behaviors.
column17: Some participants preferred the responsive-gaze robot and recognized its gaze pattern. In the core group, iconic gestures increased over three stories with the responsive robot and decreased with the avoiding robot; participants also showed frustration or tried to redirect the robot's attention.
column18: A computer-vision component based on OpenCV detected the user's face orientation and translated changes into gaze-related messages. These messages triggered the robots' responsive or aversive gaze actions; no eye-tracker calibration was required.
column19: The study used two F-2 companion robots with movable heads, eyelids, eyebrows, and arms; their head and arm movements were coordinated with speech during greetings and utterances.
column20: The paper does not explicitly describe how the robots' physical embodiment shaped the study or its effects.

column2: "i'll Be There Next": A Multiplex Care Robot System that Conveys Service Order Using Gaze Gestures
column3: The authors observed care workers using gaze and body orientation to show who would be served next and who should wait, then implemented related behaviors on a mobile care robot. In experiments, gaze toward a waiting requester often led participants to lower their hands and wait, while combining gaze with a nod sometimes suggested they would be served immediately.
column4: Ethnographic observational study and three controlled experiments examining a care robot’s gaze and gestures in multiparty service interactions.
column5: An elderly day care center in rural western Japan for the ethnographic observation; experiments with university students at Saitama University in Japan.
column6: Experiment 1: 40 participants (39 successful data sets); Experiment 2: 118 significant cases; Experiment 3: 63 students, 39 of whom are reported across the three conditions (13 per condition).
column7: Experiment 1 participants were undergraduate students, 10 male and 30 female, mean age 20.6 (SD 1.0). Experiment 2 participants were 68 male and 50 female, mean age 20.4 (SD 2.8). Experiment 3 participants were students, 39 male and 24 female, mean age 20.8 (SD 2.1). Ethnography observed care workers and elderly clients.
column8: Participants acted as the second requester while a mobile robot delivered snacks or tea to two or more people. They raised a hand to request service while the robot was already moving toward another person; the robot used different gaze and gesture patterns to acknowledge the request and indicate service order. Experiment 2 tested seven gesture patterns; Experiment 3 compared three action sequences.
column9: Experiments used multiparty scenarios with the robot and two or three human participants/users. In Experiment 1, Person A was a virtual user and Person B the target subject; Experiment 2 included three participants.
column11: Two people/users in Experiment 1 (one was a virtual control); Experiment 2 tested a setting with three participants. The paper does not state a consistent human count per session for every experiment.
column12: Video recordings analyzed for participant behavior; post-experiment questionnaire/survey; statistical tests of coded behavioral responses. No named questionnaire or scale is reported.
column13: In Experiment 1, participants in the gaze condition more often raised their hand once and lowered it shortly afterward than participants in the no-gaze condition (17/19 vs. 0/20; Fisher’s exact test, two-sided p 0.0000). In Experiment 2, gaze alone led 80% of participants to lower their hands; gaze elicited this response significantly more than hand-raising or nodding. Adding nodding after gaze reduced the response to 30% (p 0.0136).
column14: The paper frames gaze as a resource for conveying service order through two gaze functions, Type A and Type B, in multiparty interaction.
column15: Type A gaze projects that a particular client will be attended next; Type B gaze asks a client to wait until the current activity is completed, projecting that the client will be served afterward.
column16: Gaze communicates acknowledgement of a request and service order: who is being served now, who will be served next, and who should wait. Its meaning depends on other bodily orientation and movement, and can help people anticipate the next action.
column17: Gaze acknowledgement was associated with participants lowering their hands and waiting without repeating their request; the authors interpret this as recognition of acknowledgement and service order. Combined gaze and nodding could instead lead to misinterpretation that service would be immediate. The authors report that gaze alone was more effective than hand-raising or nodding for prompting hand lowering.
column18: The robot’s head gaze was controlled by a neck pan-tilt mount, with user-request recognition handled by Wizard of Oz input in the experiments. Robot movement and gaze direction were autonomously computed from user positions; other gestures played prerecorded motions. The robot acknowledged a second request by momentarily stopping and turning its gaze toward that person, then continued toward the first requester.
column19: MCR was a mobile robot built on a Segway platform, with eight upper-body joints, a rotating waist joint, a pan-tilt head mount, a skirt concealing mechanical parts, and a human face.
column20: The authors state that the human face made gaze direction visible, and the separately orientable upper and lower body enabled the robot to reproduce the bodily orientation distinctions central to Type B gaze. The paper does not directly compare effects across embodiments.
column21: The authors observed care workers using gaze and body orientation to show who would be served next and who should wait, then implemented related behaviors on a mobile care robot. column2: Designing engagement-aware agents for multiparty conversations
column3: The paper developed a physically embodied receptionist agent that estimated each person’s attention saliency and engagement intentions from visual cues, then used gaze direction and floor management in multiparty conversations. In a laboratory comparison with random gaze and floor changes, engagement-aware behavior improved several attention and user-experience measures, while information recall and physical proximity did not differ significantly.

column8: Groups consulted the receptionist agent for office-building guidance on meeting-room directions, dining, or transportation. The user evaluation used the same scenario, with participants randomly choosing among three topics; each subject’s interaction lasted about 2–3 minutes. The data-collection phase was Wizard-of-Oz; the evaluation agent operated autonomously in engagement-aware or engagement-unaware mode.

column13: Engagement-aware behavior increased participants’ gaze toward the agent (78.8% vs. 73.7%, p=.038), perceived conversation smoothness (p=.001), perceived humanness (p=.001), and perceived intelligence (p=.039). column14: Engagement-aware agent behavior, including adjusting direction of attention and managing the conversational floor based on users’ estimated attention saliency and engagement intentions.
column15: The authors define engagement evaluation as estimating involvement in a conversation and whether a participant intends to enter or leave it. They define attention saliency as how much attention a participant deserves from the agent.
column16: Attention saliency guides selection of whom the agent attends to; engagement intentions cue conversational-floor exchange, including starting, entering, taking, releasing, or ending a conversation.
column17: Compared with random gaze and floor changes, engagement-aware behavior improved gaze appropriateness, gaze toward the agent, conversation smoothness, perceived humanness, and intelligence. It did not significantly change information recall or physical proximity; intimacy, self-reported engagement, and satisfaction were reported with marginal p-values.
column18: A stereo-camera vision system extracts eight visual features for linear-regression attention-saliency estimation and changing visual-cue features for SVM engagement-intention detection. The agent directs gaze toward the highest-saliency participant and uses detected intentions to trigger floor changes. Data-collection behavior was Wizard-of-Oz; the evaluation agent operated autonomously.
column19: Physically embodied receptionist agent Olivia with a vision head and stereo camera, pan/tilt head and torso motion, and speech output using a female American English voice. Arm gestures were available but not activated.
column20: The agent’s movable head and torso enabled it to change its direction of attention through head and body pose. Arm gestures were deliberately not activated to avoid distraction and confounding effects; the paper does not report a comparative test of embodiment effects.

column2: Exploring Non-Verbal Gaze Behavior in Groups Mediated by an Adaptive Robot
column3: The paper analyzes video-coded gaze from one two-person group in each of two conditions during a collaborative word-guessing game with Furhat. The adaptive gaze condition showed more participant gaze changes and patterns of looking toward the person the robot faced, but these initial findings come from only two groups.
column4: Between-subject study with two gaze conditions; this report analyzes video annotations from one group in each condition.
column6: 72 participants in the underlying study; the current report analyzes four participants across two groups.
column7: Underlying study: pairs of differently skilled speakers, comprising a native speaker and a language learner. The two analyzed groups included Swedish speakers; reported ages were 25 and 30 in the control group and 54 and 33 in the experimental group. Gender identities were female and male in the control group and both male in the experimental group. Learner proficiency was C1 advanced in the control group and B2 high intermediate in the experimental group.
column8: Two participants collaboratively described target words shown on a tablet so Furhat could guess them. Each word could be played for up to 60 seconds; total game time was about 16 minutes per experiment. The target word was hidden after 8 seconds and could be revealed by button click. Robot gaze was either adaptive and intended to equalize participation or followed the active speaker in the control condition.
column9: Two humans and one robot per interaction session.
column12: Manual video annotations of participant gaze targets and annotation changes; robot gaze-position logs; voice activation detection to estimate participation levels in the experimental condition. The report computed gaze changes per minute and distributions of participant gaze targets in relation to robot gaze.
column13: No statistical significance tests are reported. The central descriptive findings were higher average gaze changes per minute in the experimental group than control for both participants (native speaker: 17.18 vs 12.18; language learner: 21.25 vs 13.16), and participants spent proportionally more time looking away when the robot faced them. The authors caution that only two groups were analyzed.
column14: The paper frames robot gaze as a non-verbal participation cue and mediation behavior that can balance attention and participation in collaborative learning groups.
column16: Robot gaze is used to encourage equal participation by directing attention adaptively according to participation levels; the study also describes gaze as potentially facilitating conversation cohesion and signaling a shift in focus between participants.
column17: In the analyzed groups, mediating gaze coincided with more participant gaze changes per minute and less time looking at the tablet relative to control. Participants were more likely to look at the other person when the robot gazed at that person, and three of four spent more time looking at the robot when it gazed at them. The authors describe these as initial observations based on only two groups.
column18: The adaptive condition used voice activation detection to estimate participation in real time and distribute the robot's gaze between participants based on their relative activity. column3: The study tested children’s storytelling with a Sota reader robot alone or alongside a Sota listener robot, whose presence was incorporated into the reader’s gaze model. column2: Predicting and Regulating Participation Equality in Human-robot Conversations: Effects of Age and Gender
column3: The paper analyzes 270 museum interactions in which two visitors played a collaborative card-sorting game with the Furhat robot. It finds that directing questions and gaze toward the less dominant participant can improve response balance, particularly for children, and that age and gender information helps predict participation imbalance early.
column4: Naturalistic observational analysis of recorded interactions, with randomly selected robot turn-taking behaviours used to examine their effects; the paper also evaluates an imbalance prediction model.
column5: A technical museum exhibition in which visitors interacted with a robot.
column6: 540 participants in 270 interactions.
column7: Museum visitors from the general public, categorized by manual video annotation as children or adults and female or male; users aged 16–21 were excluded. Actual ages and genders were not collected.
column8: Pairs of visitors collaboratively discussed how to sort five cards by a criterion, then could reveal the solution and play another round. The recorded interactions averaged 4.5 minutes.
column9: Three participants per session: two humans and one robot.
column12: Automated log analysis of speech activity using voice activity detection; Kinect head-pose tracking as a proxy for gaze; manual video annotation of age and gender. Outcomes included speaking time, speech overlaps, gaze proportions, and response to robot turns within three seconds.
column13: Adults spoke more than children (age main effect, F(1, 536)=52.85, p<.001), and females more than males (gender main effect, F(1, 536)=8.28, p=.004). Direct questions with gaze to the non-dominant user were associated with that user responding more often (67.8%) than the dominant user (28.0%); addressing the dominant user produced the opposite pattern (81.5% vs. 13.7%). For children, switching the addressee and establishing mutual gaze improved targeted-question response accuracy; both effects were statistically significant. Demographic information improved early prediction of final participation imbalance.
column14: The paper frames its topic as participation equality in speaking time and the use of robot gaze and turn-taking behaviour to regulate participation in multiparty human–robot conversation.
column15: Participation equality is operationalized as the relative amount of speaking time; the paper does not provide a separate definition of robotic gaze or robotic attention.
column16: Robot gaze functions as a turn-yielding cue and a means to select the next speaker; directed questions and gaze can help balance participation by encouraging the less dominant user to respond.
column17: Directly addressing a user with a question substantially increased that user's likelihood of responding, including for the non-dominant user. For children, switching the addressee and seeking mutual gaze increased response accuracy; the paper reports no significant corresponding effects for adults. The authors caution that lasting changes in self-selection were not established.
column18: Robot turn-yielding behaviour was randomly selected each turn. The robot used speech acts (questions or statements), gaze to one or both users or the table, and could include a user's name. Furhat directed gaze with combined head and eye movements; Kinect v2 tracked users’ head locations and rotations, used as a gaze proxy.
column19: Furhat is a robot head with an animated face back-projected on a translucent mask and a mechanical pan-tilt neck, allowing head and eye gaze movements.
column20: The authors state that the back-projected 3D mask makes gaze direction legible and improves turn-yielding accuracy compared with animated agents on 2D displays. The physical robot also enabled situated interaction involving references to shared objects.

column2: Gaze modeling in multi-party dialogues and extraversion expression through gaze aversion control
column3: The authors built a gaze-generation model for a robot in three-party dialogue, based on gaze patterns from two people with different extraversion scores. In video evaluations, changing gaze aversion ratios changed perceived extraversion for both dialogue voices; naturalness ratings were slightly positive across conditions.
column4: Technical/system-description study with two video-based subjective experiments.
column5: Video-based, remote/online crowdsourced evaluation; participants watched videos rather than interacting directly with the robot. The paper does not name a physical study venue.
column6: User study 1: 27 participants. User study 2: 55 participants. Across both studies: 82 participant observations.
column7: Study 1 participants were university students not involved in robotics research, average age 21.5; gender is not stated. Study 2 participants were recruited through crowdsourcing, 27 male and 28 female, average age 38.8 years (SD 10.7).
column8: Participants watched videos of an android robot in a three-party dialogue scenario with two humans and rated perceived robot extraversion and behavioral naturalness. Study 1 used seven videos; Study 2 used eight. Video clips were about 40 seconds each.
column9: Three participants per dialogue scenario: one robot and two humans.
column12: Seven-point subjective ratings of extraversion and behavioral naturalness; statistical comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni-adjusted p-values. Generated gaze aversion ratios were also measured in Study 1. The source dialogue dataset used manual annotations of dialogue roles, turn-taking, gaze events, and gaze targets.
column13: In Study 1, for Person A’s voice, PB-M elicited lower extraversion ratings than PA-R and PA-M (Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.0058 and 0.0059). For Person B’s voice, no significant differences were found. In Study 2, 20% versus 80% gaze aversion produced significantly different extraversion ratings for both voices (about 0.7–0.8 points); naturalness averages were 4–5 across conditions.
column14: The paper frames its topic as gaze control/modeling for multi-party dialogue, covering partner-directed gaze and gaze aversion. It treats gaze as a nonverbal behavior related to dialogue facilitation, turn-taking, and personality expression.
column16: The paper describes gaze as providing feedback, communicating emotional information, regulating dialogue flow, conveying turn-taking cues, and expressing personality. Its model selects gaze targets based on dialogue roles and turn-taking state.
column17: In video ratings, more gaze aversion was associated with lower perceived extraversion: the 80% aversion model scored significantly differently from the 20% aversion model for either speaker’s voice. The authors report that gaze model choice also changed extraversion impressions, although the Study 1 effect was not found for Person B’s voice. Naturalness ratings were slightly positive across models.
column18: The system uses dialogue roles and turn-taking states, then samples a gaze target, duration, and gaze-aversion eye direction from speaker-derived model parameters. Robot motion control uses look/look-away commands for eye and head movement, limits head speed, and inserts a blink for large direction changes. Dialogue roles and turns were manually annotated for this study’s analysis.
column19: The robot platform was Nikola, an android with a human-like appearance, 32 facial degrees of freedom and 3 neck degrees of freedom; gaze control used the eyeballs, eyelids, and head.
column20: The authors selected an android with human-like eye, eyelid, and head degrees of freedom because these movements were considered important for gaze expression. They also state that eye movement, in addition to head movement, can make gaze aversion more natural and human-like.
column21: The authors built a gaze-generation model for a robot in three-party dialogue, based on gaze patterns from two people with different extraversion scores. column2: Effects of gaze control strategies on the impression of robot's internal states
column3: The paper analyzed human triadic conversation data and tested gaze-control videos for two robots, varying head-to-eye ratio and whether gaze aversions were timed to thinking. More head movement and thinking-aware gaze aversion increased perceived extroversion, while thinking-aware gaze also made the robots seem more as if they were thinking; effects of low head-to-eye ratios differed by robot appearance.
column4: Two video-based evaluation experiments and an analysis of human three-party conversation data; the paper also describes a gaze-generation system.
column5: Online, video-based crowdsourced evaluations; the human conversation dataset consisted of recorded free-topic conversations. A physical laboratory or field setting for the evaluations is not stated.

column8: Participants watched video stimuli depicting robots in a triadic dialogue and rated perceived extroversion; in the second study, they rated perceived thinking and extroversion for dialogue videos with thinking intervals. column11: Two human dialogue partners per robot interaction; the paper’s source conversation dataset involved three human participants.
column12: Custom seven-point Likert questionnaire ratings of extroversion in Study 1 and thinking and extroversion in Study 2; video/audio-visual annotation of thinking intervals and gaze behavior in the conversation dataset; NEO-FFI for personality assessment. column13: Higher head-to-eye ratio (more head movement) increased extroversion ratings; gaze-control type significantly affected perceived thinking and extroversion, with the thinking-aware model scoring higher. Human conversation analysis found significantly different gaze-aversion duration distributions across interval conditions. Statistics are reported in the quotes.
column14: The paper frames robotic gaze as a means of expressing internal cognitive states and personality, with gaze behavior in multiparty dialogue organized around participants’ dialogue roles and gaze aversion during thinking.
column16: Gaze is controlled according to dialogue roles to direct attention among speaker, addressee, and side participant; gaze aversion during thinking signals cognitive processing, and gaze behavior also contributes to impressions of extroversion.
column17: More head movement increased perceived extroversion; with low HER, the humanlike Nikola was rated more introverted than CommU. Thinking-aware gaze control increased perceived thinking and slightly increased extroversion. In the human data, gaze aversion was more frequent and longer during thinking, with upward aversion particularly associated with recall.
column18: A dialogue-role based gaze model selects gaze targets; a personality adjustment layer and thinking layer modify behavior; a synthesis layer determines target, duration, aversion, direction, and head-to-eye ratio. Gaze motions were model controlled in video stimuli, with speech-driven lip and pitch motion. No sensing or Wizard-of-Oz operation is described.
column19: The study used CommU, a stylized, deformed social conversational robot, and Nikola, a highly humanlike android. CommU has large exaggerated eyes with strong black-white contrast; Nikola has smaller, more realistic eyes.
column20: At low HER, Nikola was perceived as more introverted than CommU; authors suggest CommU’s larger, high-contrast eyes may make it seem to be looking at observers across a wider range of gaze directions, reducing sensitivity to HER variation. The paper reports no significant robot-type differences in Study 2 at HER 0.5.
column21: The paper analyzed human triadic conversation data and tested gaze-control videos for two robots, varying head-to-eye ratio and whether gaze aversions were timed to thinking. More head movement and thinking-aware gaze aversion increased perceived extroversion, while thinking-aware gaze also made the robots seem more as if they were thinking; effects of low head-to-eye ratios differed by robot appearance.

column3: The authors analyzed gaze and gaze aversion in three-person human conversations, then used those patterns to build role-based gaze models for the humanoid robot CommU. In video ratings, the model combining role-based gaze with eye movement during gaze aversion was judged more natural than the other models in one of three dialogue segments.
column4: Observational analysis of human–human dialogue data followed by a robot gaze-control system implementation and a subjective evaluation experiment.

column6: 30 evaluation participants; the gaze analysis used 6 female speakers across 6 dialogue sessions.
column7: Evaluation participants: 12 male and 18 female; mean age 32.1 years (variance 10.3). Dialogue-analysis speakers: six female speakers.
column8: Evaluation participants watched four video conditions of a robot producing gaze behavior from three-party dialogue segments and rated behavioral naturalness. Each clip was about one minute long. The underlying source data consisted of three-party conversations.

column10: One robot generated the gaze motions for the videos; no live robot was present in the evaluation sessions.
column11: Three humans in each analyzed dialogue session; evaluation participants watched videos individually (individual viewing is not explicitly stated).
column12: Manual annotation of gaze targets, pupil directions, speaking-floor holder, and turn-taking points; subjective naturalness ratings of four video conditions; statistical multiple comparisons using the Ryan method.
column13: In one of three dialogue segments, the proposed role-based head-and-eye model was rated significantly more natural than the other models (p ≤ .05); no significant differences were found in the other two segments.
column14: The paper frames gaze as a nonverbal behavior that supports dialogue, including feedback, emotional communication, and regulation of dialogue flow; it studies role-based gaze and gaze aversion for multiparty dialogue.
column15: The paper describes gaze aversion as looking away from a dialogue participant’s face; it does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze-based attention.
column16: Gaze helps regulate dialogue flow and is related to turn-taking and participants’ dialogue roles, including speaker, main listener/addressee, and sub-listener. Gaze aversion is considered in relation to humanlike gaze behavior.
column17: The proposed model combining role-based gaze control and eyeball-accounted gaze aversion was judged significantly more natural than the other tested models in one segment. The study did not isolate the contributions of role-based control and gaze aversion.
column18: The authors analyzed annotated three-party dialogue gaze patterns and implemented four gaze models: same-proportion head-only, same-proportion head-and-eye, proposed role-based head-and-eye, and proposed role-based head-only. Robot head and eye movements were generated from the role and gaze-aversion analyses; lips and head motions also used speech-driven methods.

column2: Recognizing the visual focus of attention for human robot interaction
column3: The paper develops and evaluates models for recognizing people’s visual focus of attention from head pose in meetings and Nao robot recordings. Estimating the head reference direction from temporal head pose averages generally improved recognition over a fixed reference, while the unsupervised adaptation model performed similarly to the average-based model.
column4: Technical/system evaluation of VFOA recognition models, evaluated on meeting and robot-recorded datasets.
column5: Recorded multiparty meeting sessions and two video datasets recorded with a Nao humanoid robot, including a robot quiz/vernissage scenario.
column6: The paper reports dataset sizes and meeting participant counts, but does not state the total number of distinct participants across the study.
column8: In meetings, participants discussed statements displayed on slides. In Nao dataset D1, two participants sat in front of the robot and referred to a booklet. In D2, people participated in a robot-led quiz during vernissage recordings.
column9: Meeting recordings had four people and no robot is reported as present in that setting. Nao dataset D1 had two participants and one robot; D2 describes two participants and one robot.
column10: One Nao robot in each robot interaction dataset; no robot is specified in the meeting dataset.
column11: Four people in each described meeting configuration; two participants in Nao D1; D2 describes a participant and a partner.
column12: Head pose was measured using flock-of-birds sensors for meeting data and tracked head poses from a tracking/head-pose estimation method for both Nao datasets. The outcome metric was frame-based recognition rate (FRR), compared against labeled VFOA ground truth.
column13: Key technical result: G1 generally outperformed the fixed-reference baseline in meeting data and Nao D1, especially in mismatched meeting conditions and for the left participant in D1. G2 performed nearly identically to G1; the paper does not report significance tests. In Nao D2, G1 was better for the right participant but worse for the left.
column14: The paper frames visual focus of attention (VFOA) as a discrete version of gaze and studies recognizing human VFOA as a cue for multiparty human–robot interaction; it does not study robot gaze behavior.
column15: VFOA is defined as who is looking at whom or what.
column16: Human VFOA is presented as a cue for addressee-hood, interest, following discourse, and understanding interaction between people; it can support dialog modeling and robot interaction.
column17: The paper evaluates recognition performance, not effects of robot gaze on people. It reports that implicit dynamic head-reference estimation can improve VFOA recognition over a fixed reference in several settings; unsupervised adaptation did not improve results over G1.
column18: The system estimates human VFOA from head pose, using an HMM with Gaussian target models. Its gaze model maps target direction and head-reference direction to expected head pose; G1 estimates reference from the temporal average head pose, while G2 adds an unsupervised, temporally continuous reference variable. Nao data used tracked head poses.
column19: The robot platform used in the interaction recordings is the humanoid robot Nao.
column20: The paper reports that the choice of robot direction as the fixed reference was suitable for the person on the right in D1 but not for the person on the left, given the participants’ body configuration. It does not discuss the influence of the robot's physical body features.
column21: The paper develops and evaluates models for recognizing people’s visual focus of attention from head pose in meetings and Nao robot recordings. Estimating the head reference direction from temporal head pose averages generally improved recognition over a fixed reference, while the unsupervised adaptation model performed similarly to the average-based model.

It does not measure effects of robot gaze behavior on people or interaction.

column2: Verification of the effects of gaze behavior in a turn-taking task with a robot on basic psychological needs related to exclusion
column3: The authors tested whether two non-humanoid robots looking toward a participant during a voice-based turn-taking task could reduce perceived exclusion. Participants recognized the gaze and sometimes estimated that they received more turns, but gaze did not significantly improve basic psychological needs or reliably alleviate exclusion.
column4: A between-participants experiment with a 2 (Exclusion vs. Inclusion) × 2 (Gaze Behavior vs. No Gaze Behavior) design.
column5: A soundproof room in the RIKEN building at the Advanced Telecommunications Research Institute International (ATR).
column6: 125 participants in the final analysis; 137 were initially recruited.
column7: The final sample included 66 males and 59 females, with a mean age of 20.58 years (SD 1.12; range 18–22).
column8: Participants completed a voice-based turn-taking task with two robots. Turn allocation manipulated exclusion versus inclusion: participants held the turn for approximately 10% of total passes in exclusion and approximately 33% in inclusion. Gaze behavior was inserted independently of task progression, four to six times per trial.
column9: Three players per session: one human participant and two robots.
column12: Post-task questionnaire measures included custom exclusion and estimated turn-rate items, gaze-recognition items, the modified Needs Threat Scale, and other questionnaires. Participants also gave free-form written responses and took part in a brief verbal interview. Task behavior was recorded on video.
column13: Exclusion versus inclusion significantly affected perceived exclusion and all four basic-need satisfaction scores. Gaze behavior was recognized, but it did not significantly affect need satisfaction or significantly mitigate perceived exclusion. In the exclusion condition, participants estimated receiving a higher share of turns with gaze than without gaze.
column14: The paper frames gaze as a non-verbal cue that can express attention and relationship with a user; it studies direct gaze as a possible inclusion cue for alleviating perceived exclusion.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze-based attention. It defines the experimental gaze behavior as both robots simultaneously turning their gaze and bodies toward the participant.
column16: The studied gaze behavior was intended to serve as an independent cue that might alleviate users’ sense of exclusion. The authors report that gaze without a contextual link to subsequent actions may not be understood as an inclusive cue.
column17: Participants recognized the gaze behavior, and in the exclusion condition gaze increased their estimated share of received turns. The study found no evidence that gaze affected basic psychological needs or mitigated perceived exclusion.
column18: The two robots’ gaze and body orientation were controlled as a task-independent behavior triggered after a condition-specific number of consecutive robot-to-robot turn passes. column20: The authors note that using physical ball passing would require a large-scale movement-control mechanism, so they used voice turn-taking instead. column2: Towards an Engagement-Aware Attentive Artificial Listener for Multi-Party Interactions
column3: The paper analyzed human–human listener gaze and feedback in multiparty interaction, then used those patterns to build an attentive-listener system with two robot heads. Participants looked longer at the data-driven attentive robot, and third-party observers judged it more attentive than the baseline.
column4: Mixed human–human observational analysis and controlled human–robot experiment evaluating a data-driven attentive-listener system against a baseline.
column5: Laboratory human–robot interaction, plus an online crowd-sourced observer-rating study and human–human corpus analysis.

column7: Human–robot study participants were 12 KTH students or staff (9 male, 3 female); crowd observers were English-speaking US workers with the highest trust-score level. Ages and prior robot experience are not stated.
column8: Participants retold Cinderella and discussed a favorite movie while two robots listened; they then completed a social-presence questionnaire and indicated which robot seemed more attentive. Duration is not stated.

column13: Participants spent more time gazing at the attentive-listener robot than the baseline robot (one-way ANOVA, F(1,1028)=8.554, p<0.01). Third-party observers selected the attentive-listener robot as more attentive in 55/60 cases (proportion 0.92, binomial test, p<0.001). Social-presence ratings trended higher for the attentive system, but the sample was too small for statistical tests.

column16: Gaze and multimodal feedback signal listening and attentiveness, distribute attention according to listener role, and can influence the speaker’s visual attention and participant roles.
column17: The attentive-listener system received more participant gaze and was judged more attentive by third-party observers than the baseline. The attentive system generated category-specific gaze and back-channel distributions from human–human data; the baseline used flat distributions, with speaker-gaze reciprocity. Back-channels were restricted to continuers.

column2: Eyes ahead: a scoping review of technologies enabling humanoid robots to follow human gaze
column3: This scoping review synthesizes technical approaches used to let humanoid robots follow human gaze in HRI. It organizes systems by environment tracking, gaze tracking, and gaze–environment mapping, and reports varied implementations and outcomes; the authors identify robust operation in unconstrained, dynamic settings as an ongoing challenge.
column4: Scoping review synthesizing technical implementations of humanoid robot gaze-following systems.
column7: Not applicable to this review as a whole; no single participant sample is reported.
column8: The review examined studies in which humanoid robots track human gaze toward objects in shared environments and respond contingently. No single participant task applies to the review as a whole.
column12: The review extracted study setup details including outcome measures, but no single outcome measurement instrument was used across the review.
column13: The review reports heterogeneous results across included studies, including accuracy, questionnaires, video analysis, and technical performance measures; it does not report an overall statistical effect.
column14: The authors frame the behavior as robotic gaze following in human–robot triadic interaction, distinguishing it from human joint attention because robots do not possess the relevant human social-cognitive capacities. The review organizes implementations into environment tracking, gaze tracking, and gaze–environment mapping.
column15: Robotic gaze following is defined as programming a robot to recognize a human’s gaze target and respond appropriately. The review notes this behavior should not be equated with human joint attention, which presupposes social-cognitive capacities attributed to humans.
column16: Gaze following lets a robot identify what its human interaction partner attends to in the shared environment and respond contingently, for example by referring to the attended object. The review presents it as a means of supporting natural and effective HRI.
column17: The review cites studies reporting that gaze-following robots can be perceived as more socially present, engaging, and likable. In the summarized studies, reported outcomes included stronger feeling of being looked at, stronger orientation toward the robot, improved social presence for external observers, and preference toward the robot; effects differed by context and participant group.
column18: The review classifies systems by environment tracking, gaze tracking, and gaze–environment mapping. Implementations use constrained or unconstrained object tracking; eye tracking or head orientation as a proxy for gaze; and vector-based, probability-based, saccade-based, or learned mappings. The included systems were described as enabling real-time contingent responses.
column19: The review is restricted to humanoid robots, defined as physically embodied systems with a human-like head–torso structure and typically one or more human-like limbs; robotic heads qualify when part of a human-like body schema. Included platforms listed in the paper include iCub, NAO, Pepper, and robotic heads.

column3: The paper developed a system that estimates conversational dominance and uses it with participation roles to generate a humanoid robot’s gaze during group conversations. column13: In the evaluation, robot gaze condition had a significant effect on humans’ received gazes: gaze was more active and frequent in the dominant-robot condition than in the no-model condition (F(2, 69) = 3.641, p < 0.05). The no-model condition also showed a significant difference in utterance counts by dominance rank, with Rank 1 speaking more than Rank 3 (F(2, 23) = 4.695, p < 0.05). Dominant participants’ liking ratings correlated significantly with dominance in the less-dominant robot condition (r = 0.397, p < 0.05).
column14: Robot gaze behavior generation based on participation roles and conversational dominance; the authors describe gaze as an attentional behavior and nonverbal feedback signal.
column16: The paper treats gaze as feedback and as a means to coordinate multiparty communication through participation roles and dominance; gaze can direct attention to participants and facilitate turn-taking opportunities.
column17: Dominant participants rated the robot more positively when it behaved as less dominant and looked at them more. Robot gaze condition also affected gaze exchange: the dominant-robot condition produced more frequent human-to-human gaze than the no-model condition, while no-model gaze was associated with submissive participants having difficulty taking turns.
column18: The system estimates dominance with a regression model using gaze-at-others, mutual gaze, speech amount, and silence-breaking measures. Kinect face tracking estimates head direction; a Microcone microphone array provides speaker direction and speech signals. Participation roles are assigned using speaker diarization, gaze-based addressee identification, and identification of remaining people as side participants. Robot gaze transitions follow role- and dominance-based models; speech responses in the interaction were Wizard-of-Oz controlled.

column2: Footing in human-robot conversations: how robots might shape participant roles using gaze cues
column3: In a lab experiment, pairs of people interacted with a travel-agent robot whose gaze signaled whether each person was an addressee, bystander, or overhearer. People generally followed the assigned roles; gaze-based role signaling affected participation, reported attentiveness, groupness, and robot liking, but not information recall.
column4: Controlled laboratory experiment; the authors also conducted preliminary observations of human conversation to inform gaze design.
column5: Dedicated laboratory space with no outside distraction.
column6: 72 subjects in 36 trials.
column7: All-male pairs; native-Japanese-speaking university students from the Osaka area, ages 18–24 (mean 20.8). Familiarity with robots was relatively low (M=2.97, SD=1.67).
column8: Pairs interacted with Robovie as a travel agent: they selected Spain or Turkey, heard travel-package and destination information, and answered questions about preferences and destination knowledge. Three gaze-role conditions assigned the second subject as an overhearer, bystander, or addressee. Average task duration was 7.5 minutes; total procedure averaged 25 minutes.
column9: Three people per session: one robot and two human subjects.
column11: 2 subjects per experimental session.
column12: Video and audio capture for behavioral measures; post-experiment questionnaire for recall and subjective measures, including custom seven-point Likert items and manipulation-check questions; ANCOVA/ANOVA and Pearson correlations for analysis.
column13: Addressees took more speaking turns and spoke longer than bystanders and overhearers (p<.01 and p=.01); addressees reported greater task attentiveness (p<.01) and groupness (p<.01); acknowledged addressees and bystanders liked the robot more than overhearers (p=.01). Recall did not differ significantly by role.
column14: The paper frames robotic gaze as gaze cues used to signal and regulate conversational participant roles or footing, including addressee, bystander, and overhearer.
column15: Footing is described as the participant roles in conversation—who participates and in what capacity. The paper defines addressees, bystanders, and overhearers by their participation, address, and acknowledgment status.
column16: Gaze cues establish and maintain participant roles, select or signal addressees, and yield speaking turns to addressees; brief acknowledging gaze can signal a bystander’s presence without granting turns.
column17: Subjects largely interpreted and followed turn-yielding gaze, with addressees participating more. Role assignment affected reported attentiveness, groupness, and liking, but not recall. Acknowledging gaze toward bystanders was associated with higher liking than ignoring overhearers.
column18: Robovie used designed gaze behaviors based on communication theory and observations of human speakers. In the experiment, speech was scripted and the experimenter initiated turns from a preset utterance library; speech recognition was not used. Gaze was the manipulated behavior.

column2: Conversational gaze mechanisms for humanlike robots
column3: The authors modeled human conversational gaze, implemented role-signaling, turn-taking, and topic-signaling cues on a humanlike robot, and tested them in conversations with two people. Participants largely followed the robot’s turn cues; gaze-defined roles affected participation, attention, groupness, and robot liking, while recall did not differ significantly.
column4: A multi-phase study: observational modeling of human conversation, robotic system design, and a controlled laboratory experiment.
column5: Controlled laboratory experiment in a dedicated space; gaze modeling used recorded human conversations.
column6: 72 human subjects across 36 trials; 12 subjects in the modeling study (four all-male triads).
column7: Native-Japanese-speaking university students recruited from the Osaka area; ages 18–24 (mean 20.8). Participants in the modeling study were male; the evaluation recruited male subjects. Robot familiarity and gaming experience were relatively low.
column8: Participants interacted with a travel-agent robot that presented travel packages and destinations, adapted information to their choices, and asked factual questions. Two humans interacted with the robot under one of three gaze-defined participation structures: addressee plus overhearer, addressee plus bystander, or two addressees. The task averaged 7.5 minutes.
column9: Three people per experimental session: one robot and two human subjects.
column11: 2 human subjects per experimental session.
column12: Video and audio recordings for speaking-turn and speaking-duration measures; post-experiment questionnaire for recall; PANAS; a humanlike-agent perception scale; closeness scale; groupness and ostracism measures; task enjoyment and attention items; manipulation-check and custom single-item ratings; ANCOVA and correlations for analysis.
column13: Subjects interpreted 98.71% of turn-yielding signals and took 97.11% of yielded turns. Addressees took more turns and spoke longer than bystanders and overhearers (F(1, 30)=17.58, p<.01; F(1, 30)=7.41, p=0.01). Addressees reported greater task attention (F(1, 29)=12.90, p<.01) and groupness (F(1, 30)=8.95, p<.01). Addressees and bystanders liked the robot more than overhearers (F(1, 30)=7.35, p<.01); recall did not differ significantly.
column14: The paper frames robot gaze as conversational gaze mechanisms: role-signaling, turn-taking, and topic-signaling cues that communicate participation, conversation, and information structure.
column15: The authors use “mechanisms” for behavioral cues that serve particular communicative functions. The three mechanisms are defined by the conversational structure information they signal.
column16: Gaze signals whom the robot addresses and establishes participant roles, manages turn exchanges, and marks discourse or topic structure. In multiparty interaction it can designate addressees, acknowledge bystanders, or leave overhearers unacknowledged.
column17: Gaze cues shaped participation: subjects followed turn-yielding signals, while addressees took more turns, spoke longer, and reported more attention and groupness. column3: The authors developed a human-like android system that combines planned gaze with adjustable and interruptible gestures for interaction with multiple people. Speech recognition and keyword extraction were also used.

column2: Care robot able to show the order of service provision through bodily actions in multi-party settings
column3: The authors studied how a care robot could use gaze and bodily gestures to show who would receive service next in a multiparty tea-serving scenario. Participants responded to gaze by lowering their raised hands, while gaze followed by a nod sometimes suggested immediate service and produced more persistent hand-raising.
column4: Ethnographic observational study and two experiments; the paper also describes a robot system.

column7: Student participants; 118 students in the second experiment. The ethnographic study involved care workers/nurses and elderly visitors; ages and genders are not stated.
column8: Participants requested tea and snacks by raising a hand while the robot served one person at a time. Researchers compared robot responses to a second person's request, including gaze, other gestures, combinations, or no acknowledgement. In the ethnography, nurses checked visitors' vital signs and determined bath eligibility.
column9: Second experiment: three human participants and one robot in a session. The number of people per session in the first experiment is not specified.
column11: Three participants in the second experiment; group size for the first experiment is not stated.
column12: Video-recorded ethnographic observation and behavioral classification of participants' hand-raising responses; Fisher's exact tests were used. No questionnaire or eye-tracking instrument is reported.
column13: In the first experiment, hand-raising response categories differed between gaze and no-gaze conditions (Fisher’s exact test, two-sided p=0.0000); gaze was associated with more participants raising then lowering their hands. In the gesture experiment, 80% lowered their hands after gaze alone, versus 30% after gaze plus nodding (Fisher’s exact test, two-sided p=0.0136).
column14: The paper frames robot gaze as a bodily action for displaying the order of service provision and acknowledging the next person waiting for service.
column16: Gaze acknowledges and identifies the next service recipient, projects the service order, and signals that the next person should wait while the current service is completed.
column17: Gaze led participants to lower their hands after requesting service, which the authors interpret as recognizing the acknowledgement/order and accepting that they would be served next. Adding a nod after gaze reduced hand-lowering and may have confused participants by suggesting immediate service.
column18: The mobile robot stopped its torso when another user raised a hand and turned its head toward that user; tested gestures also included raising a hand and nodding, alone and in combinations. The paper does not state that gaze or gestures were selected autonomously, or describe a gaze-detection model/control architecture.
column19: Anthropomorphic mobile robot built on a Segway platform, with eight upper-body joints for human-like arm movement and a pan-tilt head; it carried tea and snacks.
column20: The paper reports that gaze was performed by turning the robot's head, and that gaze alone was more effective than some hand/nod gestures. It does not explicitly analyze how embodiment shaped the study or effects.

column2: Nonverbal Robot-Group Interaction Using an Imitated Gaze Cue
column3: In a field experiment, a mobile robot used gaze cues during a group handover to direct a salient object to a randomly selected person. When it looked at that person, they took the object more often than in the No Look condition; No Look trials also had more objects left untaken, though objects that were taken were taken sooner.
column4: Field experiment.
column5: A field experiment at a university-wide open day, in a stall in a large exhibition arena. The robot stood behind a table near the traffic corridor.
column6: 456 participants across 64 trials; 64 trials were analyzed.
column7: 283 male and 173 female participants, predominantly final-year high school students. Participants were not remunerated.
column8: Small groups gathered in front of the robot as it made cotton candy, then the robot attempted to hand a salient object to a randomly selected group member. It used a reaching physical presentation cue followed by one of two gaze conditions: Look or No Look.
column9: Groups had 3–20 people; the robot was the only robot in each interaction.
column11: 3–20 people per group; trials with fewer than three participants were excluded from analysis.
column12: Behavioral outcomes were measured from timestamped images recorded by the robot's chest camera and from experimenter review of those images. The outcomes were whether the selected participant or an onlooker took the object, whether it was not taken, and time to take.
column13: The Look condition increased selected-participant success: 32/40 trials versus 8/24 with No Look (z=3.733, p=0.0002; χ²=14.29, p<0.001). Objects were taken sooner in No Look trials (means 8.94s vs. 10.91s, p=0.019), but remained untaken more often in No Look trials (p<0.007).
column14: The paper frames gaze as a sociocontextual cue that can individualize a group member and help direct an interaction to that person. It studies gaze in a robot-group handover scenario.
column16: The Look cue was intended to individualize the selected participant and signal that the object was intended for them, reducing anonymity and equality of participation. The No Look cue was intended to avoid eye gaze and encourage deindividuation.
column17: The Look cue increased the likelihood that the selected participant took the object and decreased onlooker-taking; it also reduced the rate of objects not taken. Participants in No Look trials tended to take the object sooner, and experimenters subjectively observed confusion about whether the demonstration was over, whether the candy was offered, and to whom.
column18: The robot detected onlooker faces using OpenCV's Haar face detection, randomly selected one, then calculated its head bearing and the manipulator target pose. It randomly selected Look or No Look. Look oriented the head toward the selected participant and dipped the eyes toward the object; No Look left the head at scan-end and dipped the eyes downward. The physical handover used a reaching gesture.
column19: RobotAssist: an approximately 1.5 m tall mobile robot with a wheeled base, anthropomorphic upper body, six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, and two-degree-of-freedom sensor-laden head with separate head pan and eye tilt. The head included a brightly illuminated strip along the sagittal plane.
column20: The authors state that the robot's illuminated head strip amplified the dramatic effect of its rapid head rotation, which was designed to draw the group's visual attention. They also suggest that females' tendency not to anthropomorphize robots could reduce the social influence of individualizing cues, but describe this as a possibility requiring further investigation.
