column2: Proposal of a model to determine the attention target for an agent in group discussion with non-verbal features
column3: The paper trained SVM models to predict where an agent should direct its attention during speaking, listening, and idle moments in multiparty discussion. Using recordings of 10 groups of four humans, the models achieved F-measures of roughly 0.4–0.6; no robot or agent was tested with participants.

column8: Participants discussed and ranked 15 celebrities as candidates for a college festival guest, considering cost and audience attraction, in a 15-minute group discussion after individual preparation.
column9: Four people per discussion group; the proposed agent is modeled as one of the four participants. No robot participated in the recorded sessions.
column10: 0 in the recorded discussion sessions; the proposed agent or robot is a future application.

column13: Technical performance: F-measures for the three models were moderate, about 0.4–0.6; listening performed best, idling next, and speaking worst. The paper reports no statistical significance tests.
column14: The paper frames the target behavior as an agent’s attention in group discussion, represented by a target among other participants or the discussion material; it distinguishes this from reproducing detailed human gaze or head movements.
column15: Attention is defined as the perceived target of someone’s attention, combining gaze direction and head orientation.
column16: The behavior is intended to make an agent appear life-like in group discussion by directing its attention toward appropriate participants or the discussion material, depending on whether it is speaking, listening, or idle.
column17: No effects of robot gaze or attention on human participants were measured; the models predicted human discussion participants’ attention targets. The authors state that human participants may behave differently with agents than with other humans as a future research question.
column18: The authors train situation-specific nonlinear SVM classifiers using human-human group discussion data. They use other participants’ attention targets, speech-turn information, prosody, and head activity, extracted every 0.1 seconds with sliding windows; the models predict Table, Front, Left, or Right. Agent implementation is proposed as future work.

column2: Comparison of Human-Human and Human-Robot Turn-Taking Behaviour in Multiparty Situated Interaction
column3: The study compared turn-taking and head-pose attention in conversations between two people and a Furhat robot during a collaborative survival-ranking task. People directed attention more clearly toward the robot when yielding turns, and response timing differed when humans answered the robot; gaze patterns also varied with the kind of exchange.

column5: A controlled, seated interaction around a round table; the paper does not explicitly name the setting as a laboratory.
column6: 8 human participants, in four pairs.
column7: Participants were 23–41 years old; three were female and five male. Mean age was 30.5 (SD 5.42).
column8: Pairs of humans collaborated with a robot on an adapted Desert Survivor team-building exercise: discussing and ranking items for survival after a hypothetical plane crash. They completed three iterations of five items; recorded interactions averaged 6.5 minutes per iteration (78 minutes total, excluding instructions).
column9: 3 participants per interaction: two humans and one robot.
column11: 2 humans per interaction.

column13: Humans yielding to the robot looked at the next speaker more often than when yielding to another human (χ²=9.25, df=3, p=0.026). In human-human turn changes, head-pose targets differed by pragmatic label pair (χ²(6, N=204)=28.3722, p<0.001); the corresponding difference was not significant for human-robot changes (χ²(6, N=203)=9.1038, p=0.168). Gap lengths differed across the three speaker combinations (χ²=9.5593, df=2, p=0.008), with Robot-Human significantly different from the other two; robot response time was described as close to that of humans.
column14: The paper frames gaze and head pose as visual attention resources for coordinating turn-taking and joint attention in situated multiparty interaction. It does not give a formal definition of “robotic gaze” or “robotic attention.”
column16: Gaze/head pose helps coordinate turn-taking by indicating or selecting a next speaker, while also directing attention toward objects under discussion and supporting joint attention. The authors also describe listener gaze toward a referent as a cue for verifying common ground.
column17: Human attention patterns varied with turn type: statement-agreement exchanges showed more directed attention and gaze back from the agreeing addressee, while question-answer attention was less directed. People attended more clearly to the robot as addressee, and robot-directed questions received slower human responses than human-directed questions. The authors suggest gaze behavior may make it easier to detect when a human addresses the robot.

column2: Generation of head movements of a robot using multimodal features of peer participants in group discussion conversation
column3: The paper trained SVM models to generate a robot’s attention target and nods from other participants’ multimodal behavior in four-person group discussions. Attention prediction was moderate and performed better while listening or idling, while video evaluators found no significant condition differences in attention or overall naturalness; the proposed model received the highest nodding rating.
column4: Technical/system-development study with machine-learning model evaluation and a video-based subjective evaluation experiment.
column5: Controlled group-discussion recording experiment and online video evaluation; the human discussion corpus was recorded in a laboratory-style setup around a square table, while evaluators watched clips via a dedicated website.
column6: 40 human participants in the group-discussion data collection; 140 human evaluators in the subjective video study.
column7: Data-collection participants were Japanese college students in their third or fourth year, native Japanese speakers, ages not stated; 30 male and 10 female. Evaluators were 84 male and 56 female, mean age 39.3 years (SD 8.8).
column8: Four-person groups discussed collaboratively for 15 minutes to rank 15 celebrities for a college festival. The robot models were evaluated in video clips of about one minute, in which Sota replaced one participant and showed model-generated, human-recorded, or statistical head movements.
column9: Four people in each human data-collection discussion group. For the evaluated robot clips, Sota appeared with three human participants (four participants total).
column10: One Sota robot in each evaluated clip; the human group-discussion corpus itself used no robot.
column11: Four humans per original discussion session; three humans alongside Sota in each robot evaluation clip.
column12: Manual video coding of attention targets and nods; multimodal sensor/audio/video recordings and extracted features; model performance metrics (precision, recall, F-measure, accuracy); evaluators' 1–10 ratings of attention appropriateness, nod timing, and overall naturalness; Friedman tests.
column13: Attention prediction achieved overall F-measures of 0.460 (speaking), 0.580 (listening), and 0.528 (idling); nod prediction achieved overall F-measures of 0.645 (speaking) and 0.685 (listening). In the subjective evaluation, no significant differences were reported for attention or overall impression; the proposed model was best at nodding, but the paper does not provide a significance result for that comparison in the supplied text.
column14: The paper frames gaze-related behavior as the robot’s visual attention or attentional focus, operationalized as selecting an attention target and timing target shifts. It treats the target as a device-independent focus that can be rendered by robot head movement.
column15: The authors define the robot’s attention target as an abstract, device-independent alternative to imitating detailed human gaze or head movements: the robot should attend to the same target at the same time as a human would. They treat the attention target as the combination of head direction and eye gaze direction.
column16: The modeled attention behavior lets the robot direct its focus among discussion partners and the shared material, with behavior varying across speaking, listening, and idling. The paper also situates gaze as a potential communication signal for addresseehood and turn management, while the proposed behaviors are primarily spontaneous reactions.
column17: The study evaluated perceived naturalness of the robot’s attention target and nod timing in video clips. The proposed model was rated best for nodding; attention and overall impression did not significantly differ among conditions. No direct effect on human interaction or group outcomes was measured.
column18: Support vector machine models predicted attention targets and nods from peer participants’ multimodal features. Attention models used separate speaking, listening, and idling conditions; outputs were integrated with a dialog manager and robot controller. Sota motion filters accommodated hardware limits; the evaluation used leave-one-subject-out models on video clips.
column19: VStone Sota, a 28 cm desktop humanoid with an upper body, three head degrees of freedom (roll, pitch, yaw), horizontal torso rotation, and no moving facial parts; LEDs behind the eyes and mouth can light up.
column20: The robot’s limited degrees of freedom and lack of movable eyeballs motivated modeling attention targets instead of detailed gaze direction. Sota’s switching time and inability to interrupt movement required filtering and action sequencing; the authors note that its small physical size may affect a fully implemented system, but assume the effect was limited in the video study.
column21: The paper trained SVM models to generate a robot’s attention target and nods from other participants’ multimodal behavior in four-person group discussions. Attention prediction was moderate and performed better while listening or idling, while video evaluators found no significant condition differences in attention or overall naturalness; the proposed model received the highest nodding rating.
column22: RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper defines robotic attention as target selection represented through head and gaze direction, describes its interaction roles, and evaluates perceived naturalness and prediction performance. It details the sensing, SVM models, control integration, Sota embodiment, and how its mechanical limits shaped the implementation.

column2: Probing the Inductive Biases of a Gaze Model for Multi-party Interaction
column3: The paper builds and analyzes an embedding-based model that predicts an iCub robot’s gaze targets and head movements during a two-player collaborative game. Its learned dyad representations correlate with player speaking and gaze behavior, and changing the dyad input affects prediction performance; the study does not test effects of robot gaze on the players.
column4: Technical/system description with model evaluation and embedding analysis using cross-validation and input-swapping tests.
column5: A collaborative game interaction recorded in the RoboTrio2 corpus; the paper does not explicitly identify the setting as a lab or field study.
column6: Two human players per session across 11 sequences (11 player pairs); the total number of unique human participants is not stated.
column7: The same male pilot participated in each sequence; the player pairs differed and were either male or female pairs. Ages and prior robot experience are not reported.
column8: Two players collaboratively played a word-association game: they identified words most quoted from a theme while the pilot gave themes and scores and encouraged collaboration. Eleven sequences lasted about 20 minutes each, with nine themes per sequence.
column9: Three people (two human players and one human pilot) plus one robot in each interaction session.
column11: 3 per interaction: two players and one human pilot who teleoperated the robot and transmitted their voice.
column12: Pilot attention behavior was recorded and automatically annotated for gaze targets using Gaussian mixture models; user speech and gaze and pilot address were annotated. Model outcomes were evaluated with gaze-target F1 score and head-angle RMSE; social cues were analyzed with Spearman correlations.
column13: Key technical results: mean gaze-classification F1-score was 0.57 ± 0.01; mean head-generation RMSE was 3.0° ± 0.1 with predicted gaze and 2.1° ± 0.1 with real gaze. Dyad-number swaps changed prediction performance, with some gaze-target F1 scores falling below 0.45; correlations linked the embedding horizontal axis to players’ speaking time and looking at the robot. The authors caution that the correlational analysis cannot establish causality.
column14: The paper frames gaze as a non-verbal cue and studies a robot gaze-management model for multiparty interaction, including learned gaze targets and head movements.
column16: The modeled gaze behavior is intended to support robot behavior in a collaborative game, including adapting to players’ involvement to encourage collaboration and balance participation. The paper does not define a specific interactional function such as turn-taking.
column17: The paper evaluates model performance and reports that dyad-number inputs affect gaze and head predictions. It does not report measured effects of robot gaze behavior on the human players or interaction outcomes.
column18: A cascaded causal CNN/LSTM model predicts gaze targets and then head movements. Inputs are multimodal robot and user activity features passed through embedding layers, plus a three-dimensional dyad-number embedding. The corpus data came from an immersively teleoperated robot; the proposed model itself is evaluated as a predictive model.

column2: Data-Driven Control of Eye and Head Movements for Triadic Human-Robot Interactions
column3: The paper trains a CNN-LSTM model on teleoperated robot interactions to generate gaze targets and head movements for a robot facilitating a collaborative game with two people. In online video evaluations, context-aware head movements were preferred, and gaze/head behavior communicated the intended addressee with 78% accuracy.
column4: Technical/system description with two online third-person subjective evaluations and objective model evaluation.
column5: Online evaluations using videos replayed with a virtual Furhat robot; training data came from immersive teleoperation interactions.
column6: Study 1: 50 participants in final results (54 completed; 4 excluded). Study 2: 87 participants in final results (90 completed; 3 excluded).
column7: Online evaluators were native French speakers from France, Belgium, or Switzerland, recruited through Prolific; desktop participation only. Study 1 had gender balance and average age 34 ± 10; Study 2 had gender balance and average age 35 ± 11.
column8: A robot facilitator animates a collaborative game in which two humans identify the most frequently quoted words for a theme. Evaluators watched clips to compare head movements or identify whom the robot addressed; evaluations were online and third-person.
column9: Three agents per interaction: one robot and two humans. Online video evaluators watched as third-party observers, not as members of the interaction.
column11: 2 human players in each interaction, with the robot pilot teleoperating the robot.
column12: Model performance used gaze-target F1 score and head-angle RMSE. Subjective evaluation used online pairwise preference questions and addressee identification plus confidence ratings; statistical analyses included GLMM/logistic regression and ordinal regression. Gaze/head behavior was recorded and annotated, including eye and head trajectories.
column13: The context-aware model’s head movements were preferred over the heuristic model and rated as more attentive and engaging (all three comparisons significant). Addressee identification matched the imposed bias in 78% of cases (overall F1 = 0.78); confidence was significantly associated with agreement.
column14: The paper frames gaze as an important non-verbal cue that helps regulate turn-taking, manage conversational roles, and communicate the robot’s addressee. It treats gaze as coordinated eye and head movement.
column16: Gaze indicates whom the robot is addressing, helps regulate speaking turns and floor holding/yielding, and supports conversational role management and participation.
column17: Evaluators preferred the context-aware model’s head movements, rating the robot as more attentive and engaged than the heuristic condition. Manipulating the addressee input affected gaze/head predictions, and evaluators identified the intended addressee with 78% accuracy; confidence was lower when their answer disagreed with the bias.
column18: A causal, data-driven CNN-LSTM sequence-to-sequence model predicts discrete gaze targets and continuous head trajectories from robot speech/activity and addressee, users’ speech and gaze, and dyad identity. It was trained on annotated immersive teleoperation data; the model was evaluated via offline predictions and replayed video clips on virtual Furhat.
column19: Training corpus: teleoperated iCub robot with articulated jaw, redesigned eyes, three head degrees of freedom and three eye degrees of freedom. Video evaluations replayed the behavior on a virtual Furhat robot.
column20: The authors state that differences in robot embodiment limited their ability to assess gaze relative to evaluators: the virtual Furhat replay could be affected by the Mona-Lisa effect, although targets in the conversation were distinct and fixed. column2: Opportunities to Talk, Negotiate, and Laugh: Robot Behaviors That Shape Repeated Interactions in Groups of Older Adults
column3: In community centers, groups of three or four older adults played a word-guessing game with a facilitator robot and a guesser robot over repeated sessions. The facilitator’s autonomous gaze, which looked toward the speaker or the least active participant, was part of interventions associated with increased speech share; the study found no significant improvement in social connectedness.
column4: Exploratory mixed-method field study with repeated interactions; semi-autonomous robot system.
column5: Local community centers in real-world settings.
column6: 34 older adults recruited; 25 sessions were conducted, and 21 were included in the analysis after four exclusions.
column7: Adults aged 65 and older (25 women, 9 men); age bands ranged from 65–69 to 90+.
column8: Groups collaboratively discussed how to describe a target word, then described it to a robot guesser. Participants played for at least 20 minutes per trial, across up to three trials over two to five weeks.
column9: Three or four human participants and two robots per session.
column11: 3–4 participants per session.
column12: Social Connectedness Scale; UBC State Social Connection Scale; self-reported familiarity ratings and frequency of meeting; individual close-talk microphones with voice activity detection for speech share; video coding in ELAN; game logs; Ethnomethodological Conversation Analysis.
column13: Speech share was higher after robot interventions than before (M=.26 vs .14; b=.12, p=.001). No significant improvement in social connectedness or in-interaction social connection was found across trials. Intervention strategy did not significantly affect the change in speech share.
column14: The paper frames robotic gaze as reactive active-listening behavior and proactive support for participation, with proactive gaze directed toward the least active participant during silence.
column16: Gaze demonstrates listening and encourages participation; the proactive gaze targets the least active participant to support participation balance.
column17: Speech share increased after interventions, and the authors report that gaze behaviors encouraged participation in groups beyond dyads and across repeated trials. The paper does not report a significant difference in the increase between gaze and verbal strategies. No significant social-connectedness improvement was found.
column18: The facilitator's reactive and proactive gaze behaviors were fully autonomous. Reactive gaze turned to the speaker; proactive gaze was triggered after one second of group silence and targeted the participant with the lowest speaking share in that discussion phase. Minimum gaze duration was one second. Verbal support was wizard-selected.
column19: The study used Furhat as facilitator and Misty as guesser. Furhat used the “Titan” facial appearance; Furhat and Misty used low-pitched Swedish voices.
column20: Pilot studies informed the choice of Furhat and Misty because older adults had difficulty understanding or hearing other robot platforms. The paper does not describe an effect of robot body form on gaze findings.

column3: The paper presents a reinforcement-learning system that selects where a humanoid robot should direct its gaze among people and other salient targets in multiparty scenarios. column13: Real-world gaze-target prediction accuracy was 95.1% across 448 trials. In simulation, habituation significantly degraded MOL success rate (99.9% to 97.8%; p=0.001, Cohen’s d=2.28), increased average steps (7.84 to 16.14; p<0.001, d=2.24), and reduced transfer score (0.717 to 0.684; p=0.007, d=1.67); DQL and VQL success rates remained 100%.
column14: The paper frames its approach as stimulus-driven, policy-based allocation of robotic gaze/attention to salient targets, integrating perceptual saliency, social context, and learned preferences. It distinguishes this from joint attention, which coordinates shared focus between agents.
column15: Attention is defined as policy-driven allocation of gaze direction toward salient environmental targets, with saliency determined by learned policy and integrating perceptual, social, and policy-driven selection.
column16: Attention allocates the robot's gaze among available social stimuli, prioritising targets and enabling redirection as people enter, disengage, or compete for attention. The authors describe it as supporting gaze control in multiparty social interaction.
column17: The system produced 95.1% real-world target-prediction accuracy and showed immediate gaze redirection, disengagement, recovery after departures, and dynamic priority adjustment in multiparty scenarios. The paper reports effects on system performance, not measured participant-level or interaction-quality outcomes.
column18: Autonomous value-based reinforcement learning with a habituation-modulated epsilon-greedy exploration rate; DQL uses a neural network and experience replay. Kinect sensing supplies activity, proximity, and person-count state features; gaze actions select among up to six people, an object, or the environment. Reward uses the Elicited Attention model and proxemics. The policy was pretrained in IsaacSim and deployed on ARI.

column2: The Robot in the Room: Influence of Robot Facial Expressions and Gaze on Human-Human-Robot Collaboration
column3: The study tested one iCub humanoid robot with two people playing a collaborative shape-sorter game. Looking at the guide increased the robot’s perceived intelligence, while gaze direction did not significantly affect completion time; happy facial expressions were associated with faster collaboration and higher intelligence ratings.
column4: Experimental study
column5: Laboratory study at the University of Hamburg; the paper describes a controlled experimental setup with a round table and iCub robot.
column6: 50 participants total; the reported repeated-measures analyses include 25 pairs (degrees of freedom 1, 23 and 24).
column7: 50 adults: 13 female and 37 male; ages 21–55 years (mean 29.02, SD 5.60). Participants reported no history of neurological conditions and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing.
column8: A triadic collaborative shape-sorter game: a robot instructor gave a target object, one person guided a blind-to-the-objects actor using speech and gestures, and the actor inserted the object. Pairs played 10 rounds, switching roles after five rounds; rounds had a 30-second completion threshold and robot facial-expression and gaze conditions.
column9: 3 participants/entities per interaction session: two human participants and one robot.
column12: Task completion time; the guide participant’s per-round two-button rating of the robot as intelligent or random; and the Godspeed questionnaire after all rounds. Analyses used ANOVAs, paired/independent t-tests, and correlations.
column13: Happy initial facial expression was associated with faster completion than neutral (38.66 vs. 54.22 seconds; F(1,23)=15.73, p<.01, ηp²=.40). Initial gaze toward the guide led to higher intelligence ratings than gaze toward the actor (means .70 vs .59; F(1,23)=4.94, p<.05, ηp²=.17). Final happy expression led to higher intelligence ratings than sad (means .81 vs .61; t(24)=−2.46, p<.05).
column14: The paper frames gaze as a non-verbal social cue and as gaze communication used by a humanoid robot in triadic collaboration; it does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or gaze-based attention.
column16: The robot directs its gaze toward either the actor or guide as a social cue in the triadic interaction; the study tests whether that direction changes collaboration and perceptions of the robot. The authors report that gaze toward the guide increased perceived robot intelligence, while gaze direction did not significantly affect completion time.
column17: Initial gaze toward the guide increased perceived robot intelligence compared with gaze toward the actor, but initial gaze direction did not significantly affect task completion time. Final gaze direction did not significantly change robot ratings. Happy facial expressions also affected collaboration and robot ratings.
column18: The robot controller sent control signals to iCub to direct its head gaze toward the actor or guide based on predefined estimated positions, and sent emotion templates through the emotion interface. column2: Optimization and improvement of a robotics gaze control system using LSTM networks
column3: The paper develops and evaluates gaze control for a projected-face robotic head in interactions involving multiple people. Its competitive network achieved 85.0% expected behavior, while the LSTM model reached 82.80% test accuracy and was described as easier to train.
column4: Technical system-development and evaluation study comparing an optimized competitive neural network with an LSTM gaze-control model.
column6: Three people participated in the training and dataset preparation; total study sample size is not stated.

column11: 3 people in training; operational tests included more than 8 participants.
column12: Teacher annotations of focus-of-attention winners; technical performance measures including accuracy, validation accuracy, test accuracy, loss, confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 score, Cohen's kappa, and ROC AUC. No named questionnaire or interview is reported.
column13: The competitive system behaved as expected in 85.0% of cases. The LSTM model achieved 82.80% test accuracy; the authors report no statistical significance testing.
column14: Gaze control is framed as choosing and shifting the robot’s focus of attention among people in a multiparty conversation, based on interaction stimuli.
column15: The paper does not provide a formal definition; it describes gaze control as deciding whom to attend to or selecting a focus of attention.
column16: The gaze behavior selects whom the robot attends to and supports following a multiparty conversation with smooth transitions; the paper also associates mutual gaze with increased engagement.
column17: The authors report that the robotic head showed natural interaction behavior similar to the teacher-annotated behavior and improved the sensation of naturalness and realism. No participant-reported outcome measure is described.
column18: The system detects seven per-person stimuli: presence in the robot’s field of view, speaking, looking at the robot, movement/restlessness, audio from a person outside the field of view, being in another participant’s VFOA, and proxemics. A competitive network uses optimized stimulus weights, habituation, and short-term memory; an alternative model processes sequences of 30 frames with per-person LSTM layers and a classification output. The robot runs in a ROS-based architecture.
column19: A self-developed robotic head with a projected face/3D facial display, simulated eye movement, and combined neck/body and eye movement.
column20: The authors state that the humanoid design and gaze-control system make the HRI system more realistic and acceptable to interlocutors; they do not isolate or experimentally test embodiment effects.

column2: Joint Attention Estimation during Multi-party Facilitation Using Multi-Modal Fusion
column3: The paper trains and evaluates a multimodal model to estimate shared attention in recorded human group discussions, using talking status, body language, head position, and gaze data. Temporal modeling with an LSTM improved reported performance, while ablations found that excluding gaze could improve performance; no robot embodiment or robot interaction was studied.
column4: Technical/system description and quantitative model evaluation.
column5: Video data from facilitated and non-facilitated group discussions; the paper describes no robot-involving setting.

column8: Participants took part in group discussions, including music appreciation discussions, in facilitated or non-facilitated conditions. The paper evaluates a model on recorded discussion videos, not a robot interaction task.
column9: Group sizes varied; the number of people per discussion is not specified.
column12: Tobii Glasses 3 eye-tracking glasses and microphones; Theta fisheye camera; outsourced body-language annotations; YOLOv5-based head detector and L2CS gaze-estimation network. Model performance was evaluated with Euclidean distance and detection rate.
column13: Key technical result: adding LSTM temporal dependency improved model performance in the reported comparisons; excluding gaze improved results in the ablation tests. The paper reports detection rates and distances but no statistical significance tests.
column14: The paper frames the concept as joint attention estimation, describing joint attention as shared focus or attention among individuals.
column15: Joint attention is defined as shared focus or attention among individuals; this paper models it using multimodal interaction data and predicts attention heatmaps.
column16: The paper describes joint attention as supporting shared understanding and communication, and as a target for estimating where group participants' shared attention is directed. It does not study a robot's gaze behavior in interaction.
column17: The paper reports model-performance effects, not measured effects of robot gaze or attention on people. LSTM inclusion improved performance across metrics, while excluding gaze improved performance in ablation tests.
column18: The model fuses talking status, gaze angles, upper-body body-language classes, and head positions through a Transformer encoder, then uses a three-layer LSTM over three consecutive frames and fully connected layers to produce joint-attention heatmaps. Inputs are derived from human-human discussion recordings; no robot sensing or control implementation is reported.

column2: Forming shared attention between robot and users in conversational situations
column3: The paper presents and tests a robot system that follows alternating conversation between two users, identifies the current speaker and estimates what that speaker is attending to. In its demonstration, the system detected attention targets as speakers changed; combining audio localization with image-based skin-color information also improved reported speaker-location accuracy.
column4: Technical system description with experimental evaluation.
column5: A conversational scene tested in a general environment with noise and reverberation; no specific site is stated.
column8: Two users alternated conversation while teaching each other the names of handheld objects and asking and answering questions. The robot detected the active speaker and that speaker’s attention target, then displayed the target image to indicate shared attention.
column9: 3 people total per interaction: two human users and one robot.
column12: System-level evaluation using synchronized audio, texture and depth images; speaker-location estimation error; and frame-by-frame system outputs for speaker and attention-target detection. No named questionnaire, interview, or human-rated scale is stated.
column13: The authors report that integrating skin-color information with audio/depth-based sound localization reduced errors: localization error was within 0.1 m for all 87 voiced frames, versus within 0.15 m for 94.3% of frames using audio alone. column14: The paper frames the behaviour as forming shared attention between a robot and users in conversation. It specifically targets overt attention, where the user's attention target matches the object being fixated on.
column15: Shared attention is defined as the robot identifying what a user attends to and sharing that object as an attention target. The paper treats overt attention as the case where the attention target and fixation target coincide.
column16: The robot detects and selects the current speaker, identifies the speaker's attention target, and shares it to support communication in turn-taking conversation.
column17: The system demonstrated alternating shared attention with speakers and detected their attention targets. The paper does not report measured effects on users or interaction outcomes beyond system performance.
column18: An autonomous algorithm fuses a five-channel microphone array, three-eye stereo camera texture/depth images, and skin-color likelihood maps to locate the speaker. column2: A Gaze Controller for Coordinating Mutual Gaze During Conversational Turn-Taking in Human-Robot Interaction
column3: This report proposes a data-driven mutual-gaze controller for iCub that coordinates gaze with dialogue turn-taking in one-to-one face-to-face conversation. It outlines a planned comparison with iCub’s saliency-based gaze controller and lists measures of impressions and interaction quality, but reports no results.

Eye tracking is used to obtain human gaze direction input.
column14: The paper frames its subject as conversational mutual gaze, coordinated with turn-taking in dyadic human–robot interaction. It explicitly distinguishes this from joint attention and multiparty interaction, which it excludes from the study.
column16: Mutual gaze is coordinated with turn-taking and is intended to support naturalistic interaction dynamics; the broader background also identifies gaze as a cue for regulating turn-taking.

column18: A proposed data-driven gaze controller is trained from human–human dyadic conversational interaction data. It receives dialogue state and speech-event input from a dialogue manager, plus human gaze direction from an eye tracker, and produces gaze motion in a human face-centric coordinate system. The proposed model uses a semi-Markov or time-indexed HMM/POMDP variant; the robot platform is iCub.
